article_title: Instructional Practices and Student Math Achievement Correlations from a Study of Math Curricula (Issue Brief)
citation: Douglas H. Clements, Roberto Agodini, Barbara Harris. (2013). Instructional Practices and Student Math Achievement: Correlations from a Study of Math Curricula (Issue Brief). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Use correlational evidence on instructional practices to generate specific hypotheses for future experimental study
description: The brief positions correlational evidence on instructional practices as a hypothesis-generating step: additional relationships observed in large studies "can suggest specific hypotheses for the future study of such instructional practices". Those future studies, in turn, are expected to produce research evidence that could inform teacher professional development and the writing of instructional materials. The principle treats correlation-based findings as inputs to a research pipeline rather than as directly actionable causal conclusions.
requirements: Correlational studies large enough to detect relationships between specific instructional practices and achievement
constraints: The brief states the results reveal relationships "largely consistent with earlier research, but not in every case", so hypotheses require further study before informing practice
target_learners: Elementary school students learning mathematics
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement in early elementary grades
examples: The brief reports its correlational findings explicitly as evidence that can suggest hypotheses for future study of instructional practices.
key_sources: Douglas H. Clements, Roberto Agodini, Barbara Harris. (2013). Instructional Practices and Student Math Achievement: Correlations from a Study of Math Curricula (Issue Brief). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/

article_title: Statistical Power for School-Based RCTs with Binary Outcomes
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2013). Statistical Power for School-Based RCTs with Binary Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 6, issue 3. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/statistical-power-for-school-based-rcts-with-binary-outcomes
title: Plan larger school samples when designing clustered education RCTs with binary outcomes
description: Because binary outcomes demand larger samples than continuous test-score or behavioral-scale outcomes, designers of clustered school-based RCTs should plan for more schools than the 40 to 60 typically used. The article's key finding is that "sample sizes of 40 to 60 schools that are typically included in clustered RCTs for student test score or behavioral scale outcomes will often be insufficient for binary outcomes," so power calculations should use the article's logit-based approach.
requirements: Power planning must be conducted before the trial using the logit-based sample size formulas for the planned binary outcome
constraints: Applies to clustered designs with school- or teacher-level random assignment and binary outcomes
target_learners: K-12 students in school-based intervention studies
target_learning_goals: Adequately powered education RCTs measuring binary outcomes
examples: The article derives sample size formulas for clustered designs using generalized estimating equation methods to support this planning
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2013). Statistical Power for School-Based RCTs with Binary Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 6, issue 3. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/statistical-power-for-schoolbased-rcts-with-binary-outcomes

article_title: Measurement Models for Behavioral Frequencies: A Comparison Between Numerically and Vaguely Quantified Reports
citation: Jamie Lynn Marincic. (2012). Measurement Models for Behavioral Frequencies: A Comparison Between Numerically and Vaguely Quantified Reports. Working Paper 10. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Choose behavioral frequency report formats with awareness that quantification format shapes measurement structure and findings
description: Survey designers collecting behavioral frequency information should treat the choice between "numerically or vaguely quantified frequency reports" as a measurement decision, not a cosmetic one. The working paper shows the two formats yield measurement models with different structure, so the format chosen "directly influences substantive findings." Format selection should therefore be justified against the intended analyses.
requirements: Researchers must anticipate the measurement model they intend to build before selecting a frequency report format.
constraints: Support comes from one experiment embedded in the 2006 National Survey of Student Engagement; the available text prints no effect sizes.
target_learners: Postsecondary students surveyed about engagement behaviors
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of behavioral frequencies in survey-based educational research
examples: The article compared measurement models built from the two report formats using data from an experiment embedded in the 2006 National Survey of Student Engagement.
key_sources: Jamie Lynn Marincic. (2012). Measurement Models for Behavioral Frequencies: A Comparison Between Numerically and Vaguely Quantified Reports. Working Paper 10. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/measurement-models-for-behavioral-frequencies-a-comparison-between-numerically-and-vaguely-quantified-reports

article_title: Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? (Journal Article)
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2011). Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 36, no. 4. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Researchers should assess statistical power for mediator-outcome linkage analyses before relying on them to interpret RCT results
description: Because the article develops power formulas specifically for exploratory analyses linking teacher practice outcomes to student achievement outcomes in clustered school-based RCTs, it implies that researchers should evaluate power for these analyses when designing studies. The simulated power analysis exists to inform such assessments, indicating that typical RCTs may face power limitations for linking impacts on teacher practice and student achievement.
requirements: Access to the article's power formulas and design parameters for the planned RCT
constraints: Applies to clustered school-based RCT designs using OLS or IV estimators
target_learners: Education researchers and evaluators
target_learning_goals: Designing adequately powered analyses of teacher practice mediators
examples: The article conducts a simulated power analysis to illustrate power for these linkage analyses in typical RCTs
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2011). Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 36, no. 4. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/ja-do-typical-rcts-of-education-interventions-have-sufficient-statistical-power-for-linking-impacts

article_title: Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs
citation: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2011). Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 36, no. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs
title: Report CACE significance findings using correct variance formulas, but simplified formulas may suffice for similar conclusions
description: The article's comparison implies that analysts estimating CACE in clustered education RCTs should base significance findings on correct variance formulas that account for the relevant sources of error. Because the commonly used simplified formulas "lead to very similar significance findings" across the 10 RCTs examined, the practical stakes of formula choice may be limited, though correct formulas remain the benchmark.
requirements: Clustered RCT data with noncompliance, and variance formulas appropriate to the design
constraints: Similarity of findings is demonstrated for the 10 large-scale RCTs studied; the article does not claim universal equivalence
target_learners: Students in education RCTs
target_learning_goals: Accurate inference about intervention effects for compliers
examples: The authors compared significance findings for the CACE estimator across 10 large-scale RCTs using correct versus commonly used variance formulas.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2011). Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 36, no. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs

article_title: The Effects of Charter High Schools on Educational Attainment
citation: Kevin Booker, Tim R. Sass, Brian Gill, Ron Zimmer. (2011). The Effects of Charter High Schools on Educational Attainment. Journal of Labor Economics, vol. 29, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Consider charter high school continuity when designing middle-to-high-school transition supports for charter middle school students
description: The article's findings suggest that where students enroll after charter middle school is consequential for attainment: continuing into a charter high school was associated with higher diploma earning and college attendance than "transitioned to a traditional public high school". School systems and families weighing high school options for charter middle school graduates may treat high school sector continuity as a relevant consideration, alongside the study's Florida and Chicago scope.
requirements: Applies to students who attended a charter middle school and are choosing between charter and traditional public high schools.
constraints: Evidence is limited to Florida and Chicago as analyzed in this study.
target_learners: Charter middle school students transitioning to high school
target_learning_goals: High school diploma attainment
College attendance
examples: The study compared charter middle school graduates who continued into charter high schools with those who entered traditional public high schools in Florida and Chicago.
key_sources: Kevin Booker, Tim R. Sass, Brian Gill, Ron Zimmer. (2011). The Effects of Charter High Schools on Educational Attainment. Journal of Labor Economics, vol. 29, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/the-effects-of-charter-high-schools-on-educational-attainment

article_title: The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions (Journal Article)
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2010). The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 35, no. 4. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Use pretest-posttest designs in education RCTs to improve precision of estimated treatment effects, but weigh the bias risk of late pretests
description: Education RCTs often use pretest-posttest designs because including pretests improves the precision of estimated treatment effects. However, when pretests are collected after random assignment, analysts should not automatically include them: the decision "involves a variance-bias trade-off" that should be evaluated using a loss function approach before late pretest data are used in impact estimation.
requirements: RCT designs where pretest data collection timing relative to random assignment is known
constraints: Bias risk applies specifically when pretest data are collected after random assignment for logistical reasons
target_learners: Education researchers, evaluators, and analysts conducting randomized control trials
target_learning_goals: Designing RCT analyses that balance precision against bias in treatment effect estimates
examples: The article analyzes the trade-off theoretically and empirically for several commonly used impact estimators in education RCTs.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2010). The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 35, no. 4. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/journal-article-the-late-pretest-problem-in-randomized-control-trials-of-education-interventions

article_title: An Experimental Evaluation of Four Elementary School Math Curricula
citation: Roberto Agodini, Barbara Harris. (2010). An Experimental Evaluation of Four Elementary School Math Curricula. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 3, no. 3. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/an-experimental-evaluation-of-four-elementary-school-math-curricula
title: Curriculum choice as a lever for early-grade math achievement gains
description: The article treats the selection among comprehensive elementary math curricula as a school-level design decision with measurable achievement consequences: switching curricula changed an average first-grader's math percentile rank by "9 to 12 points" in its estimates. The pattern is choosing a demonstrably more effective curriculum package rather than altering instruction within an existing one. It operates at the whole-curriculum grain, affecting the year's math instruction as a unit.
requirements: School must be choosing among the curricula evaluated (or similarly structured comprehensive math curricula)
constraints: The estimated advantage applies to first-grade math as reported in this evaluation
target_learners: First-grade students in elementary schools
target_learning_goals: Early-grade mathematics achievement
examples: The evaluation estimated that a school using Math Expressions or Saxon instead of Investigations or SFAW would raise an average first-grader's math percentile rank by 9 to 12 points
key_sources: Roberto Agodini, Barbara Harris. (2010). An Experimental Evaluation of Four Elementary School Math Curricula. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 3, no. 3. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/an-experimental-evaluation-of-four-elementary-school-math-curricula

article_title: Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs
citation: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.
title: Establish the integrity of the forcing variable both institutionally and statistically before trusting RD impact estimates
description: Standard 1 requires that no systematic manipulation of the forcing variable occurred, since manipulation makes "the true relationship between the outcome and forcing variable can no longer be identified, which could lead to biased impact estimates." Institutional integrity requires describing who scored, who chose the cutoff, and when; statistical integrity requires a density test or graphical analysis around the cutoff. Both criteria must be satisfied to meet the standard without reservations.
requirements: An adequate description of the scoring and treatment assignment process showing scorers had little opportunity or incentive to change true scores
A statistical test failing to reject continuity of the forcing variable density at the cutoff, or a graphical density analysis without strong evidence of a discontinuity at the cutoff
constraints: If there is both a clear opportunity to manipulate scores and a clear incentive, the study does not satisfy this standard
target_learners: students
teachers
schools
target_learning_goals: credible causal estimates of education intervention effects
examples: Manipulation is likely to be less plausible if the forcing variable is a standardized test score than if it is a teacher-conducted assessment where teachers also influence treatment assignment.
key_sources: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.

article_title: Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs
citation: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.
title: RD studies must meet RCT attrition standards, reporting overall and differential attrition
description: Standard 2 requires RD studies to report the numbers assigned to treatment and comparison samples and response rates, with both overall attrition and attrition by treatment status. To meet the standard without reservations, "an RD study must meet the WWC randomized control trial (RCT) standards for attrition," calculated for the entire sample or only for units near the cutoff. A study failing this standard may still be reviewed as a QED if baseline equivalence is established.
requirements: Report overall attrition and attrition by treatment status
Meet WWC RCT attrition standards
constraints: A study that fails this standard could potentially be reviewed as a QED if equivalence is established on key baseline covariates, with the forcing variable not exempt from the equivalence requirement
target_learners: students
teachers
schools
target_learning_goals: credible causal estimates of education intervention effects
examples: Attrition may be calculated either for the entire research sample or for only students near the cutoff value of the forcing variable.
key_sources: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.

article_title: Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs
citation: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.
title: Demonstrate continuity of the outcome-forcing variable relationship at the cutoff via covariate equivalence and placebo tests away from the cutoff
description: Standard 3 addresses the untestable smoothness condition underlying RD estimates through two indirect approaches: testing whether key baseline covariates correlated with the outcome are continuous at the cutoff, and testing for discontinuities at values away from the cutoff "where there should be no impacts." Both criteria must be satisfied to meet the standard without reservations; the covariate requirement is waived for the forcing variable itself.
requirements: Baseline equivalence on key covariates demonstrated at the cutoff value (waived for the forcing variable)
No evidence of an unexplainable discontinuity in the outcome-score relationship at score values other than the cutoff
constraints: The smoothness condition cannot be checked directly; the two approaches are indirect
target_learners: students
schools
target_learning_goals: credible causal estimates of education intervention effects
examples: Discontinuities away from the cutoff are tested at values such as the medians of points above or below the cutoff, following Imbens and Lemieux (2008); a discontinuity corresponding to another known intervention with a different cutoff is explainable.
key_sources: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.

article_title: Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs
citation: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.
title: Estimate RD impacts with a statistical model controlling for the forcing variable, an appropriate functional form, and a justified bandwidth
description: Standard 4 sets five criteria for statistical modeling, which "plays a central role in estimating impacts in an RD study." It is "never acceptable to estimate an impact by comparing the mean outcomes of treatment and comparison group members without adjusting for the forcing variable." Studies must include a graphical analysis, justify the parametric or nonparametric specification, support any slope constraint, and estimate site impacts separately for multi-site averages.
requirements: A statistical model controlling for the forcing variable
A graphical analysis with scatter plot and fitted curve consistent with the chosen bandwidth and functional form
Evidence that an appropriate parametric, semi-parametric, or nonparametric model was fit
Empirical support for any constraint that the relationship is the same on both sides of the cutoff
Separate site-level estimation when impacts are averaged across multiple sites
constraints: Meeting with reservations requires Criteria A and D plus either B or C; the study fails if Criterion A is not satisfied, or Criterion D is not satisfied, or both B and C are not satisfied
target_learners: students
schools
target_learning_goals: credible causal estimates of education intervention effects
examples: A polynomial degree could be chosen to minimize the Akaike Information Criteria, or a local regression bandwidth justified using cross-validation; sensitivity of impacts to tail observations can assess bandwidth choice.
key_sources: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.

article_title: Survey of Outcomes Measurement in Research on Character Education Programs
citation: Person, Ann E., Emily Moiduddin, Megan Hague-Angus, and Lizabeth M. Malone (2009). Survey of Outcomes Measurement in Research on Character Education Programs (NCEE 2009-006). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncee.ed.gov
title: Character education evaluators should ground measure selection in a theory of change or work backward from an outcome taxonomy, and choose measures with demonstrated reliability and validity
description: The report recommends that researchers selecting outcome measures for character education evaluations first reference "a clear theory of how program elements are linked to specific out comes" to identify the constructs a program is most likely to affect; in the absence of such a theory, they can "work backward" from the report's taxonomy to select appropriate constructs. It further advises selecting or developing measures with demonstrated reliability and validity, given the complexity of character as a construct, and calls for more consistent reporting of psychometric properties across studies.
requirements: Access to the report's outcome taxonomy and its crosswalk of measures with reported reliability of .70 or greater
constraints: The measures presented are not necessarily representative of the universe of character education research nor necessarily the best measures available; the report provides no guidance on or recommendations of specific measures
target_learners: K-12 students in character education programs, including PCEP grantees
target_learning_goals: character development outcomes across cognitive, affective, and behavioral domains
examples: The report highlights misalignment risks it observed: scale items that do not hang together, and mismatches between the construct a measure actually captures and the construct the researcher reports
key_sources: Person, Ann E., Emily Moiduddin, Megan Hague-Angus, and Lizabeth M. Malone (2009). Survey of Outcomes Measurement in Research on Character Education Programs (NCEE 2009-006). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/survey-of-outcomes-measurement-in-research-on-character-education-programs

article_title: Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes?
citation: Schochet, Peter Z. (2009). Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? (NCEE 2009-4065). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncee.ed.gov
title: Size RCT data collection for teacher practice mediators according to the power needed for mediator-achievement analyses
description: Because teacher practice mediators are costly to obtain through classroom observations, videotaping, and coded protocols, the report argues power results "may have design implications for the scope of the data collection effort for obtaining costly teacher practice mediators." If power is low, mediator analyses reduce to a heuristic qualitative linking of outcomes. Designers should therefore decide the scope of mediator data collection in light of the school sample needed for precise mediator-achievement estimates.
requirements: Sufficient study schools (about 150 to 200 under OLS assumptions) to power mediator-achievement association tests
Reliable mediator measures, since measurement error further reduces power
constraints: For typical RCTs with 60 schools, power is likely to be limited, especially for IV methods
target_learners: elementary school students in low performing schools
target_learning_goals: identifying teacher practice pathways through which interventions improve student achievement
examples: The report's simulated power analysis computes the number of schools required to detect mediator effects explaining 5, 10, and 20 percent of classroom-effect variation at different power levels
key_sources: Schochet, Peter Z. (2009). Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? (NCEE 2009-4065). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/do-typical-rcts-of-education-interventions-have-sufficient-statistical-power-for-linking-impacts-on-teacher-practice-and-student-achievement-outcomes

article_title: Technical Methods Report: The Estimation of Average Treatment Effects for Clustered RCTs of Education Interventions
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2009). Technical Methods Report: The Estimation of Average Treatment Effects for Clustered RCTs of Education Interventions. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Test the sensitivity of RCT impact findings using different estimation methods and cluster-level weighting schemes
description: Because standard errors from alternative estimators of treatment effects in clustered RCTs can differ, the report's key recommendation is that analysts "test the sensitivity of their impact findings using different estimation methods and cluster-level weighting schemes". This guards policy conclusions against dependence on a single estimator choice.
requirements: Access to data from the clustered RCT so impacts can be re-estimated under alternative estimators and weighting schemes
constraints: The recommendation is made in the context of two-stage clustered RCTs of education interventions
target_learners: students in education interventions evaluated through clustered RCTs
target_learning_goals: robust estimation and reporting of intervention effects
examples: The report's empirical analysis re-estimated impacts and standard errors for five large-scale clustered education RCTs using the considered estimators
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2009). Technical Methods Report: The Estimation of Average Treatment Effects for Clustered RCTs of Education Interventions. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/

article_title: An Evaluation of the Teacher Advancement Program (TAP) in Chicago: Year One Impact Report
citation: Steven Glazerman, Allison McKie, Nancy Carey. (2009). An Evaluation of the Teacher Advancement Program (TAP) in Chicago: Year One Impact Report. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: TAP's four-component whole-school design combining growth, leadership, feedback, and performance pay
description: TAP bundles four school-wide components: professional growth opportunities, promotion to school leadership roles without leaving the classroom, structured feedback, and performance-based compensation. The report describes it as "a whole-school intervention that aims to improve schools by raising teacher quality," evaluating whether these combined changes affect teachers and students.
requirements: Implementation across the whole school rather than for individual teachers only
constraints: First-year implementation in Chicago; effects on student outcomes may lag implementation
target_learners: K-8 classroom teachers
target_learning_goals: Improving teacher quality, support, and retention
examples: Chicago Public Schools implemented TAP beginning in 2007 in K-8 schools
key_sources: Steven Glazerman, Allison McKie, Nancy Carey. (2009). An Evaluation of the Teacher Advancement Program (TAP) in Chicago: Year One Impact Report. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/an-evaluation-of-the-teacher-advancement-program-tap-in-chicago-year-one-impact-report

article_title: The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2008). The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: In education RCTs, prefer impact estimators that include late pretests over those that exclude them, provided early-year impact growth is not very rapid
description: Design principle for RCT analysis: when pretests can only be collected after random assignment, analysts should generally use estimators that include the late pretest data rather than dropping them or substituting other baseline scores, because the precision gains typically outweigh the bias risk. The paper grounds this in a "loss function approach grounded in the causal inference literature" and conditions it on impact growth rates.
requirements: Knowledge of whether test score impacts are likely to grow slowly early in the school year
Availability of late pretest data collected after random assignment
constraints: Does not apply when test score impacts grow very quickly early in the school year
target_learners: Education researchers and evaluators conducting randomized control trials
target_learning_goals: Designing RCT analyses that yield precise and unbiased estimates of education intervention effects
examples: The paper's analysis covers RCTs of interventions to improve student test scores, where pretest data are often collected after random assignment for logistic reasons.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2008). The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee

article_title: Small class sizes for improving student achievement in primary and secondary schools: a systematic review
citation: Filges, T., Sonne‐Schmidt, C. S., Nielsen, B. C. V. (2018). Small class sizes for improving student achievement in primary and secondary schools: a systematic review. Campbell Systematic Reviews 2018:10. https://doi.org/10.4073/csr.2018.10
title: Target class size reductions at schools with high concentrations of socioeconomically disadvantaged students rather than implementing universal reduction
description: Because class size reduction is costly, the review's background argues it may be more economically efficient to concentrate reductions where benefits are largest. Evidence it cites indicates smaller class size is more beneficial for disadvantaged students, and STAR and SAGE evidence indicates minority, low-income, and educationally disadvantaged students benefited most. The review therefore suggests that "rather than implementing costly universal class size reduction policies, it may be more economically efficient to target schools with high concentrations of socioeconomic disadvantaged students for class size reductions."
requirements: Knowledge of which student groups benefit most from smaller classes, since the efficiency argument rests on differential benefit by socioeconomic background
constraints: The supporting evidence cited (STAR, SAGE) is described in the review's background rather than synthesised in this review's own meta-analysis
target_learners: students from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds
minority students
students living in poverty
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in reading and mathematics
examples: The review cites the Tennessee STAR randomised controlled trial and Wisconsin's SAGE program as evidence that disadvantaged students benefited most from reduced class size
key_sources: Filges, T., Sonne‐Schmidt, C. S., Nielsen, B. C. V. (2018). Small class sizes for improving student achievement in primary and secondary schools: a systematic review. Campbell Systematic Reviews 2018:10. https://doi.org/10.4073/csr.2018.10

article_title: The effects of inclusion on academic achievement, socioemotional development and wellbeing of children with special educational needs
citation: Dalgaard, N. T., Bondebjerg, A., Viinholt, B. C. A., & Filges, T. (2022). The effects of inclusion on academic achievement, socioemotional development and wellbeing of children with special educational needs. Campbell Systematic Reviews, 18, e1291. https://doi.org/10.1002/cl2.1291
title: Hegarty's seven factors associated with positive student outcomes in inclusive settings
description: The review reports, citing Hegarty (1993), a narrative review identifying "a number of factors are associated with positive student outcomes in inclusive settings": instruction based on student achievement needs, materials and procedures allowing students to proceed at their own pace, additional time for students who need it, increased student responsibility for their own learning, co-operation among students in achieving goals, support teaching, and collaboration among special and general education teachers. The pattern describes a configuration of instructional and organisational conditions under which inclusive placements are reported to work well.
requirements: Inclusive settings must provide the listed supports, including support teaching and collaboration among special and general education teachers
constraints: The factors come from a narrative review cited second-hand by this review; the review did not meta-analyse them as moderators
target_learners: children with special educational needs in inclusive general education settings
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
social adjustment in inclusive classrooms
examples: The review quotes Hegarty's enumerated list of seven factors in its background section on how the intervention might work.
key_sources: Dalgaard, N. T., Bondebjerg, A., Viinholt, B. C. A., & Filges, T. (2022). The effects of inclusion on academic achievement, socioemotional development and wellbeing of children with special educational needs. Campbell Systematic Reviews, 18, e1291. https://doi.org/10.1002/cl2.1291

article_title: Elementary-Grade Math Programs in the Pittsburgh Public Schools: A Comparison of Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math
citation: Catherine Nelson, Julia Kaufman, Kevin Booker, Brian Gill. (2007). Elementary-Grade Math Programs in the Pittsburgh Public Schools: A Comparison of Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/elementary-grade-math-programs-in-the-pittsburgh-public-schools-a-comparison-of-everyday-mathematics-and-harcourt-math
title: Evaluate curriculum programs as implemented, since implementation similarity can mask theoretical differences between programs
description: When comparing curricula, program effects depend on how programs are actually enacted in classrooms, not only on their theoretical design. The Pittsburgh comparison found no achievement difference between Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math, and the authors suggest this "may be related to the fact that" the programs "were more similar in practice than they are in theory." Evaluations should therefore attend to implementation when interpreting program comparisons.
requirements: Assessment of how the programs were actually implemented in classrooms, so that implementation similarity can be taken into account when interpreting outcome differences.
constraints: The article states this interpretation only for the Pittsburgh implementation of these two programs; it is offered as a possible explanation, not a tested finding.
target_learners: Elementary-grade students in public school districts
target_learning_goals: Elementary mathematics achievement
examples: The Pittsburgh quasi-experimental comparison of Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math, in which the authors attributed the null achievement difference to the programs' similar implementation in practice.

Elementary-Grade Math Programs in the Pittsburgh Public Schools: A Comparison of Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math. article_title: Ingredients of a Successful Summer Learning Program: A Case Study of the Building Educated Leaders for Life (BELL) Accelerated Learning Summer Program
citation: Jeffrey Capizzano, Kendra Bischoff, Nicola Woodroffe, Duncan Chaplin. (2007). Ingredients of a Successful Summer Learning Program: A Case Study of the Building Educated Leaders for Life (BELL) Accelerated Learning Summer Program. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Describe the specific elements of an effective program so it can be replicated
description: After an intervention is shown effective, document its specific program elements so practitioners can replicate it. This paper follows that approach: given positive random-assignment results, "this new paper describes the specific elements of the successful program so it can be replicated." The elements documented are those present in the successful BELL summer program.
requirements: A prior evaluation establishing the program as effective, so that the documented elements come from a demonstrably successful program
constraints: The authors state they cannot distinguish which elements caused the positive impacts, so documented elements are of potential rather than proven importance
target_learners: Elementary school students in summer learning programs
target_learning_goals: Literacy and academic skill retention over the summer
examples: The paper describes the elements of the BELL Accelerated Learning Summer Program, which a prior random-assignment evaluation had found effective.

Ingredients of a Successful Summer Learning Program: A Case Study of the Building Educated Leaders for Life (BELL) Accelerated Learning Summer Program. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/ingredients-of-a-successful-summer-learning-program-a-case-study-of-the-building-educated-leaders-for-life-bell-accelerated-learning-summer-program

article_title: National Evaluation of Early Reading First
citation: Jackson, R., McCoy, A., Pistorino, C., Wilkinson, A., Burghardt, J., Clark, M., Ross, C., Schochet, P., Swank, P., & Schmidt, S. (2007). National Evaluation of Early Reading First: Final Report to Congress. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Enhance preschool teacher practices, instructional content, and classroom environments to prepare children for school
description: The Early Reading First program embodies the principle that improving preschool quality on three fronts — teacher practices, instructional content, and classroom environments — helps children start school ready. Grants were "designed to enhance teacher practices, instructional content, and classroom environments in preschools to ensure that young children... start school with the skills needed for academic success."
requirements: Funding (grants) to preschools to support changes across teacher practices, instructional content, and classroom environments.
constraints: Evaluated in preschool settings serving young children, especially those from low-income families.
target_learners: preschool children, especially those from low-income families
target_learning_goals: school-entry language and literacy skills
examples: The federal program awarded grants to preschools, and the national evaluation found significant positive impacts on classroom and teacher outcomes and on children's print and letter knowledge.

article_title: Expanding Beyond Academics: Who Benefits and How?
citation: John Deke, Joshua Haimson. (2006). Expanding Beyond Academics: Who Benefits and How? Trends in Education Research, Issue Brief #2. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Individualize competency development rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach
description: Because students differ in which competencies predict their later success, the brief suggests education should be individualized rather than uniform. It concludes that "not all students would benefit from improving the same competencies," so schools should tailor which competencies they help each student develop.
requirements: Schools must be able to identify which competencies matter for individual students' later success.
constraints: The brief frames this as a suggestion based on predictive associations, not a tested intervention.

labor market earnings
leadership skills
work habits
prosocial behavior
locus of control
examples: The brief analyzed how high school competencies including academic achievement, leadership skills, sports-related skills, work habits, prosocial behavior, and locus of control relate to later attainment and earnings.

citation: Duncan Chaplin, Jeffrey Capizzano. (2006). Impacts of a Summer Learning Program: A Random Assignment Study of Building Educated Leaders for Life BELL. Washington, DC: Urban Institute. https://www.urban.org/
title: Invest in out-of-school-time summer programming for low-income children
description: The article recommends continued investment in summer out-of-school-time programming for low-income children, because its random assignment study found a well-implemented summer program "can improve reading test scores" and increase parents' encouragement of reading. It names current funding streams such as the 21st Century Community Learning Centers program and Title I Supplemental Services as examples of such investment.
requirements: The program must be well-implemented, as the finding is qualified by implementation quality.
constraints: Support is stated as "some support" for investments, not definitive proof of scale-up.
target_learners: Low-income children
target_learning_goals: Reading achievement
Home literacy support
examples: The study evaluated the BELL (Building Educated Leaders for Life) summer learning program using random assignment.

article_title: Alternative Routes to Teaching: The Impacts of Teach For America on Student Achievement and Other Outcomes
citation: Steven Glazerman, Daniel Mayer, Paul Decker. (2006). Alternative Routes to Teaching: The Impacts of Teach For America on Student Achievement and Other Outcomes. Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, vol. 25, no. 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/alternative-routes-to-teaching-the-impacts-of-teach-for-america-on-student-achievement-and-other-outcomes
title: Evaluate alternative teacher preparation routes with randomized experiments before judging their effects on students
description: The article's approach is to base judgments about an alternative teacher preparation route on a randomized experiment rather than on claims or assumptions. It used "a randomized experiment to study the impact of Teach For America on student achievement and other outcomes," measuring math and reading achievement plus attendance, promotion, and disciplinary incidents. This design allowed the authors to report both positive and null findings and to test claims that such programs harm students.
requirements: Random assignment of students or classrooms to teachers from the alternative route versus comparison teachers, as the study used a randomized experiment
constraints: Findings apply to the studied program (Teach For America) and outcomes measured in the 2001-2004 evaluation; the article does not claim generalization to all alternative routes
target_learners: K-12 students taught by alternatively certified and comparison teachers
target_learning_goals: Math achievement
Reading achievement
examples: The National Evaluation of Teach For America (2001-2004) used a randomized experiment to estimate TFA's impacts on math and reading achievement and other outcomes.

article_title: Maximizing Learning Across Investments Recommendations for Funders
citation: Kara Conroy, Kate Place, Greg Chojnacki. (2023). Maximizing Learning Across Investments: Recommendations for Funders. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/maximizing-learning-across-investments-recommendations-for-funders
title: Structure an M&E process that supports cross-grantee learning while balancing funder, grantee, and community priorities
description: The brief's recommendations aim to help funders "structure an M&E process that supports cross-grantee learning while balancing the priorities of the funder, the grantees, and the communities where research will take place." Cross-grantee learning is presented as a design goal for multi-solution portfolios, with community priorities treated as a party whose interests must be balanced, not overridden.
requirements: The M&E process must be structured to support learning across grantees, not only within single grants.
constraints: The process must balance the priorities of the funder, the grantees, and the communities where research will take place.
target_learners: Funders investing in multiple learning solutions at the same time
target_learning_goals: Cross-grantee learning about whether solutions work, for whom, and in what context
examples: The brief positions this balancing principle as the purpose of its recommendation set for funders.

article_title: Outcomes, Impacts, and Processes: A Framework for Understanding School Performance
citation: Brian Gill, Laura Dyer. (2023). Outcomes, Impacts, and Processes: A Framework for Understanding School Performance. U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/
title: Three-question structure for school performance inquiry
description: The framework structures school performance inquiry around three questions: "1. How are students doing? 2. How much does the school contribute to how students are doing? and 3. What is happening in the school?" Each question maps to a complementary grouping of measures—student outcomes, school impacts on outcomes, and processes driving those impacts—so the three together give a rounded picture of school performance.
requirements: Measure data organized into the three complementary groupings must be valid, reliable, and robust
target_learners: K-12 students in states and districts
target_learning_goals: Comprehensive understanding of school performance
examples: The framework pairs each question with a measure grouping: outcomes with how students are doing, impacts with school contribution, processes with what is happening in the school
key_sources: Brian Gill, Laura Dyer. (2023). Outcomes, Impacts, and Processes: A Framework for Understanding School Performance. U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/outcomes-impacts-and-processes-a-framework-for-understanding-school-performance

article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Assess for Early Evidence of Success (Phase 3)
citation: Ruggiero, R., Manley, M., Knechtel, V., Place, K., & Shoji, M. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Assess for Early Evidence of Success (Phase 3). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/
title: Treat evidence building as iterative learning that may loop back or end in abandonment
description: The checklist's activities are built around "iterative learning, which may mean completing a phase multiple times, moving backwards to a previous phase, or abandoning a solution altogether." Evidence building should therefore not be treated as a one-way pipeline: teams should expect to revisit earlier phases when pilot or refinement evidence warrants it, and to stop pursuing solutions that evidence does not support.
requirements: Willingness to repeat phases, return to previous phases, or discontinue a solution based on evidence
target_learners: students in a priority community
target_learning_goals: evidence-based refinement and validation of learning solutions
examples: The checklist explicitly instructs users that a phase may be completed multiple times or that users may move backwards to a previous phase

citation: Ruggiero, R., Manley, M., Knechtel, V., Place, K., & Shoji, M. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Assess for Early Evidence of Success (Phase 3). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/

requirements: Identification of a priority community and engagement of its stakeholders in each evidence-building phase

target_learning_goals: solutions associated with improved outcomes for priority-community students
examples: The checklist's stated purpose names stakeholder collaboration as part of designing, refining, and testing the solution

article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Refine the Solution (Phase 2)
citation: Ryan Ruggiero, Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Kate Place, Megan Shoji. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Refine the Solution (Phase 2). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/
title: Treat evidence building as iterative learning that may loop back or end a solution
description: The M&E Checklist frames evidence building as iterative learning rather than a one-way sequence: checklist activities may mean completing a phase multiple times, moving backwards to a previous phase, or abandoning a solution altogether. This principle positions refinement and even termination as legitimate outcomes of evidence gathering, encouraging solution developers to act on what implementation reveals rather than proceeding rigidly through phases.
requirements: Users must engage in checklist activities focused on iterative learning, remaining open to repeating phases, moving backwards, or abandoning a solution.
target_learners: Students in priority communities served by the solutions being developed and refined
target_learning_goals: Building descriptive and causal evidence that solutions work for the intended community
examples: The checklist explicitly allows moving backwards to a previous phase or abandoning a solution altogether as part of the evidence-building process.

article_title: Sample Size Guide
citation: Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Gregory Chojnacki. (2023). Sample Size Guide. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/sample-size-guide
title: Engage a research partner to set sample sizes for validation-phase studies
description: Because rigorous effectiveness validation requires study-specific statistical planning, the guide recommends that organizations treat its general guidance as a starting point rather than a prescription. It states that in Phase 3 and Phase 4, "organizations can use this guidance as a starting point but should work with a research partner to determine the specific sample size needed for their study", pairing self-service tools with expert methodological support.
requirements: Access to a research partner with methodological expertise for Phase 3 and Phase 4 studies.
constraints: The guide's own sample size guidance is explicitly insufficient on its own for determining the specific sample size of a Phase 3 or Phase 4 study.
target_learners: students who are Black, Latino, and/or experiencing poverty
target_learning_goals: validating effectiveness of educational solutions
examples: The guide directs Phase 3 and Phase 4 users to work with a research partner to determine the specific sample size needed for their study.

article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Validate Effectiveness (Phase 4)
citation: Ryan Ruggiero, Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Kate Place, Megan Shoji. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Validate Effectiveness (Phase 4). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/measurement-and-evaluation-checklist-validate-effectiveness-phase-4
title: Treat evidence building as iterative learning that may loop back or end a solution
description: The checklist's activities are built around iterative learning rather than a one-way pipeline. This principle positions evidence gathering as a feedback loop that can redirect or terminate development, not merely confirm it.
requirements: Willingness to revisit earlier phases or abandon a solution when evidence warrants
target_learners: students in a priority community
target_learning_goals: evidence-based improvement of learning solutions
examples: The checklist explicitly permits completing a phase multiple times or moving backwards to a previous phase

citation: Kate Place, Gregory Chojnacki, Virginia Knechtel, Andy Gothro, Megan Shoji, Lindsay Fox. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Plan Template. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Seven-component structure of a complete M&E plan
description: The template enumerates what a complete M&E plan includes: "A description of a solution and theory of change"; information on prior research; detail on how priority communities were and will be involved; the study research questions; the measures and approach for answering them; "Ambitious targets (or goals) for each intended outcome"; and a timeline to carry out the work. This list defines the plan's organizing structure.
requirements: Each plan component must be completed for the plan to be complete, as enumerated by the template

target_learning_goals: structuring a complete measurement and evaluation plan
examples: The template's own list of plan contents, from theory of change through timeline

title: Co-develop the M&E plan with the implementing organization, research partner, and priority communities
description: The authors recommend that "the implementing organization and research partner work together to co-develop the M&E plan, in partnership with representatives from the priority communities." target_learning_goals: community-involved evaluation planning
examples: The template includes a component documenting how priority communities were and will be involved in the design of the solution and the evaluation

title: Equity must be embedded in the learning and decision-making approach, not only in organizational goals
description: The article argues that goal statements alone are insufficient for equity-centered strategic learning. It states that "strong equity-centered strategic learning is demonstrated when equity is considered in not only the organization's goal but also in its learning and decision-making approach." Organizations should therefore examine how learning processes and decisions, not just stated goals, address equity for Black and Latino students and students experiencing poverty.
requirements: An organization adopting this principle must review both its goals and its learning and decision-making processes for attention to equity.
target_learners: K–12 education grantee organizations
target_learning_goals: Embedding equity in organizational learning and decision making
examples: The CBSL partnership applied this criterion in defining what counts as strong equity-centered strategic learning among pilot grantees.

article_title: Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field
citation: Kara Conroy, Annalisa Mastri, James Wholley. (2021). Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Six-element pattern for engaging training and technical assistance design
description: A reusable design pattern for training and technical assistance (TA) consisting of six elements the brief identifies as necessary for engagement: grounding in "clear expectations and common understanding," being "designed around the needs of the recipients," being "developed using ongoing recipient input," being "accessible for recipients," being "delivered by providers equipped to meet recipients' needs," and being "framed as a partnership between the provider and recipient." Ongoing recipient input during development

article_title: Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field
citation: Kara Conroy, Annalisa Mastri, James Wholley. (2021). Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Frame training and technical assistance as a partnership between provider and recipient, working with recipients to gather and incorporate their input
description: The brief recommends treating training and TA as "a partnership between the provider and recipient" rather than a one-way delivery. It emphasizes "how to work with recipients to gather and incorporate their input on the training and TA they will receive," so that TA is designed around recipient needs and developed using ongoing recipient input. This principle directs providers to build recipient voice into design, delivery, and iteration.
requirements: Ongoing mechanisms for gathering recipient input on the training and TA they will receive
target_learners: Training and technical assistance recipients in human services and employment programs
target_learning_goals: Recipient engagement with and ownership of training and technical assistance
examples: The brief presents strategies such as written TA requests, needs and assets assessments, and TA menus as ways providers work with recipients to gather and incorporate their input.

article_title: Identifying Students At Risk Using Prior Performance Versus a Machine Learning Algorithm
citation: Lindsay Cattell, Julie Bruch. (2021). Identifying Students At Risk Using Prior Performance Versus a Machine Learning Algorithm. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic, U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs
title: Choose between prior-performance flags and algorithmic risk scores by weighing accuracy needs against cost, ease of setup, and the value of fine-grained risk information
description: The report presents the choice of early warning approach as a tradeoff rather than a single best option. It notes the prior performance system "is just as accurate as the algorithm for some purposes and is cheaper and easier to set up, but it does not provide fine-grained information." Districts needing to distinguish degrees of risk can use the algorithm to set cutoffs matched to outcome prevalence, the harms of over- versus under-identifying students, and available intervention resources.
requirements: Districts must decide which outcomes matter, how harmful over- versus under-identification is, and what intervention resources are available before setting algorithm cutoffs.
constraints: The prior performance approach does not provide fine-grained information identifying students at greatest risk.
target_learners: K-12 students at risk of chronic absenteeism, low GPA, course failure, or suspension
target_learning_goals: Accurate early identification of students at academic risk so resources can be targeted before students drop out
examples: The report compares a prior performance early warning system to two algorithm cutoff options: one matching the same percentage of students as the flags, and one identifying the 10 percent of students most at risk.
key_sources: Lindsay Cattell, Julie Bruch. (2021). Identifying Students At Risk Using Prior Performance Versus a Machine Learning Algorithm. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic, U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs

article_title: Using Promotion Power to Identify the Effectiveness of Public High Schools in the District of Columbia
citation: Max Gross, Menbere Shiferaw, Jonah Deutsch, Brian Gill. (2021). Using Promotion Power to Identify the Effectiveness of Public High Schools in the District of Columbia. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs
title: Use promotion power alongside status and value-added measures when evaluating high schools
description: The study positions promotion power as a complement to existing school-effectiveness indicators: promotion power scores "are distinct from status measures such as graduation rate and college enrollment rate" because they account for prior achievement and background, and they "complement value-added measures by using similar methods to examine additional, longer-term outcomes." Districts and researchers evaluating high schools should therefore report promotion power together with, not instead of, status and value-added measures.
requirements: Prior student achievement and background data, and longer-term outcome data such as graduation and college enrollment, to estimate promotion power
constraints: Developed and illustrated for public high schools in the District of Columbia
target_learners: Public high school students
target_learning_goals: High school graduation
College enrollment
College readiness
examples: The study estimated promotion power for DC public high schools on college-ready SAT scores, high school graduation, and college enrollment as longer-term outcomes beyond value-added measures

article_title: The Community Ecocycle in Place-Based Systems Change: A Tool for Funder and Community Reflection and Action
citation: Meg Long, Wanda Casillas, James Liou. (2021). The Community Ecocycle in Place-Based Systems Change: A Tool for Funder and Community Reflection and Action. Equal Measure and Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Funder reflection on community developmental phase should precede and shape place-based investment
description: The article's guiding principle is that funders should first use the tool "to consider the dynamic, natural, and necessary developmental phases through which communities move" before committing investment approaches. Because communities' assets and needs differ by phase, reflection on phase is positioned as a necessary precursor to action, making investments more likely to fit community circumstances.

title: Adult education programs should use evidence-based strategies to improve services and participant success

high school equivalency

title: Pair hybrid instruction with precautions such as mask-wearing and physical distancing to mitigate in-school virus transmission
description: The report's central design recommendation is that districts can educate students in person while mitigating COVID-19 spread by combining hybrid scheduling with precautions. article_title: Too Scared to Learn? The Academic Consequences of Feeling Unsafe in the Classroom
citation: Johanna Lacoe. (2020). Too Scared to Learn? The Academic Consequences of Feeling Unsafe in the Classroom. Urban Education, vol. 55, issue 10. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Treat a safe classroom environment as a prerequisite for productive learning
description: The article opens from the position that "a safe environment is a prerequisite for productive learning," and its empirical finding of a consistent negative relationship between feeling unsafe and test scores grounds this principle. It implies that efforts to improve achievement in middle schools should attend to students' feelings of safety in the classroom.
requirements: Schools need a way to measure students' reported feelings of safety, such as annual student surveys
constraints: The supporting evidence is an observational relationship, not a tested intervention

examples: The study analyzed survey-reported feelings of safety alongside test scores for more than 340,000 students annually

District central office leaders

article_title: The Choice Architecture of School Choice Websites
citation: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Jesse Chandler, Alyson Burnett. (2020). The Choice Architecture of School Choice Websites. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 13, issue 2. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Design the choice architecture of school choice websites deliberately, because small display manipulations shift which schools parents choose
description: This principle holds that how school information is displayed on choice websites — default ordering, icon versus graph versus number formats, and concise versus detailed summaries — is itself a design decision that shapes parental choices. The article's experiment shows that "a small design manipulation... induced meaningful changes in the types of schools selected," so website designers should treat display choices as consequential rather than neutral.

constraints: Evidence comes from a hypothetical school district choice task with low-income parents; the article reports trade-offs, e.g. graphs maximized satisfaction at the expense of understanding

target_learning_goals: informed school selection based on academic performance information
examples: In the experiment, changing the default order in which schools were presented and swapping graphs or numbers for icons changed the types of schools parents selected

citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2020). Analyzing Grouped Administrative Data for RCTs Using Design-Based Methods. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 45, issue 1.
title: Use grouped administrative data with design-based methods to improve data access for RCT analysis
description: The article recommends analyzing RCTs with grouped administrative data "to help improve data access," using design-based estimators formed as group-level averages. This allows evaluators to estimate average treatment effects when individual-level data cannot be obtained, provided the design conditions the article identifies are met.
requirements: RCT designs of the types covered: clustered and blocked designs, and models with weights and covariates
constraints: Subgroup analyses via ecological inference yield large design effects and are not covered by the tolerability result
target_learners: education researchers and evaluators conducting RCT analyses
target_learning_goals: estimating average treatment effects with restricted data access

citation: Max, Jeffrey; Tuttle, Christina; Gleason, Philip; McCallum, Diana; Gill, Brian. (2019). How Does School Choice Affect Student Achievement in Traditional Public Schools? Washington, DC: Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Policymakers evaluating school choice should account for its effects on students who remain in traditional public schools, not only on participants

article_title: A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research
citation: Brian Goesling. (2019). A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research. Journal of School Health, vol. 89, issue 11. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-practical-guide-to-cluster-randomized-trials-in-school-health-research

examples: The guide frames this as one of several practical steps researchers can take to meet growing demands for evidence and accountability in education policy and programming.

article_title: A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research

article_title: Use of Evidence to Drive Decision-Making in Government
citation: Julieta Lugo-Gil, Dana Jean-Baptiste, Livia Frasso Jaramillo. (2019). Use of Evidence to Drive Decision-Making in Government. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Leadership support and staff buy-in are needed for evidence use in government decision-making
description: This principle holds that government agencies seeking to use evidence in program and policy decisions need leaders who actively promote evidence use and staff who accept and support that practice. Interview respondents identified "having leadership that supports and promotes the use of evidence and buy-in from the organization's staff" as a factor facilitating evidence use. article_title: Reforming School Discipline: School-Level Policy Implementation and the Consequences for Suspended Students and Their Peers
citation: Matthew P. Steinberg, Johanna Lacoe. (2018). Reforming School Discipline: School-Level Policy Implementation and the Consequences for Suspended Students and Their Peers. American Journal of Education, vol. 125, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reforming-school-discipline-school-level-policy-implementation-and-the-consequences-for-suspended-students-and-their-peers
title: District discipline reforms should be monitored for school-level implementation because peer consequences depend on it
description: The article's findings indicate that a district-level prohibition on out-of-school suspensions for classroom disorder produced different peer consequences depending on how schools implemented it: "in schools that eliminated classroom disorder OSS, peer math achievement and attendance were unaffected, whereas peer math achievement declined and attendance decreased in schools that did not fully implement the district-level reform." constraints: Evidence comes from one district's reform (Philadelphia) prohibiting out-of-school suspension for classroom disorder infractions
target_learners: K-12 students in district schools, including suspended students and their peers
target_learning_goals: Maintaining attendance and math achievement for all students during discipline policy reform
examples: Philadelphia prohibited out-of-school suspension for classroom disorder infractions; schools varied in whether they eliminated classroom disorder OSS, and peer outcomes differed accordingly.

article_title: Nudging Parents to Choose Better Schools: The Importance of School Choice Architecture
citation: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Jesse Chandler, Alyson Burnett. (2018). Nudging Parents to Choose Better Schools: The Importance of School Choice Architecture. Working Paper 65. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/nudging-parents-to-choose-better-schools-the-importance-of-school-choice-architecture
title: Design the architecture of school choice interfaces to nudge parents toward better-informed choices
description: The article's central design principle is that the architecture of school choice — how school information is presented in chooser interfaces — shapes parents' decisions. It argues that "simple design choices, such as  setting the default sort order to academic performance instead of distance from home, could induce parents to choose academically higher performing schools," so interface defaults and information presentation should be treated as policy-relevant design levers.
requirements: An online chooser interface whose information presentation and defaults can be configured
constraints: Evidence comes from a factorial experiment with low-income parents choosing schools; effects on other populations are not established in the supplied text
target_learners: Low-income parents choosing schools for their children
target_learning_goals: Choosing academically higher performing schools
Better knowledge about schools
examples: The study tested five presentation design factors, including default sort order, in an online school chooser tool
key_sources: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Jesse Chandler, Alyson Burnett. (2018). Nudging Parents to Choose Better Schools: The Importance of School Choice Architecture. Working Paper 65. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/nudging-parents-to-choose-better-schools-the-importance-of-school-choice-architecture

article_title: Presenting School Choice Information to Parents: An Evidence-Based Guide
citation: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Alyson Burnett. (2018). Presenting School Choice Information to Parents: An Evidence-Based Guide. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Present school choice information in a form that is understandable and user-friendly so parents can make informed decisions
description: Because choosing a school is difficult for parents, agencies presenting school information should ensure it is "understandable and user-friendly to help make an informed decision." The article grounds this principle in experimental evidence that the visual representation, amount, and organization of information affect parents' understanding, ease of use, satisfaction, and school rankings.
requirements: Information presented to parents about schools must be understandable and user-friendly.
constraints: The article notes there is little pre-existing evidence-based guidance on presenting school information to the public.
target_learners: Parents choosing schools for their children
target_learning_goals: Informed school choice decision-making
examples: The guide's underlying experiment varied the visual representation, amount, and organization of information presented for a hypothetical school district.

article_title: Can More Teachers Be Covered? The Accuracy, Credibility, and Precision of Value-Added Estimates with Proxy Pre-Tests
citation: Elias Walsh, Dallas Dotter, Albert Y. Liu. (2018). Can More Teachers Be Covered? The Accuracy, Credibility, and Precision of Value-Added Estimates with Proxy Pre-Tests. Working Paper 64. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Use proxy pre-tests to extend value-added coverage to grades and subjects lacking same-subject prior tests, while weighting estimates appropriately
description: The article's central design recommendation is that states and districts can use proxy pre-tests—prior-grade test scores from other subjects—as controls in value-added models for grades where same-subject prior tests are unavailable, thereby increasing the number of covered teachers, for example "by including science teachers, rather than only teachers of math and English language arts." Because such estimates carry bias, the article recommends giving them "more appropriate weights in teachers' evaluations," for instance via empirical Bayes shrinkage.
requirements: Prior-grade test scores from other subjects must be available as proxy pre-test controls
constraints: Proxy pre-test estimates show evidence of bias compared with same-subject pre-test models, so they should be weighted appropriately in evaluations
target_learners: K-12 students in grades and subjects without consecutive-grade same-subject testing
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of teachers' contributions to student achievement for evaluation purposes
examples: The study used statewide Oklahoma data to investigate whether proxy pre-test value-added models can credibly, accurately, and precisely measure teacher contributions.

article_title: Causal Validity Considerations for Including High Quality Non-Experimental Evidence in Systematic Reviews
citation: John Deke. (2018). Causal Validity Considerations for Including High Quality Non-Experimental Evidence in Systematic Reviews. OPRE Report #2018-63, Office of Planning, Research, and Evaluation, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. https://www.acf.hhs.gov/opre
title: Systematic reviews should consider causal validity when deciding whether to include high quality non-experimental evidence
description: The report's title and framing advance a review-design principle: rather than excluding all non-experimental evidence, systematic reviews should assess the causal validity of high quality non-experimental studies when deciding what to include. The provided text states the motivation — reviews "seek to assist decision makers by rating the quality of and summarizing the findings from research evidence" — and notes RCTs cannot cover all programs. The report itself is the vehicle for developing these causal validity considerations.
requirements: Review processes must rate the quality of research evidence and summarize findings to assist decision makers
constraints: The provided text does not state the specific validity criteria; it only announces the report's purpose
target_learners: Policy makers and researchers who conduct or use federally funded systematic reviews of intervention evidence
target_learning_goals: Understanding when and how non-experimental evidence can be credibly incorporated into evidence reviews for policy decisions
examples: The OPRE report itself, titled Causal Validity Considerations for Including High Quality Non-Experimental Evidence in Systematic Reviews, is the artifact developing this principle
