article_title: Changing Special Education Enrollments
citation: Shazia Rafiullah Miller and Robert M. Gladden. (2002). Changing Special Education Enrollments: Causes and Distribution Among Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. http://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Consider elementary school policies in light of their possible long-term effects on high schools before adopting them
description: This principle holds that district policymakers should project the downstream consequences of elementary school reforms for high schools before adoption. The report's central finding is that the eighth-grade promotion gate, an elementary policy, reshaped high school composition by retaining general education students while students with disabilities advanced under IEP requirements, concentrating them in neighborhood schools. As the report puts it, "before the system adopts a policy to prompt change in the elementary schools, it should be considered in light of its possible long-term effects on high schools."
requirements: Requires longitudinal enrollment and classification data spanning grade levels so cross-level effects can be projected before adoption
constraints: The report grounds this in one district (Chicago, 1993–2000) and one policy (the 1995–96 eighth-grade promotion gate) with its specific retention, APC, and IEP rules
target_learners: district administrators and policymakers
eighth-grade students transitioning to high school
students with disabilities in neighborhood high schools
target_learning_goals: equitable distribution of students with disabilities across schools
inclusion of students with disabilities in general education classrooms
system-level policy design that anticipates cross-level consequences
examples: The report traces how the 1995–96 eighth-grade promotion gate produced higher general education retention, a smaller better-prepared ninth-grade cohort, and concentrations of students with disabilities reaching 30 percent in eleven high schools
key_sources: Shazia Rafiullah Miller and Robert M. Gladden. (2002). Changing Special Education Enrollments: Causes and Distribution Among Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/changing-special-education-enrollments-causes-and-distribution-among-schools

article_title: Declining High School Enrollment
citation: Elaine M. Allensworth & Shazia Rafiullah Miller. (2002). Declining High School Enrollment: An Exploration of Causes. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Consider a district policy's long-term effects on downstream schools before adopting it
description: The report argues that elementary-school policies reverberate through high schools in ways that should be anticipated. It shows the eighth-grade promotion gate reduced high school enrollment through retention, APC placement, faster progression, and changed special education concentrations, concluding that "before the system adopts a policy to prompt change in the elementary schools, it should be considered in light of its possible long-term effects on high schools."
requirements: District-level administrative data linking student progression across school levels, so downstream effects can be traced
constraints: The report could not isolate the promotion gate's effects from simultaneous policy changes such as new magnet schools and course-taking requirements
target_learners: district policymakers
high school students in urban districts
target_learning_goals: system-level policy design that anticipates cross-level consequences for student progression and school composition
examples: The 1996 CPS promotion gate shrank ninth-grade cohorts and reduced grade repetition, depressing enrollment by 11.5 percent by 1999-00 while graduation rates held steady.
key_sources: Elaine M. Allensworth & Shazia Rafiullah Miller. (2002). Declining High School Enrollment: An Exploration of Causes. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/declining-high-school-enrollment-exploration-causes

article_title: Improving Chicago's Schools
citation: Luppescu, S., Hart, H., Nagaoka, J., Easton, J. Q., & Sweeney, R. E. (2001). Pablo Neruda High School: Improving Chicago's Schools, 2001 Survey Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Enhance teachers' knowledge and skills through coherent, sustained professional development as the leading school improvement initiative
description: The report holds that enhancing teachers' knowledge and skills is arguably the single most important initiative schools can undertake to improve student learning. It warns that in many schools professional development is happenstance, left to individual choice and not organized or supported by any coherent and sustained school improvement plan. Schools should therefore assess whether learning opportunities are in place so new instructional initiatives have a greater likelihood of being implemented well.
requirements: Professional development must be organized and supported by a coherent and sustained school improvement plan rather than left to individual choice
constraints: The report notes uncoordinated professional development is a negative measure on which low levels are more desirable
target_learners: Teachers in Chicago public schools
target_learning_goals: Improved instructional practice to enhance student learning
examples: The report provides measures of Access to New Ideas, Quality Professional Development, and Uncoordinated Professional Development so schools can assess whether learning opportunities are in place before improvement initiatives
key_sources: Luppescu, S., Hart, H., Nagaoka, J., Easton, J. Q., & Sweeney, R. E. (2001). Pablo Neruda High School: Improving Chicago's Schools, 2001 Survey Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/improving-chicagos-schools-pablo-neruda-high-school

article_title: Instruction and Achievement in Chicago Elementary Schools
citation: Julia B. Smith, Valerie E. Lee, and Fred M. Newmann. (2001). Instruction and Achievement in Chicago Elementary Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Promote interactive instruction through teacher preparation, collegial dialogue, and principal instructional leadership
description: Because interactive instruction was associated with greater learning gains while didactic instruction and review were associated with smaller gains, the report recommends building the conditions linked to interactive teaching. These include educating teachers in interactive methods through pre-service education and high-quality professional development, supporting collegial dialogue about practice, and encouraging principals to provide instructional leadership. The authors conclude that "Chicago students’ achievement could improve further if teachers across the school system were encouraged to achieve a better balance among their use of review, interactive teaching, and didactic teaching practices."
requirements: Teachers with advanced degrees, substantial coursework in their subject, or high-quality professional development; school organizational supports of innovation orientation, reflective dialogue, and instructional leadership
constraints: The associations are observational and controlled for student, classroom, and school characteristics; causal direction for some contextual links (e.g., problem behaviors) is acknowledged as complicated
target_learners: Elementary school students in grades 2-8 in urban districts
target_learning_goals: Reading and mathematics achievement gains on standardized assessments
examples: The study found teachers reporting high-quality professional development used interactive instruction most (.21 effect-size units), and schools with strong instructional leadership showed more interactive and less didactic instruction
key_sources: Julia B. Smith, Valerie E. Lee, and Fred M. Newmann. (2001). Instruction and Achievement in Chicago Elementary Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/instruction-and-achievement-chicago-elementary-schools

article_title: Authentic Intellectual Work and Standardized Tests
citation: Fred M. Newmann, Anthony S. Bryk, Jenny K. Nagaoka. (2001). Authentic Intellectual Work and Standardized Tests: Conflict or Coexistence? Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Organize instruction around authentic intellectual work rather than choosing between basic skills and ambitious intellectual work
description: The report argues that the debate posing basic-skills teaching against ambitious intellectual work "rests on a false dichotomy." Its evidence shows that "organizing instruction around challenging, authentic intellectual work can achieve both goals simultaneously": students produced more complex work and also achieved greater gains on standardized tests of basic skills. The principle directs teachers, administrators, and policymakers to emphasize authentic assignments without fearing basic-skills losses.
requirements: Assignments must meet the three AIW criteria: construction of knowledge, disciplined inquiry, and value beyond school
constraints: Evidence comes from writing and mathematics in grades 3, 6, and 8 of disadvantaged Chicago elementary schools; high-quality assignments were not commonplace in the Chicago Public Schools
target_learners: elementary students in grades 3, 6, and 8 in disadvantaged urban schools
target_learning_goals: basic skills in reading and mathematics alongside complex intellectual work
examples: The study linked scored writing and mathematics assignments from 19 Chicago elementary schools to ITBS and IGAP outcomes for almost 5,000 students, finding higher gains in high-quality-assignment classrooms
key_sources: Fred M. Newmann, Anthony S. Bryk, Jenny K. Nagaoka. (2001). Authentic Intellectual Work and Standardized Tests: Conflict or Coexistence? Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/authentic-intellectual-work-and-standardized-tests-conflict-or-coexistence

article_title: School Instructional Program Coherence
citation: Newmann, F. M., Smith, B., Allensworth, E., & Bryk, A. S. (2001). School Instructional Program Coherence: Benefits and Challenges. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Schoolwide coherence through a common literacy framework with sustained coaching support
description: Chelsea Elementary achieved strong instructional program coherence by implementing a schoolwide literacy framework based on Reading Recovery, with sustained investment in training and school-based literacy coordinators who coached teachers daily. At the time of the visit, 60 percent of teachers had taken a six-month intensive training course, and three full-time literacy coordinators visited classrooms regularly to observe, demonstrate, coach, and co-teach. An external partner staff person described it as "an 'in-your-face' approach."
requirements: Sustained investment in school-based coaching staff
All teachers, regardless of grade or assignment, working with the same framework
Leadership that persuades reluctant teachers to adopt the framework
constraints: The coherent vision of language arts instruction did not carry over into math, social studies, or science at Chelsea
target_learners: Elementary school students from working poor families in urban schools
target_learning_goals: Literacy development across all grades through common instructional practices and assessment
examples: Chelsea hired three full-time school-based literacy coordinators who offered after-school workshops, searched for materials, and visited classrooms regularly to observe, demonstrate, coach, and co-teach
key_sources: Newmann, F. M., Smith, B., Allensworth, E., & Bryk, A. S. (2001). School Instructional Program Coherence: Benefits and Challenges. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED

article_title: School Instructional Program Coherence
citation: Newmann, F. M., Smith, B., Allensworth, E., & Bryk, A. S. (2001). School Instructional Program Coherence: Benefits and Challenges. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Schoolwide coherence through coordinated adoption of a structured direct instruction program
description: Ackerman Elementary achieved the highest coherence ratings among the 11 field study schools by adopting a Direct Instruction program providing scripted lessons and matching assessments in mathematics and reading for grades one through six, supplemented by grade-level literacy leaders and classroom libraries. Teachers met in within-grade and across-grade teams, often twice weekly, to coordinate curriculum, instruction, and assessment. The report notes "The fully articulated instruction and assessment scheme provided by the Direct Instruction program, along with schoolwide implementation of the literacy/library supplement, were leading reasons for Ackerman's high rating on instructional program coherence."
requirements: A fully articulated instructional and assessment scheme
Ongoing whole-school staff development for implementing the program
Grade-level literacy leaders to support peers
constraints: Not every school would agree with Ackerman's decisions to adopt Direct Instruction and to focus its program so much on improved test scores
target_learners: Elementary school students in grades one through six in high-poverty urban schools
target_learning_goals: Raising reading and mathematics achievement through a common scripted instructional framework
examples: Ackerman staff decided after discussion to use Direct Instruction for grades one through six, and funded one teacher per grade as a literacy leader to assist peers with classroom libraries
key_sources: Newmann, F. M., Smith, B., Allensworth, E., & Bryk, A. S. (2001). School Instructional Program Coherence: Benefits and Challenges. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED

article_title: Annual CPS Trend Review, 2000
citation: John Q. Easton, Todd Rosenkranz, Anthony S. Bryk. (2001). Annual CPS Test Trend Review, 2000: Elementary School Test Score Trends in Chicago Public Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. http://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Report test score trends by age groupings rather than grade groupings to keep the comparison group constant when retention policies change
description: This data brief diverges from official CPS reporting by grouping students by age rather than grade, because large-scale grade retention changes grade composition over time and can inflate higher-grade scores. The authors state they "report student scores by age groupings rather than grade groupings" to distinguish retention effects from changing test score trends, keeping the comparison group constant across years.
requirements: Age must be defined consistently with school entry requirements, as the brief does by assigning students to age groups by birthday within the academic year.
constraints: The brief applies this specifically in the context of CPS retention policies beginning in fall 1997, primarily in grades three, six, and eight.
target_learners: Elementary school students in grades 3-8
target_learning_goals: Accurate system-level monitoring of academic achievement trends
examples: The brief shows fifth-grade trend interpretation became unreliable as retained third graders moved through grades, motivating the age-based grouping.
key_sources: John Q. Easton, Todd Rosenkranz, Anthony S. Bryk. (2001). Annual CPS Test Trend Review, 2000: Elementary School Test Score Trends in Chicago Public Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/annual-cps-trend-review-2000

article_title: Annual CPS Trend Review, 2000
citation: John Q. Easton, Todd Rosenkranz, Anthony S. Bryk. (2001). Annual CPS Test Trend Review, 2000: Elementary School Test Score Trends in Chicago Public Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. http://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Use mean grade equivalent scores rather than percent-at-or-above-norms indicators when reporting systemwide test trends
description: The brief argues the mean is the most sensible single statistic for reporting test score trends because it is sensitive to the performance of all included students. It states that other indicators, such as percent at or above national norms, median percentile, or median grade equivalent, "can be strongly influenced by the performance of relatively small subgroups of students."
requirements: A common inclusion standard applied consistently over the entire trend period, as the brief sets for bilingual education students.
constraints: The brief notes grade equivalents can be very sensitive to test level differences, so it re-analyzed trends using equated Rasch scores as a check.
target_learners: Elementary school students in grades 3-8
target_learning_goals: Accurate system-level monitoring of academic achievement trends
examples: The brief reports mean ITBS grade equivalent scores by age group and race/ethnicity in Tables C and D for 1992 through 2000.
key_sources: John Q. Easton, Todd Rosenkranz, Anthony S. Bryk. (2001). Annual CPS Test Trend Review, 2000: Elementary School Test Score Trends in Chicago Public Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/annual-cps-trend-review-2000

article_title: Trust in Schools
citation: Bryk, A. S. and Schneider, B. (1988). Trust in Schools: A Core Resource for Improvement. https://www.amazon.com
title: Build and sustain a broad base of trust across a school community as a critical resource when embarking on major school reform
description: The principle follows from the book's central finding: relational trust should be treated as a core resource for improvement, not an intangible afterthought. Bryk and Schneider "show how a broad base of trust across a school community can provide a critical resource as education professional and parents embark on major school reforms," and the book "offer insights into how trust can be built and sustained in school communities." It also "identifies some features of public school systems that can impede such development," so reformers should attend to those impediments while cultivating trust.
requirements: Requires attention to the social exchanges of daily school life that generate or fail to generate trust
constraints: Features of public school systems can impede the development of trust, as the book identifies
target_learners: Elementary school students
target_learning_goals: Successful implementation of school reform and improved student learning
examples: In the 12 Chicago elementary schools studied, high-trust schools saw educators experiment with new practices and work with parents, alongside marked gains in student learning.
key_sources: Bryk, A. S. and Schneider, B. (1988). Trust in Schools: A Core Resource for Improvement. https://www.amazon.com

article_title: Chicago Classroom Demands for Authentic Intellectual Work
citation: Anthony S. Bryk, Jenny K. Nagaoka, and Fred M. Newmann. (2000). Chicago Classroom Demands for Authentic Intellectual Work: Trends from 1997-1999. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Analyze actual classroom assignments as a direct complement to standardized test scores when judging instructional improvement
description: Because high-stakes test score trends can improve for reasons unrelated to instruction, this report argues that collecting and scoring the assignments teachers give daily offers a direct window into instructional quality. As the authors put it, "These assignments—what teachers ask stu- dents to do on a day-to-day basis—are direct indica- tors of the quality of instruction." The principle was implemented by gathering typical and challenging writing and math assignments annually and scoring them against authenticity rubrics.
requirements: Teachers must submit both typical and challenging assignments, and a rubric-based scoring process with rater-bias adjustment is needed to produce comparable measures
constraints: Changes in the sample of schools over time and variable amounts of data from different teachers required statistical modeling to estimate trends
target_learners: elementary school students in grades three, six, and eight in urban public schools
target_learning_goals: quality of instruction in writing and mathematics
examples: The project collected 349 assignments from 74 teachers in 1997, 953 assignments from 116 teachers in 1998, and 715 assignments from 87 teachers in 1999, scoring them with many-facet Rasch measurement.
key_sources: Anthony S. Bryk, Jenny K. Nagaoka, and Fred M. Newmann. (2000). Chicago Classroom Demands for Authentic Intellectual Work: Trends from 1997-1999. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/chicago-classroom-demands-authentic-intellectual-work-trends-1997-1999

article_title: School Leadership and the Bottom Line in Chicago
citation: Penny Bender Sebring and Anthony S. Bryk. (2000). School Leadership and the Bottom Line in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research. http://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Four leadership-style characteristics of principals in productive Chicago elementary schools
description: The article enumerates a recurring pattern of leadership-style characteristics shared by principals of improving schools: an inclusive, facilitative orientation in which principals articulate a "vision-in-outline" and invite teachers and parents to elaborate it; an institutional focus on student learning; efficient management; and the use of support and pressure to catalyze initiatives. As printed, "Principals in productive schools set high standards for teaching, understand how children learn, and encourage teachers to take risks and try new methods of teaching." Regular classroom visits demonstrate conviction and give principals a pulse on instruction, and efficient management ensures teachers have needed materials and students receive support services so disruptions are minimized.
requirements: Change requires the commitment, talent, and energy of many, so principals bring parents, teachers, and other staff into leadership positions
target_learners: Elementary school teachers and students in improving Chicago schools
target_learning_goals: Improved quality of teaching and student learning opportunities
examples: Principals make regular visits to classrooms and secure academic and social support services for students in need
key_sources: Penny Bender Sebring and Anthony S. Bryk. (2000). School Leadership and the Bottom Line in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/school-leadership-and-bottom-line-chicago

article_title: The Chicago Annenberg Challenge
citation: Dorothy Shipps, Karin Sconzert, with Holly Swyers. (1999). The Chicago Annenberg Challenge: The First Three Years. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Network structure: clusters of at least three like-minded schools aided by an external partner, restructuring time, size, and isolation
description: The Chicago Annenberg Challenge's core design pattern required schools to apply not individually but in networks—clusters of at least three like-minded schools aided by an external partner—to enhance collaboration and community support. Grantees were asked to focus on how they might "alter the basic elements of time, size, and isolation": reorganizing the school day, creating smaller personalized environments, and connecting educators to the communities they serve. External partners were intended to provide community resources, develop the pool of assisting organizations, and build adult leadership at schools.
requirements: At least three schools per cluster; an external partner for each network; a rich invitational application process
constraints: Funds were stipulated not to go to the CPS central administration; the pattern was grounded in the 1988 decentralization context
target_learners: students and educators in Chicago Public Schools network schools
target_learning_goals: school restructuring to improve students' opportunities to learn through collaboration and community support
examples: The Working Group's proposal required implementation-grant clusters of at least three schools with external partners, and first-year grantees were selected largely from existing school-partner collaborations
key_sources: Dorothy Shipps, Karin Sconzert, with Holly Swyers. (1999). The Chicago Annenberg Challenge: The First Three Years. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/chicago-annenberg-challenge-first-three-years

article_title: The Chicago Annenberg Challenge
citation: Dorothy Shipps, Karin Sconzert, with Holly Swyers. (1999). The Chicago Annenberg Challenge: The First Three Years. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Privately funded reform organizations must build a distinct identity and locally rooted legitimacy to influence public schooling
description: The report distills the Challenge's dilemmas into three overlapping influence requirements: identity, legitimacy, and legacy. To be influential, it argues, a reform organization "must distinguish its vision of school change in clear terms that permit it to have a meaningful identity in a crowded field of organizational change agents," and must "develop resource ties and cultural and political support from among the existing institutions in the city so that it develops its own locally rooted organizational legitimacy." The report warns that seeking legitimacy risks stretching the organization's theory of action beyond current plans.
requirements: A clear, distinct vision of school change; resource ties and cultural and political support from existing local institutions
constraints: Pursuing local legitimacy risks compromising the founding theory of action by stretching beyond current plans; strategic flexibility is constrained by early grant decisions and a changing institutional environment
target_learners: civic, business, political, and education leaders shaping urban school reform
target_learning_goals: building organizational influence for large-scale, privately funded school improvement
examples: The report concludes that the Challenge's pursuit of policy influence while remaining faithful to its initial vision may restrain its long-term reform legacy to one less deep and thorough than hoped
key_sources: Dorothy Shipps, Karin Sconzert, with Holly Swyers. (1999). The Chicago Annenberg Challenge: The First Three Years. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/chicago-annenberg-challenge-first-three-years

article_title: It's About Time
citation: BetsAnn Smith. (1998). It's About Time: Opportunities to Learn in Chicago's Elementary Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research.
title: Nest a full 300-minute instructional program within a school day of 360-400 minutes
description: The report argues that instructional time policy must build in realistic room for the human and operational demands of elementary classrooms rather than a maximally compressed schedule. Its observations showed schools operating "a highly compressed schedule" in which non-instructional demands spill into officially allotted instruction time. It concludes that a 300-minutes-a-day instructional program must be nested within a school day of 360-400 minutes, depending on lunch organization and whether recess is restored.
requirements: School day length must be extended beyond the current 330-minute closed campus schedule to absorb operational demands without eroding instruction.
constraints: The report notes Chicago's largely disadvantaged schools are asked to make achievement gains in less time than more advantaged surrounding systems; new charter schools chose 60-90 minutes longer days.
target_learners: Chicago Public Schools elementary students
target_learning_goals: Increasing delivered instructional time across the full academic program
examples: The report observes that most new Chicago charter schools chose to operate 60 to 90 minutes longer each day than the standard CPS school day.
key_sources: BetsAnn Smith. (1998). It's About Time: Opportunities to Learn in Chicago's Elementary Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/its-about-time-opportunities-learn

article_title: Adjusting Citywide ITBS Scores for Student Retention in Grades Three, Six, and Eight
citation: John Q. Easton, Brian Jacob, Stuart Luppescu, Melissa Roderick. (1998). Adjusting Citywide ITBS Scores for Student Retention in Grades Three, Six, and Eight. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Use the mean grade equivalent, not the median or percent at norms, when examining achievement score trends over time
description: The article argues that the mean (arithmetic average) is superior for examining trends because it takes into account the performance of all students, whereas the median is most influenced by students right at the middle of the distribution and percent at or above grade level by students closest to the national average. The brief reports mean grade equivalents in Figures 1-12 while also calculating percent at or above grade level in Figure 15 for comparability with CPS reports.
requirements: Access to full score distributions so means can be computed, rather than only medians or cutoff percentages
constraints: The article acknowledges the other statistics can provide useful information about the school system; the choice is specific to examining trends and changes over time
target_learners: all tested students in a public school district
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of systemwide achievement trends
examples: The brief reports mean grade equivalents by grade for 1990-1998 with 1998 adjusted values (Figure 13), and shows in Figure 15 that the percent-at-norms results are similar to the mean-based results
key_sources: John Q. Easton, Brian Jacob, Stuart Luppescu, Melissa Roderick. (1998). Adjusting Citywide ITBS Scores for Student Retention in Grades Three, Six, and Eight. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/adjusting-citywide-itbs-scores-student-retention-grades-three-six-and-eight

article_title: The Quality of Intellectual Work in Chicago Schools
citation: Newmann, F. M., Lopez, G., & Bryk, A. S. (1998). The Quality of Intellectual Work in Chicago Schools: A Baseline Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research.
title: Apply authentic intellectual work standards across almost any content at any grade level to bridge curricular disagreements
description: The report argues that because the standards define the nature of intellectual work needed for vocation, citizenship, and personal life rather than specific content, they provide a common intellectual mission across disciplines. It states that "one virtue of the standards for authentic intellectual work is that they can be applied to the teaching of almost any content at any grade level," bridging otherwise divisive preferences about what to teach.
requirements: Scoring against grade-level expectations and trained scorers using the developed rubrics
constraints: The standards deliberately avoid prescribing precise curriculum content, which the report notes remains contested among schools, districts, states, and professional organizations
target_learners: students at any grade level, illustrated here in grades three, six, and eight
target_learning_goals: authentic intellectual work across writing and mathematics content
examples: The report applied the same standards to score writing and mathematics assignments and student work in grades three, six, and eight in 12 Chicago schools
key_sources: Newmann, F. M., Lopez, G., & Bryk, A. S. (1998). The Quality of Intellectual Work in Chicago Schools: A Baseline Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/quality-intellectual-work-chicago-schools-baseline-report

article_title: Changing Standards, Changing Relationships
citation: Roderick, M., Stone, S., with Arney, M., Chiong, J., DaCosta, K., & Waxman, E. (1998). Changing Standards, Changing Relationships: Building Family-School Relationships to Promote Achievement in High Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/publications/changing-standards-changing-relationships-building-family-school-relationships-promote
title: Increasing parental involvement in high schools requires changing teachers' and schools' outreach practices, not just expecting parents to engage
description: The brief argues that raising parental involvement at the high school level must begin with changes in what high schools and teachers do: communicating about academic goals, giving parents direction for supporting learning, and making schools more inviting. It finds that "High schools have discouraged parent involvement by being less inviting to parents and by making it harder for parents to get information and resources." Schools that improved instruction also improved parent relationships, supporting a dual-focus approach.
requirements: High school teachers and administrators must see working with parents as part of their role
constraints: High schools face structural barriers including larger workloads, fewer informal contact opportunities, and in Hispanic-serving schools, language barriers and overcrowding
target_learners: high school students, particularly ninth graders
target_learning_goals: academic achievement through increased home support and monitoring of schoolwork
examples: Fenger High School adopted family math nights, parent orientations, a parent advisory council, a paid parent aide, and informal family social nights to open communication and build parent skills
Roosevelt High School's Parent Center combined monthly workshops in Spanish and English, volunteer coordination, and individualized family counseling services
key_sources: Roderick, M., Stone, S., with Arney, M., Chiong, J., DaCosta, K., & Waxman, E. (1998). Changing Standards, Changing Relationships: Building Family-School Relationships to Promote Achievement in High Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/publications/changing-standards-changing-relationships-building-family-school-relationships-promote

article_title: Academic Productivity of Chicago Public Elementary Schools
citation: Anthony S. Bryk, Yeow Meng Thum, John Q. Easton, Stuart Luppescu. (1998). Mining Productivity: How to Read Your Productivity Profile. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Group grade-level profiles into primary, intermediate, and upper-grade summaries so accountability promotes cooperative improvement across grade levels
description: Because adjacent-grade profiles are negatively related and single-grade judgments mislead, the guide recommends grouping two or three grades together for accountability analyses. It argues "a good accountability system should promote cooperative improvement efforts among faculty across grade levels," creating incentives for teachers to work cooperatively. Chicago elementary schools' K-8 structure supports summaries of primary (grades two to four), intermediate (five and six), and upper (seven and eight) grades.
requirements: Sufficient matched two-year data within each grade grouping to report the summary
constraints: Summary labels are based on the output trend of the final grade in the grouping and the average gain trends of the grades in the grouping
target_learners: Students in Chicago public elementary schools, kindergarten through grade eight
target_learning_goals: School-level improvement in reading and mathematics achievement
examples: The guide reports Primary Grades Summary (grades two, three, and four), Intermediate Grades Summary (grades five and six), and Upper Grades Summary (grades seven and eight) where information suffices
key_sources: Anthony S. Bryk, Yeow Meng Thum, John Q. Easton, Stuart Luppescu. (1998). Mining Productivity: How to Read Your Productivity Profile. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: Charting Reform
citation: Susan Ryan, Anthony S. Bryk, Gudelia Lopez, Kimberley P. Williams, Kathleen Hall, Stuart Luppescu. (1997). Charting Reform: LSCs - Local Leadership at Work. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Require and expand training for all incoming Local School Council members
description: The report endorses mandatory, expanded training for incoming council members, finding that even under voluntary training most members received preparation in core areas yet a substantial minority felt underprepared. The authors write that the 1995 legislative provision to expand training "and require it for all incoming LSC members seems well-founded," because 40 percent reported not receiving enough preparation to do their job well. Training is most useful when tailored to the particular council, as principal-provided training was.
requirements: Training must cover essential areas: LSC roles and responsibilities, principal evaluation, the School Improvement Plan, and the school budget.
constraints: The article notes less common training topics included analyzing achievement data, good educational practices, and school and community partnerships.
target_learners: parent and community members serving on Local School Councils
target_learning_goals: governing a local school: principal evaluation, school improvement planning, and budget oversight
examples: The survey found most members received training from the principal, school reform groups, and the Board of Education, with principal-delivered training rated most useful.
key_sources: Susan Ryan, Anthony S. Bryk, Gudelia Lopez, Kimberley P. Williams, Kathleen Hall, Stuart Luppescu. (1997). Charting Reform: LSCs - Local Leadership at Work. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/charting-reform-lscs%E2%80%94local-leadership-work

article_title: School Reform, Retention Policy, and Student Achievement Gains
citation: Stuart Luppescu, Anthony S. Bryk, Paul Deabster, John Q. Easton, and Yeow Meng Thum. (1995). School Reform, Retention Policy, and Student Achievement Gains. University of Chicago draft report.
title: Do not rely on grade retention to help lagging students catch up, since promoted comparable students make larger gains
description: The article concludes that if retention's purpose is to let lagging students catch up, its results indicate the opposite effect: promoted students out-gain comparable retained students, so retention leaves students falling further behind. This is the authors' policy conclusion drawn from their matched propensity comparisons of achievement gains in Chicago elementary schools.
requirements: Comparisons should match retained and promoted students on a propensity for retention so the groups are comparable
constraints: The finding comes from one district's 1987-1992 data, with third grade a notable exception and the gain difference averaging about one-quarter of a logit
target_learners: Elementary students at risk of grade retention
target_learning_goals: Improving annual achievement gains in reading and mathematics
examples: The study compared gains of retained versus promoted students within cohorts (diagonal comparisons) and of first-time versus repeating grade-takers (vertical comparisons), finding promoted students ahead in almost all cases
key_sources: Stuart Luppescu, Anthony S. Bryk, Paul Deabster, John Q. Easton, and Yeow Meng Thum. (1995). School Reform, Retention Policy, and Student Achievement Gains. University of Chicago draft report. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/school-reform-retention-policy-and-student-achievement-gains

article_title: Charting Reform in Asbury School
citation: Sebring, P. A., Bryk, A. S., Luppescu, S., & Thum, Y. M. (1995). Charting Reform in Asbury High School: Results of Student and Teacher Surveys. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: School report pattern: summary profiles plus detailed scale distributions with quartile benchmarks
description: Each school report has two parts: Part I gives five profile graphs summarizing each essential support, allowing a school to compare itself with all participating schools and alerting it to possible strengths and weaknesses; Part II details how students and teachers responded to each contributing scale. Each scale section shows item endorsement percentages, an interpretation table mapping scale scores to qualitative descriptions, and bar charts comparing the school's score distribution with top- and bottom-quartile schools.
requirements: A separate guide on how to read the report and familiarity with the Self-Analysis Guide are recommended before beginning the analysis.
constraints: The report is intended to assist schools in assessing strengths and weaknesses and improvement efforts, not to prescribe actions.
target_learners: school staff and Local School Council members conducting self-analysis
target_learning_goals: school self-assessment and improvement planning
examples: The LSC Contribution section reports that in bottom-quartile schools about 35 percent of teachers see a limited contribution and 40 percent no contribution, while in top-quartile schools a little over half judge the LSC has made significant contributions.
key_sources: Sebring, P. A., Bryk, A. S., Luppescu, S., & Thum, Y. M. (1995). Charting Reform in Asbury High School: Results of Student and Teacher Surveys. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/charting-reform-asbury-school-results-student-and-teacher-surveys

article_title: Charting Reform in Prairie School
citation: Sebring, P. A., Bryk, A. S., Luppescu, S., & Thum, Y. M. (1995). Charting Reform in Prairie School: Results of Student and Teacher Surveys. Consortium on Chicago School Research.
title: School report pattern: summary profiles plus detailed scale distributions benchmarked against similar and quartile schools
description: The report follows a two-part design: Part I gives five profile graphs, one per essential support, offering a quick comparison of the school with all participating schools and with similar schools matched on IGAP scores and school size; Part II details each scale with item-level endorsement percentages, an interpretation table for scale scores, and distributions comparing the school with top and bottom quartile schools. This design is intended to alert schools to possible strengths and weaknesses and guide deeper examination.
requirements: Comparison groups of schools similar with respect to IGAP scores and school size, and sufficient respondent counts per scale
constraints: The report advises reading a separate guide on how to read the report and the Self-Analysis Guide before beginning analysis
target_learners: school staff and Local School Council members conducting school self-analysis
target_learning_goals: diagnosing school strengths and weaknesses to guide improvement efforts
examples: The report suggests staff study Part I summary profiles while assigning Part II subsections such as Parent Community Partnerships to smaller groups with specialized interest.
key_sources: Sebring, P. A., Bryk, A. S., Luppescu, S., & Thum, Y. M. (1995). Charting Reform in Prairie School: Results of Student and Teacher Surveys. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/charting-reform-prairie-school-results-student-and-teacher-surveys

article_title: A View from the Elementary Schools
citation: Bryk, A. S., Easton, J. Q., Kerbow, D., Rollow, S. G., & Sebring, P. A. (1993). A View from the Elementary Schools: The State of Reform in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research.
title: Judge urban school reform mid-course by organizational direction, not short-term achievement trends
description: The report argues that a mid-course assessment of a systemic urban reform should examine whether ongoing organizational rearrangements are occurring and whether new arrangements operate as planned, rather than judging by short-term test-score changes. It reasons that "short-term profits might plummet as losses are incurred in the process of reshaping the basic mission and operating procedures," and that even the best cases of significant individual school improvement often required five or more years to culminate in comprehensive restructuring.
requirements: An assessment framework organized around the reform's own theory of change, in this case enhanced participation as a lever for improvement
constraints: The report explicitly rejects the legislation's 1994 national-norms timetable as not defensible for a system of over 400,000 students and 25,000 teachers
target_learners: Students in large urban school systems undergoing systemic reform
target_learning_goals: Improving student learning through governance restructuring and instructional improvement
examples: The report redirects its evaluative questions toward how new governance structures function, what types of improvement efforts are underway, and whether participation provides an effective lever for improvement
key_sources: Bryk, A. S., Easton, J. Q., Kerbow, D., Rollow, S. G., & Sebring, P. A. (1993). A View from the Elementary Schools: The State of Reform in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/view-elementary-schools-state-reform-chicago

article_title: Achieving School Reform in Chicago
citation: Consortium on Chicago School Research. (1991). Achieving School Reform in Chicago: What We Need To Know — A Research Agenda. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Research serving school reform must address multiple audiences and function as community education
description: The Consortium grounds its agenda in the conviction that a responsive research agenda must address public officials, school-based decision makers, and citizens broadly, since important decision making now occurs in individual school communities. It argues that the most effective research does not simply support administrative control but helps identify new concerns and offers concepts for discussing problem situations. Research reporting should therefore encourage a broad-based public conversation about educational issues.
requirements: Information must meet the quality test of deepening understanding and stimulating discourse about the aims and means of education
constraints: Good research is a slow and difficult process, so an infrastructure must be created in advance of the questions that will arise
target_learners: citizens of Chicago, public officials, principals, teachers, parents, and community members
target_learning_goals: public understanding of school reform progress and educational improvement
examples: The Consortium adopts a pluralistic policy, seeking open access to information and the ability of diverse groups to act on that information
key_sources: Consortium on Chicago School Research. (1991). Achieving School Reform in Chicago: What We Need To Know — A Research Agenda. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/achieving-school-reform-chicago-what-we-need-know

article_title: Achieving School Reform in Chicago
citation: Consortium on Chicago School Research. (1991). Achieving School Reform in Chicago: What We Need To Know — A Research Agenda. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Assessment should move beyond standardized tests toward authentic measures such as portfolios and projects
description: Stakeholders in the consultation process expressed dissatisfaction with the ITBS as too narrow and voiced widespread interest in new measures of student performance that move beyond paper-and-pencil standardized tests. The report recommends investigating authentic measures such as portfolios and projects, linked to clearly articulated objectives, warning that without such progress Chicago will be left with a minimalist accounting system. The Consortium recommends immediate and sustained attention to revamping testing and assessment.
requirements: Assessment must be linked to a clearly articulated set of objectives establishing what an individual should know and be able to do
constraints: Testing is mired in controversies about purpose, validity and reliability of measurement, test security, cost, and information use and abuse, which must be confronted for adequate measures of learning
target_learners: Chicago Public Schools students in grades one through twelve
target_learning_goals: measuring higher order thinking skills, problem solving, and communication alongside basic skills
examples: The Chicago Teachers' Union advocated abandoning standardized testing for primary grades and encouraging instructionally focused processes such as portfolios and instruments allowing creative thinking and expression
key_sources: Consortium on Chicago School Research. (1991). Achieving School Reform in Chicago: What We Need To Know — A Research Agenda. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/achieving-school-reform-chicago-what-we-need-know

article_title: Data for Improvement and Data for Accountability: Considerations for State Boards
citation: Title as printed: Overview, State Education Standard. (2024). The Journal of the National Association of State Boards of Education. https://www.nasbe.org/the-state-education-standard/
title: Treat malleability and predictive validity as non-negotiable criteria when selecting accountability indicators
description: The article argues that when states choose indicators for accountability systems, malleability and predictive validity should function as "non-negotiable criteria". An indicator should be something schools can genuinely influence within an improvement cycle and should predict meaningful student outcomes. The article directs this principle at state boards of education evaluating proposed indicators.
requirements: State boards should seek evidence of both malleability and predictive power for any proposed indicator before adopting it.
constraints: The article warns that bringing school-level improvement data into public accountability frameworks carries risks, since pressure to perform can suppress honest inquiry and incentivize superficial fixes.
target_learners: K-12 students in states designing accountability systems
target_learning_goals: Selection of accountability and improvement indicators that support genuine school improvement
examples: The article describes examining how malleability and predictive validity should serve as criteria when selecting accountability indicators.
key_sources: Title as printed: Overview, State Education Standard. (2024). The Journal of the National Association of State Boards of Education. https://www.nasbe.org/the-state-education-standard/

article_title: Research Agenda 2026–30
citation: Porter, S., Ramirez Richter, R., de la Torre, M., & Allensworth, E.M. (2026). Research and Engagement for Systems Transformation: Building Knowledge, Capacity, and Coherence for Equitable Education Systems. UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Democratize data and elevate community expertise through a distributed model of inquiry
description: The agenda commits to making data and research accessible to everyone through "a distributed model of inquiry—one that supports shared questioning, interpretation, and meaning-making across researchers, practitioners, families, and students." It works through accessible tools, synthesis, and engagement so evidence strengthens collective understanding and local capacity, treating data use as something communities participate in rather than receive. This principle underlies initiatives such as Evidence to Action, which convenes parent and community leaders to engage with rigorous evidence and their own lived expertise.
requirements: Accessible tools, synthesis, and engagement structures that support shared questioning and interpretation across researchers, practitioners, families, and students
constraints: The document notes limited tools and practices currently exist for democratizing data and research use
target_learners: Students and families in urban public school systems, particularly historically underserved communities
target_learning_goals: Building local capacity to interpret and act on school and student data
examples: The Evidence to Action initiative brings together Local School Council members, Bilingual Advisory Committees, Community Action Councils, Parent Advisory Councils, and elected school board members to make meaning of school improvement data.
key_sources: Porter, S., Ramirez Richter, R., de la Torre, M., & Allensworth, E.M. (2026). Research and Engagement for Systems Transformation: Building Knowledge, Capacity, and Coherence for Equitable Education Systems. UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: Co-Designing New Approaches to School Safety
citation: Johnson, D.W. (2026). Co-designing new approaches to school safety: District and community perspectives on Chicago's Whole School Safety Framework. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Four key features of the WSS co-design model: inclusive design, restorative orientation, addressing institutional harm, and demonstrated possibility
description: The interpretive summary distills the co-design process into four key features participants highlighted as it evolved into a template for future efforts. "Inclusive design: The process intentionally centered diverse perspectives—students, families, community members, and district staff—in shaping policy." The restorative orientation was grounded in "relationship-building, trust, and reciprocal accountability," and the process was seen as evidence that authentic collaboration is feasible and replicable in other contexts.
requirements: Sustained participatory structures such as a steering committee including district staff and community-based organizations with their constituencies
constraints: The article notes sustaining this degree of partnership amid leadership turnover at CPS and the CBOE is a defining challenge as WSS scales from framework to policy to practice
target_learners: district officials
community-based organization leaders
students and families in school communities
target_learning_goals: community-engaged policymaking
equity-focused collaboration
school safety planning
examples: Between December 2020 and January 2021, CPS and CBO leaders co-designed common questions for CBO-led public meetings held in February 2021, then synthesized learnings into consensus recommendations shared with the CBOE on March 24, 2021
key_sources: Johnson, D.W. (2026). Co-designing new approaches to school safety: District and community perspectives on Chicago's Whole School Safety Framework. article_title: Parent Advisory Councils
citation: Building Better Parent Councils: A Research Brief. (2024). National Center for Families Learning. https://www.familieslearning.org
title: Clearly define parent council roles and decision-making authority to engage and satisfy members
description: The brief recommends that sponsoring organizations co-design a shared understanding of a parent council's purpose among parents, educators, and administrators before the council operates. informed contribution to school decision-making

article_title: Parent Advisory Councils
citation: Building Better Parent Councils: A Research Brief. (2024). National Center for Families Learning. https://www.familieslearning.org
title: Shift from top-down leadership to collaborative family engagement to empower parent councils

Professional development on consensus-building and shared decision-making is offered as the supporting mechanism for leaders.

school administrators
family-facing practitioners

consensus-building
empowering families in school operations

article_title: Parent Advisory Councils
citation: Building Better Parent Councils: A Research Brief. (2024). National Center for Families Learning. https://www.familieslearning.org
title: Set a shared vision with attainable goals and track progress to sustain council engagement
description: The brief recommends that parent councils orient their work around collectively developed aims tied to real school and community needs. Attainable goals addressing key school and community issues
Progress tracking and celebration of successes

school and community stakeholders

sustained engagement in school improvement

article_title: Using Data to Improve Schools
citation: Elaine Allensworth. (2025). Using Data to Improve Schools. Corwin. https://www.corwin.com
title: Focus improvement effort on high-impact metrics rather than overwhelming or irrelevant data
description: The article argues that educators are often "inundated with data that feels overwhelming, irrelevant, or unhelpful" and that improvement efforts should instead concentrate on identifying high-impact metrics. It states that schools can improve key performance areas by identifying such metrics and fostering a collaborative culture of improvement, countering common myths and assumptions that divert attention from the data that matter most.

constraints: Common myths and assumptions can divert attention from the data that matter most, per the article

target_learning_goals: improving attendance, test scores, and graduation rates through data-informed improvement

article_title: How Did Chicago Connected Broadband Access Affect Remote Learning During COVID-19?
citation: Schachner, J.N., Marwell, N.P., de la Torre, M., Gwynne, J.A., & Allensworth, E.M. (2025). How did Chicago Connected broadband access eligibility and participation affect remote learning engagement and achievement during the COVID-19 pandemic? Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai25-1153

article_title: Kindergarten Redshirting: What Families Should Know
citation: Kindergarten redshirting: What families should know. (2026). NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/should-kindergartners-be-redshirted-costs-likely-outweigh-academic-benefits/
title: Advise against redshirting for most children, reserving it for children with significant developmental delays or major behavioral or emotional regulation struggles
description: The fact sheet's guidance for families weighing redshirting is that "For most children, the answer is likely no," while identifying a narrower group more likely to benefit. It names two exception groups: children with significant developmental delays and children who majorly struggle with behavioral or emotional regulation. The recommendation rests on the balance of short-lived academic benefits against costs such as childcare expense, dropout risk, and earnings effects.

constraints: The fact sheet states the recommendation applies to most children and identifies exceptions rather than a universal rule

target_learning_goals: kindergarten readiness and school entry timing decisions
examples: The fact sheet lists children with significant developmental delays and children who majorly struggle with behavioral or emotional regulation as more likely to benefit from redshirting

article_title: The Development of Racial/Ethnic and Socioeconomic Achievement Gaps During the School Years
citation: Megan Kuhfeld, Elizabeth Gershoff, Katherine Paschall. (2018). The development of racial/ethnic and socioeconomic achievement gaps during the school years. Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology 57, 62-73. https://www.journals.elsevier.com/journal-of-applied-developmental-psychology
title: Study race and poverty in interaction when measuring achievement gaps
description: The article concludes that achievement-gap measurement should treat race/ethnicity and poverty jointly rather than separately, because their association with math and reading achievement varies together across development. The results "highlight the importance of studying race and poverty in interaction when measuring achievement gaps." The authors support this with TVEM estimates showing that gaps among poverty groups differ by race/ethnicity and widen at specific ages.
requirements: Longitudinal achievement data spanning school entry through middle school, analyzed with a method such as TVEM that estimates associations across continuous age
constraints: Findings are based on two large longitudinal data sets covering ages 5 to 15 in math and reading achievement; the abstract does not report effects outside this range or domain
target_learners: students from age 5 to age 15 in U.S. schools
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
reading achievement
examples: The study modeled developmental trends in achievement gaps between poverty and race/ethnicity groups from school entry to middle school using two large longitudinal data sets

Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology 57, 62-73. https://www.journals.elsevier.com/journal-of-applied-developmental-psychology

article_title: Seven Successful Strategies for Literate Assessment
citation: Beth Tarasawa, Amelia Wenk Gotwals, Cara Jackson. (2018). Seven successful strategies for literate assessment. Principal Leadership 18. https://www.nwea.org/research/publications/

use of assessment data in classroom planning

article_title: Longitudinal Models of Reading and Mathematics Achievement in Deaf and Hard of Hearing Students
citation: Stephanie Cawthon, Johny Daniel, North Cooc, Ana Vielma. (2022). Longitudinal models of reading and mathematics achievement in deaf and hard of hearing students. The Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education. https://doi.org/10.1093/deafed/enac033
title: Use longitudinal data analysis to understand how DHH students' achievement progresses over time and where they need additional support
description: This principle holds that educators and researchers should use longitudinal data analysis to track how academic achievement for DHH students progresses over time. The article argues that "Longitudinal data analysis is critical to understanding how academic achievement for DHH students progresses over time and where they may need additional support on their academic journey to achieve at the level of their hearing peers." Achieving at the level of hearing peers

article_title: Understanding the Initial Educational Impacts of COVID-19 on Communities of Color
citation: Megan Kuhfeld, Erik Ruzek, Karyn Lewis, Jim Soland, Angela Johnson, Beth Tarasawa, & Lindsay Dworkin. (2021). Understanding the initial educational impacts of COVID-19 on communities of color. NWEA Research Report. https://www.nwea.org
title: Analyze achievement equity without centering whiteness as the default comparison standard
description: The report's authors, in line with Critical Race and Critical Whiteness Theorists, explicitly chose to exclude White students from their analyses to avoid centering whiteness as the default academic standard, instead comparing BIPOC students' pandemic-era performance to same-race/ethnicity students' pre-pandemic performance. They also acknowledge the risk that enumerating inequities adopts a deficit-based perspective that perpetuates a victim-blaming orientation, and state that focus should be on dominant power systems rather than fixing BIPOC students.
requirements: Comparisons must be framed against same-race/ethnicity pre-pandemic baselines rather than against White students as the reference group
constraints: The authors note this descriptive framing does not by itself explain why gains were lower; their data cannot speak to why academic gains were lower during the pandemic
target_learners: Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC) students
target_learning_goals: Equitable interpretation and monitoring of academic achievement and growth
examples: The report adopted the gender-neutral term Latinx and compared students to same race/ethnic peers before and after the pandemic rather than to White students

article_title: Examining the State-Trait Composition of Social-Emotional Learning Constructs: Implications for Practice, Policy, and Evaluation
citation: James Soland, Megan Kuhfeld, Emily Wolk, Sharon Bi. (2019). Examining the state-trait composition of social-emotional learning constructs: Implications for practice, policy, and evaluation. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness 12(3), 550-557. https://www.tandfonline.com
title: Treat SEL measures cautiously in school accountability systems because SEL constructs are more context-dependent than achievement
description: Because the study finds SEL domains "seem to be more strongly influenced by contextual factors" than the highly stable rank ordering of math and reading skills, the authors argue that SEL measures should be interpreted differently from achievement measures in evaluation and policy settings. The abstract states that "Implications for school accountability systems and intervention approaches are discussed," positioning state-trait composition as a consideration when using SEL scores for accountability or judging intervention effects.
requirements: Awareness of the state-trait composition of the specific SEL construct being used in evaluation or accountability
constraints: The article's evidence base covers four SEL domains and math/reading achievement; the text provided does not print specific accountability recommendations

target_learning_goals: Appropriate interpretation of SEL measures in policy and evaluation

article_title: The Forgotten 20 Percent: Achievement and Growth in Rural Schools Across the Nation
citation: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2021). The forgotten 20 percent: Achievement and growth in rural schools across the nation. AERA Open. https://aeraopen.org
title: Interpret rural school performance using seasonal learning patterns, not just year-end scores
description: The article argues that achievement comparisons across school settings should account for when learning happens — during school years versus summers. Because "The divergence is driven by larger summer losses for rural students," the authors state that "These findings highlight the importance of seasonal learning patterns in interpreting rural school performance." Year-end snapshots alone can misattribute rural–nonrural differences to school quality when they arise over summers.
requirements: Achievement data from both fall and spring administrations to distinguish school-year growth from summer loss
target_learners: Kindergarten through eighth-grade students in rural and nonrural public schools
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of achievement gaps and school performance for rural students
examples: The study decomposed rural–nonrural achievement trajectories into school-year growth and summer loss components across grades K–8.
key_sources: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2021). The forgotten 20 percent: Achievement and growth in rural schools across the nation. AERA Open. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-forgotten-20-percent-achievement-and-growth-in-rural-schools-across-the-nation/

article_title: Does Four Equal Five? Implementation and Outcomes of the Four-Day School Week
citation: M. Rebecca Kilburn, Andrea Phillips, Celia Gomez, Louis Mariano, Christopher Doss, Wendy Troxel, Emily Morton, Kevin Estes. (2021). Does four equal five? Implementation and outcomes of the four-day school week. NWEA Research report. https://www.nwea.org
title: Communities should weigh mixed four-day-week evidence against their own goals and local context when deciding on adoption
description: Because the study's findings on the four-day school week are mixed — small cost savings, no quantitative attendance evidence, qualitative support for teacher recruitment, high stakeholder satisfaction, but lower ELA and math scores over time — the report concludes that "communities are likely to make different choices about the 4dsw depending on their goals and the local context." Adoption decisions should therefore weigh the academic tradeoff against the non-academic benefits stakeholders value.
requirements: Decision-makers need local information on their own goals (e.g., teacher recruitment, family time, cost) and context, since the evidence does not point uniformly in one direction.
constraints: The academic evidence points to lower ELA and math scores over time on the 4dsw, which any adoption decision must confront.
target_learners: K-12 students in districts considering a four-day school week, especially rural districts in the western United States
target_learning_goals: Maintaining student academic achievement in English language arts and math while managing costs, attendance, and teacher recruitment and retention
examples: The study compared 4dsw and 5dsw districts in Idaho, New Mexico, and Oklahoma using original qualitative data and administrative data from these and other states.
key_sources: M. Rebecca Kilburn, Andrea Phillips, Celia Gomez, Louis Mariano, Christopher Doss, Wendy Troxel, Emily Morton, Kevin Estes. (2021). Does four equal five? article_title: Progress Towards Pandemic Recovery: Continued Signs of Rebounding Achievement at the Start of the 2022-23 School Year
citation: Karyn Lewis, Megan Kuhfeld. (2022). Progress towards pandemic recovery: Continued signs of rebounding achievement at the start of the 2022-23 school year. NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org/research-publications/
title: Use achievement data to identify the most harmed students and provide supports proportional to unmet needs
description: The brief recommends that schools and districts continue using assessment data to understand which students have been most harmed by pandemic disruptions and to allocate supports in proportion to students' unmet needs. It states: "Schools and districts should continue to use data to understand which students have been most harmed and to provide supports in proportion to students’ unmet needs." This follows its finding that rebounding is uneven and youngest readers are furthest behind.
requirements: Ongoing assessment data (such as MAP Growth) on student achievement relative to pre-pandemic levels
constraints: Recovery is projected to take several years, so supports must be sustained rather than one-time
target_learners: Students in grades 3-8 affected by pandemic learning disruption
target_learning_goals: Recovery of reading and mathematics achievement to pre-pandemic levels
examples: The brief analyzed MAP Growth reading and mathematics data from 7 million students in grades 3-8 in 25,000 schools to identify which students were most harmed.

article_title: Achievement and Growth for English Learners
citation: Johnson, A. (2022). Achievement and growth for English Learners. (NWEA Center for School and Student Progress Working Paper). https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/08959048211049419
title: Use learning gains over time, and bilingual or home-language assessments, as key indicators of EL academic progress
description: The article argues that cross-sectional English-only achievement scores understate ELs' skills and fuel deficit framing, so "measures of learning gains should be considered the key indicator of EL academic progress in both instruction and accountability." It further recommends that "dual-language or home-language assessments should be provided in addition to English assessments" for high-stakes decisions, since home-language assessment removes language barriers and the English assessment tracks improvement as measured in English.
requirements: Assessment practices must align with accurately measuring and affirming students' skills and progress
Appropriate accommodations should be provided on monolingual English assessments to reduce bias from unnecessary linguistic complexity
constraints: Applies in contexts where all students must be assessed in English; the precise extent to which English scores underestimate individual EL achievement is unknown

multilingual students developing English proficiency
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of academic achievement and growth
equitable accountability and service-eligibility decisions
examples: The study disaggregated ever-EL data into always-EL and dually-identified subgroups to target services and address deficit-based narratives

article_title: Dual Language Education and Academic Growth
citation: Angela Johnson. (2020). Dual language education and academic growth. NWEA Research Working Paper. https://www.nwea.org
title: Programs aimed at addressing achievement gaps need to consider summer as well as school-year learning for historically-underserved student populations
description: The article draws a design implication from its seasonal growth findings: "programs aimed at addressing achievement gaps need to consider summer as well as school-year learning for historically-underserved student populations." Because dual language participants showed opposite seasonal patterns in math and reading, interventions targeting achievement gaps must account for both school-year and summer learning rather than school-year growth alone.
requirements: Programs must be evaluated with measures that separate school-year growth from summer learning loss, as the piecewise growth model does.
constraints: The finding comes from one large school district enrolling a substantial English Learner population and one Spanish-English dual language program.
target_learners: Hispanic students in grades 2 to 8
English Learner student populations
target_learning_goals: Math achievement growth
Reading achievement growth
Closing achievement gaps with the national average
examples: The study applied a piecewise multilevel growth model to administrative data from a large school district, separating school-year growth from summer loss for dual language participants and nonparticipants.

article_title: High Dosage Tutoring for Academically At-Risk Students
citation: Davison, M., Postell, S., Isaacs, J., & Hashim, A. K. (2024). High dosage tutoring for academically at-risk students. Research brief. https://www.nwea.org
title: High dosage tutoring implementation factor set: frequency and scheduling, group size, qualified personnel, outcome measurement, curriculum, tutor-to-student relationships, and removing barriers to access

The set functions as a design checklist for schools or districts planning tutoring programs for at-risk students.
requirements: Implementation must attend to frequency and scheduling, group size, qualified personnel, measurement of outcomes, curriculum, and tutor-to-student relationships for the tutoring to work as described.
constraints: The brief notes that some components, such as removing barriers to access, are new additions to the factor set.
target_learners: Academically at-risk K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Accelerated academic growth in core academic subjects
examples: The brief reviews the research collection on high dosage tutoring and enumerates these factors as those that must be considered and included for effective implementation.

article_title: High Dosage Tutoring for Academically At-Risk Students
citation: Davison, M., Postell, S., Isaacs, J., & Hashim, A. K. (2024). High dosage tutoring for academically at-risk students. Research brief. https://www.nwea.org

examples: The brief lists removing barriers to access among the factors that must be considered and included to implement high dosage tutoring effectively.

article_title: Post-Pandemic School Closure Trends: Schools Serving Black Students Disproportionately Closed
citation: Isaacs, J., Kuhfeld, M., Postell, S., & Hashim, A. (2025). Post-Pandemic School Closure Trends: Schools Serving Black Students Disproportionately Closed. NWEA White Paper. https://www.nwea.org

description: Because closures disproportionately affect schools serving Black and high-poverty students even after controlling for enrollment declines and poverty, the paper argues closure policy conversations must address racial discrimination. target_learning_goals: Equitable protection of educational continuity and community institutions during closure decisions
examples: The paper's logistic regression showed a 7.3% predicted closure rate for an entirely Black, high-poverty, 50%-enrollment-drop school versus 3.6% for an otherwise identical school with no Black students.

article_title: Practitioner's Guide to Integrating Literacy and Science
citation: Practitioner's guide to integrating literacy and science. (2025). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Nine-lesson phenomenon-driven sequence: introduce phenomenon, observe, question, experiment, share data, read, revise model, extend
description: The guide sketches a nine-lesson sequence (approximately 45 minutes each) driven by a single phenomenon: why some playground surfaces are hotter than others. Students read an engaging narrative, record initial ideas in journals, make playground observations, narrow a testable question, design and conduct experiments, share and argue over data, read with a need to know, revise a class consensus model, and design engineering solutions. The guide notes "the entire set of lessons are driven by the single phenomenon."
requirements: A puzzling everyday phenomenon that can be explained if students master the focal science concepts
constraints: Lessons 1-3 are appropriate for grades K-6; Lessons 4-9 are most appropriate for grades 3-6
The sequence takes place over nine lessons of approximately 45 minutes each, daily or across weeks
target_learners: Elementary students in grades K-6
target_learning_goals: Explaining a scientific phenomenon (Sun's effect on Earth's surface)
Authentic reading, writing, and scientific discourse
examples: Students touch surfaces or use infrared thermometers to observe temperature patterns, then design poster-board color experiments.
