article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Breakthrough Innovation: A Working Definition
citation: Friedman, K., Benge-Steele, C., & Woods, A.D. (2026). ATS Field Note: Breakthrough Innovation. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/297
title: Pursue education advances through use-inspired, iterative research in partnership with practitioners and communities
description: Because education systems are structurally resistant to change, the article argues that "advances in education often depend on use-inspired, iterative research conducted in partnership with practitioners and communities." It further notes that breakthroughs can emerge not only from new ideas but from reframing entrenched problems or recombining existing capabilities in novel ways. The principle underpins the ATS Hub's vision of an infrastructure fostering a community of innovators for rapid development and scaling of breakthrough educational solutions.
requirements: Research must be use-inspired and iterative, conducted in partnership with practitioners and communities rather than detached from them
constraints: Education systems are shaped by deeply embedded norms, routines, and institutional infrastructure that resist change
target_learners: Practitioners, communities, and learners served by education innovation efforts
target_learning_goals: Developing and scaling breakthrough educational solutions addressing urgent educational challenges
examples: The ATS Hub, an IES-funded project, supports the Accelerate Transform Scale Initiative by building a field of education innovators developing use-inspired, evidence-based products harnessing emerging technologies
key_sources: Friedman, K., Benge-Steele, C., & Woods, A.D. (2026). ATS Field Note: Breakthrough Innovation. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/297

article_title: Breaking With the Past: Embracing Digital Transformation in Education
citation: Brizard, J.-C. (2023). Breaking with the past: Embracing digital transformation in education. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/176
title: Adaptive AI edtech should be deployed as a supplement to, never a replacement for, teacher-led instruction
description: The publication describes AI-powered adaptive products (e.g., Woot Math, MyPath K-5, Amplify Reading, Quill) that immediately adapt to students' learning levels, reducing the time teachers spend assessing, placing, and adjusting learning activities, and accelerating catch-up for learners who are behind. It insists these tools "are typically supplemental and can be employed in station rotations, during specific instructional blocks of time, or at home" and augment but can never replace the skilled practice of teachers.
requirements: Products used should be employed within station rotations, instructional blocks, or at home alongside teacher-led one-on-one and group instruction
constraints: The publication notes the listed products each received Digital Promise Product Certifications for research-based design and/or learner variability, while some (e.g., Quill) are not certified
target_learners: K-12 learners who are behind and need to catch up, across grades 3-8 mathematics and reading and ELA
target_learning_goals: Rapid closing of skill gaps; personalized placement on learning progressions
examples: Woot Math supplements learning for grades 3-6 and intervenes in grades 6-8; Quill's diagnostic assesses more than 300 concepts and generates a 10-week individualized plan of 10-to-15-minute activities
key_sources: Brizard, J.-C. (2023). Breaking with the past: Embracing digital transformation in education. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/176

article_title: Research and Development in America's Schools
citation: Smith, K. A., & Stewart, J. (2026, January). Research and development in America’s schools: How school systems drive sustainable improvement and innovation. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/283
title: R&D should be treated as a core function of healthy school systems, like budgeting, curriculum, and assessment
description: The report argues that school-system R&D is not optional but essential infrastructure. It states that "R&D must be considered a core function of healthy school systems, just like budgeting, curriculum, and assessment", positioning systematic inquiry and development alongside standard operational functions. The report frames this as what allows systems to become "engines of improvement and innovation" that design, implement, and scale solutions responsive to student needs.
requirements: System-level commitment to embedding inquiry, evidence, and collaboration into daily routines rather than isolated pilots
constraints: The report notes many systems engage in R&D without formal structures, and efforts "can be difficult to operationalize or scale" without a systematic structure
target_learners: K-12 students in school districts and charter networks
target_learning_goals: Improving teaching and learning outcomes through system-level improvement and innovation
examples: The report's framework, rubric, and three use cases (rural, suburban, charter network) are offered as ways to operationalize R&D as a core function
key_sources: Smith, K. A., & Stewart, J. (2026, January). Research and development in America’s schools: How school systems drive sustainable improvement and innovation. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/283

article_title: Research and Development in America's Schools
citation: Smith, K. A., & Stewart, J. (2026, January). Research and development in America’s schools: How school systems drive sustainable improvement and innovation. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/283
title: Micro-R&D: teachers test new tools and ideas on a small scale before successful practices enter the broader curriculum
description: At South Fayette Township School District (PA), R&D operates as a culture of experimentation rather than a department. The report describes that "This approach empowers teachers to test new tools and ideas on a small scale, often in after-school clubs, summer programs, or elective courses, before integrating successful practices into the broader curriculum." Success is measured by student interest and engagement—elective signups, club attendance, word-of-mouth—rather than standardized metrics, with leadership intentionally flat and distributed so teachers, students, and community members co-design programs.
requirements: Leadership trust, autonomy, and strategic risk-taking; administrators acting as facilitators connecting educators to grants and partners
constraints: The report notes traditional data may be sparse in this approach, with engagement indicators serving as evidence of impact
target_learners: K-12 students in a suburban district; teachers as innovators
target_learning_goals: Iterative local innovation in curriculum and programs, student engagement and interest
examples: Programs cited include drone academies, vertical horticulture, blockchain courses, esports, and Mini-THON
key_sources: Smith, K. A., & Stewart, J. (2026, January). Research and development in America’s schools: How school systems drive sustainable improvement and innovation. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/283

article_title: Privacy Enhancing Technologies in Digital Learning Platforms
citation: Dorie, Vincent. (2025, December). Privacy enhancing technologies in digital learning platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/278
title: Design PETs into digital learning platforms from the ground up as core infrastructure
description: The long-term recommendation is that PETs be considered integral parts of DLPs both to protect data and further trust, and as purpose-limiting, research-enabling tools. They should be designed into DLPs from the ground up, not layered on to existing systems, with a privacy-by-design mindset applied to each step of the data lifecycle for each data source. The article argues this sustains the social license needed for long-term viability of educational research.
requirements: Data governance that considers each step of the data lifecycle for each data source
constraints: Adoption requires stakeholder buy-in and concerted efforts such as participatory design of PET adoption
target_learners: students on digital learning platforms
educational institutions and platform developers
target_learning_goals: sustainable, trustworthy educational research infrastructure
examples: The article recommends communities of practice discuss PETs at educational research conferences and share templated data sharing agreements
key_sources: Dorie, Vincent. (2025, December). Privacy enhancing technologies in digital learning platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/278

article_title: Unlocking the Potential of Technology Innovations: A Vision for Supporting Multilingual Learners
citation: Danae Kamdar, Tiffany Leones, Amanda LaTasha Armstrong, Shelton Daal & Ximena Dominguez. (2025). Unlocking the Potential of Technology Innovations: A Vision for Supporting Multilingual Learners. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Asset-based, culturally and linguistically responsive design pattern for MLL edtech
description: This pattern treats multilingual learners' languages, cultures, and communities as assets to design around rather than obstacles, moving beyond simple translation. The report recommends that "efforts that move beyond simple translation and consider issues of cultural and linguistic sensitivity are needed." Interview exemplars include a studio that prioritized creating a product in Spanish first for Puerto Rican and Mexican communities before translating to English, recognizing that language and culture are interconnected, and recruiting a native speaker of the community as narrator so the community's language is authentically reflected.
requirements: Design teams must meaningfully include voices of MLLs, families, communities, and educators early and often throughout product development
Cultural and linguistic specificity must be addressed, since Spanish-speaking populations vary widely in cultural traditions and vocabulary
constraints: Interviewees noted that diversity among Spanish-speaking populations makes standardized best practices difficult and that addressing power dynamics among diverse team members takes time
target_learners: Young multilingual learners ages 3-8 and their families and communities
target_learning_goals: Engagement, comprehension, and enjoyment of learning content
Identity affirmation and authentic cultural and linguistic representation
examples: One studio developed a product for Spanish-speaking communities by designing in Spanish first, then translating to English; another recognized the need for a community native speaker as narrator during design
key_sources: Danae Kamdar, Tiffany Leones, Amanda LaTasha Armstrong, Shelton Daal & Ximena Dominguez. (2025). Unlocking the Potential of Technology Innovations: A Vision for Supporting Multilingual Learners. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/f37dc670-36a6-4f6e-a6c4-bf312be4fac0

article_title: Expected and Emerging Requirements for Digital Learning Platforms as Research Infrastructure
citation: Roschelle, J., Wortman, A., & Pautz Stephenson, S. (2025, January). Expected and Emerging Requirements for Digital Learning Platforms as Research Infrastructure. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/241
title: Platform-specific content authoring pathways let researchers run A/B tests on curricular variations within each platform's structure
description: Each SEERNet platform gives researchers a distinct way to author or modify content for comparative experiments, matched to the platform's architecture. E-TRIALS can randomize new versus existing presentations of mathematical symbols; Terracotta works with any content entered into the Canvas LMS, letting researchers test alternative versions of assigned content; OpenStax Kinetic lets researchers create Qualtrics surveys or interventional activities students access from Kinetic dashboards, with Qualtrics chosen because many learning scientists already use it. E-TRIALS also supports conditional assignment based on student responses, enabling evaluation focused on students who could most benefit.
requirements: Platform tools that preserve randomization and single-factor variation; E-TRIALS monitors studies to ensure supports vary by a single factor
constraints: Platform scope limits apply: OpenStax Kinetic supports changes in labs but not in its core textbooks, and some content is blocked by school firewalls, which E-TRIALS works around via the ASSISTments YouTube channel
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students on the platforms
target_learning_goals: testing whether modified curricular supports increase learning via A/B experiments
examples: Dr. Avery Closser's SEERNet study adjusts how symbolic math is presented to help students visualize expression structure via E-TRIALS randomization
key_sources: Roschelle, J., Wortman, A., & Pautz Stephenson, S. (2025, January). Expected and Emerging Requirements for Digital Learning Platforms as Research Infrastructure. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/241

article_title: Connecting SEERNet and Improvement Science to Pursue Better Outcomes in Schools
citation: Manai, J., & Roschelle, J. (2024, November). Connecting SEERNet and Improvement Science to Pursue Better Outcomes in Schools. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/234
title: Combining Improvement Science with SEERNet data capabilities as complementary engine and framework
description: The paper's central pattern pairs what it calls an "engine of improvement" — SEERNet's data and malleability of digital learning platforms — with Improvement Science as "a broader framework to keep the improvements accountable to important school challenges and educators' wisdom". SEERNet supplies learning-process data and rapid comparative testing; Improvement Science contributes problem identification, root-cause analysis, and iterative refinement via NICs and PDSA cycles, so interventions are both theoretically sound and practically applicable.
requirements: Collaboration between researchers and practitioners, with clear data-sharing protocols and professional development for interpreting platform data
constraints: Most SEERNet research questions to date have come from scientific theories and may not address educators' most pressing challenges; Integration requires addressing data privacy and security
target_learners: Students in schools and districts using digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Precise identification of student needs and continuous, scalable improvement of interventions
examples: A district uses SEERNet data showing uneven math performance to prompt systematic inquiry into causes and to test alternative solutions with data close to the learning process
key_sources: Manai, J., & Roschelle, J. (2024, November). Connecting SEERNet and Improvement Science to Pursue Better Outcomes in Schools. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/234

article_title: Connecting SEERNet and Improvement Science to Pursue Better Outcomes in Schools
citation: Manai, J., & Roschelle, J. (2024, November). Connecting SEERNet and Improvement Science to Pursue Better Outcomes in Schools. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/234
title: Ground SEERNet research in educators' problems of practice rather than only in theory-driven questions
description: The paper argues SEERNet's contribution "could be enhanced by integrating a problem-based approach inspired by Improvement Science—that is, by collaborating with educators to identify the right problem of practice to focus on". Starting from educators' sense of what is important enables context-sensitive, precisely targeted interventions that are practically applicable and sustainable, while still using rigorous comparative testing within the platforms.
requirements: Collaboration between researchers and practitioners to identify pressing problems of practice
constraints: Researchers must adapt methodologies to fit the data actually available via the platforms; Practitioners must find solutions that fit what digital learning platforms can reasonably do
target_learners: All students in schools using digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Addressing the educational challenges educators consider most pressing
examples: The paper recommends using both practitioners' accounts of problems and SEERNet DLP data to uncover underlying issues and develop targeted interventions
key_sources: Manai, J., & Roschelle, J. (2024, November). Connecting SEERNet and Improvement Science to Pursue Better Outcomes in Schools. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/234

article_title: Practitioner-reported Needs for Enacting, Implementing, and Adopting OpenSciEd Curriculum Materials
citation: McElhaney, K., Urban, R., Kamdar, D., Baker, A., Tsai, K., and Roschelle, J. (2024). Practitioner-reported Needs for Enacting, Implementing, and Adopting OpenSciEd Curriculum Materials [White paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/215
title: District implementation of OpenSciEd should value teachers' assets and give teachers agency and voice in adoption and enactment decisions
description: The report's focus groups indicate that district adoption approaches promoting teacher agency support buy-in, particularly from experienced teachers accustomed to non-practice-based pedagogy. One leader described balancing non-negotiable core principles with "negotiable" elements such as lesson sequence and timing, so that teachers "felt like they had some say in what was going to be most important." The report concludes that such an approach "promotes teachers’ agency in the process" and that valuing teachers' assets could especially help create buy-in from experienced teachers.
requirements: District culture of enabling and supporting teachers, including time and space for peer collaboration and support for finding and accessing OpenSciEd resources
constraints: The authors note such adoption and implementation models could introduce new organizational tensions, such as with districts' accountability to state standards or allocation of time and resources for teacher PL
target_learners: middle and high school science teachers
district and school leaders implementing OpenSciEd
target_learning_goals: teacher buy-in and sustained implementation of phenomenon-based science instruction
examples: A district leader described designating some enactment elements as negotiable, such as lesson sequence and timing, while holding all teachers to shared core principles
key_sources: McElhaney, K., Urban, R., Kamdar, D., Baker, A., Tsai, K., and Roschelle, J. (2024). Practitioner-reported Needs for Enacting, Implementing, and Adopting OpenSciEd Curriculum Materials [White paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/215

article_title: Social Regulation of Learning
citation: Hampton, S., Glazer, K., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., & Fusco, J. (2025). Social Regulation of Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/249
title: Gradually release teacher control so students can develop socially shared regulation of learning
description: The primer recommends that teachers deliberately reduce control over group dialogues, because students develop socially shared regulation of learning only when given opportunities to practice regulating without the teacher. "If a teacher does not offer a release, students will not have the opportunity to develop socially shared regulation of learning as the teacher is controlling the regulation." Development is "nonlinear and highly dynamic," so teachers should adjust the pace and intensity of interventions.
requirements: Teachers must monitor groups and intervene minimally yet impactfully, timely yet infrequently, and provide structure and support rather than expecting regulation to occur naturally
constraints: Students may need more intervention when encountering a brand new topic and less as they become familiar with one another; the process should be treated as nonlinear and highly dynamic
target_learners: K-12 students in collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: Socially shared regulation of learning
student agency and ownership of learning
examples: The primer suggests teachers pause 30 seconds and observe before intervening, and describes Dragnić-Cindrić et al.'s (2023) finding that teacher-controlled groups used less socially shared regulation
key_sources: Hampton, S., Glazer, K., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., & Fusco, J. (2025). Social Regulation of Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/249

article_title: Social Regulation of Learning
citation: Hampton, S., Glazer, K., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., & Fusco, J. (2025). Social Regulation of Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/249
title: Observable indicators distinguish low-quality from high-quality socially shared regulation of learning
description: The primer offers a side-by-side table of observable behaviors so observers "can quickly discern what a student could experience in a classroom environment with low-quality versus high-quality socially shared regulation of learning." Low-quality indicators include sustained off-task behavior, unequal contributions, frequent hostility, and frequent need for teacher intervention; high-quality indicators include balanced contributions, mutual support and respect, and the group working together to overcome challenges.
requirements: Because observing inside a learner's mind is not possible, practical and observable indicators are needed; many indicators are likely to be present simultaneously and intermittently
constraints: Indicators are observational proxies, not direct measures of regulation; the primer notes regulation's impact on learning can be hard to measure
target_learners: K-12 students in group learning
target_learning_goals: Recognizing and fostering socially shared regulation of learning
examples: High-quality student behaviors listed include asking clarifying questions, using reasoning phrases such as "I think X because of Y," managing conflicts without teacher intervention, and referencing additional materials with little or no prompting
key_sources: Hampton, S., Glazer, K., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., & Fusco, J. (2025). Social Regulation of Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/249

article_title: Collaborative Argumentation for Learning
citation: Schank, P., Barth, C., Crawford, V., and Fusco, J. (2025, May). Collaborative Argumentation for Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/251
title: Use peer review of arguments to improve learning while reducing teacher workload
description: The primer recommends peer review as a strategy that accounts for teachers' limited time: "Through a powerful approach called peer review, students review and assess each other's arguments, serving to both improve student learning and reduce teacher workload". It works especially well when teachers use role-playing games, prompts, and other scaffolds to seed peer reviewing of discussions as students practice argumentation skills (Clark et al., 2009).
requirements: Scaffolds such as role-playing games and prompts to seed peer reviewing of discussions
constraints: The primer notes teachers do not want to be the sole source of feedback, and a trust-based classroom culture supports students giving and receiving critical feedback
target_learners: Middle school and secondary STEM students
target_learning_goals: Argumentation skills
Learning from evaluating peers' arguments
examples: The primer's recommendation of peer review as one of the promising strategies that take teachers' available time into account
key_sources: Schank, P., Barth, C., Crawford, V., and Fusco, J. (2025, May). Collaborative Argumentation for Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/251

article_title: Assessment During Collaborative Learning
citation: Fusco, J., DiMaria, S., Yeadon, B., Kolodner, J., & Shell, A. (2025). Assessment During Collaborative Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/252
title: Balancing individual and group assessment in collaborative learning with pre-, checkpoint, and follow-up individual measures
description: The primer recommends a deliberate mix of individual and group assessments so that collaborative work stays meaningful while individual learning remains visible. Some practitioners find "a mix of 40% collaborative group grades and 60% individual grades encourages students to engage seriously in collaborative work" while still showing individual abilities. Concrete moves include documenting individual thinking before collaboration, checkpoint assessments during the process, follow-up individual assessments after group activities, and assessments capturing collective learning.
requirements: Preplanning what to assess and when; individual knowledge checks follow up when collaborative assessments do not reveal what each student can do
constraints: Students and parents typically prefer individual assessment and may find grades for collaborative work confusing or disappointing
target_learners: K-12 and STEM students working in collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: Content mastery
collaborative skills
individual accountability
examples: Practitioners use pre/post individual assessments of growth or individual quizzes after group tasks when group work does not uncover what each student can do
key_sources: Fusco, J., DiMaria, S., Yeadon, B., Kolodner, J., & Shell, A. (2025). Assessment During Collaborative Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/252

article_title: Classroom Discourse
citation: Schank, P., Jenks, L., Barth, C., Crawford, C., Powers, K., & Fusco, J. (2025, May). Classroom Discourse. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/250
title: Establishing and reinforcing ground rules for respectful, equitable discussion
description: The primer recommends that teachers work with students to establish a shared understanding of norms for communication and engagement. Key ground rules include "listening attentively to classmates, speaking respectfully, using evidence to support claims, and taking turns to speak." Once established, norms should be consistently reinforced to become ingrained in classroom culture; some teachers hang posters of the agreed-upon norms.
requirements: Building rapport and practice with students initially takes time as expectations are laid out and students develop their skills
constraints: The primer notes that when students feel safe to share and challenge ideas without fear of ridicule, disagreements and dispute resolution become productive for learning
target_learners: K-12 STEM students
target_learning_goals: participation in productive, accountable classroom discussion
examples: Some teachers hang posters in their classrooms of the agreed-upon norms
key_sources: Schank, P., Jenks, L., Barth, C., Crawford, C., Powers, K., & Fusco, J. (2025, May). Classroom Discourse. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/250

article_title: Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses
citation: Koch, M., & Peters Hinton, V. (2025). Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses [Project Report]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/242
title: Pair digital courseware with active instructor involvement and intentional integration, since courseware alone entails risks for abstract subjects like statistics
description: The report concludes that Lumen One "pairs nicely with the evidence-based teaching approach of formative practice and feedback, but it can be a challenging courseware if the professor has little involvement in the student's learning process." Instructors should be intentional about integrating the courseware regardless of modality, actively orienting students to its features and providing feedback beyond what the courseware supplies. This recommendation arises directly from student reports that instructor outreach, availability, and responsiveness shaped their engagement and confidence.
requirements: Instructors must actively orient students to the courseware and provide outreach, availability, and responsiveness beyond the courseware's own feedback
constraints: Relying solely on digital software to guide students through abstract statistics content entails risks, per the report
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory statistics courses, particularly students of color
target_learning_goals: engagement with course material
sense of belonging
confidence and motivation in statistics
examples: Students described instructors noticing slipping quiz scores and reaching out individually, staying after class to explain step by step, and demonstrating courseware use in class
key_sources: Koch, M., & Peters Hinton, V. (2025). Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses [Project Report]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/242

article_title: ATS Field Note — Using AI in Prototyping
citation: McGurl, C. & Maisscotte, B. (2026). ATS Field Note: Using AI in Prototyping. In ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/298
title: Pair AI-supported prototyping with clear team roles, recurring review cycles, and systematic educator feedback
description: The article reports that AI prototyping is most effective when embedded in workflows with clear roles, regular review cycles, and ongoing educator input. Its team established weekly sessions with practicing educators and weekly sessions with internal experts, creating a "build → review → refine" cycle that let them respond quickly, as when teachers called a dashboard "overwhelming" and a revised version was tested the following week.
requirements: Clarified team roles, frequent team check-ins, consistently and systematically gathered educator feedback, and clear guidance on the development process
constraints: Progress slowed when there was no clear system for getting feedback, even though AI enabled rapid generation of multiple feature variations
target_learners: K-2 educators using the literacy decision support tool
target_learning_goals: Usable, classroom-fit literacy workflow and decision support tools refined through educator feedback
examples: The team held weekly sessions with practicing educators and weekly sessions with internal experts; after teachers said a prototype dashboard felt overwhelming, the team simplified the design and tested a revised version the following week
key_sources: McGurl, C. & Maisscotte, B. (2026). ATS Field Note: Using AI in Prototyping. In ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/298

article_title: ATS Field Note — Using AI in Prototyping
citation: McGurl, C. & Maisscotte, B. (2026). ATS Field Note: Using AI in Prototyping. In ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/298
title: Test designs in working prototype form rather than as polished concepts or wireframes
description: The article recommends using AI to move quickly from concepts such as wireframes to functional prototypes users can interact with and give feedback on. AI-generated wireflows looked logical and complete on paper, but once turned into a simple working prototype, problems became obvious: too many clicks, poor timing of key information, and recommendations that did not match teacher needs.
requirements: Small, testable prototypes updated more often, so educators can interact with the tool and give concrete feedback
constraints: Paper wireframes alone hid usability problems such as excessive clicks, poor information timing, and mismatched recommendations
target_learners: K-2 educators providing feedback on literacy tool prototypes
target_learning_goals: Early surfacing of usability issues and avoidance of costly rework
examples: Educators interacting with a working prototype gave feedback such as "I need this earlier," or "I wouldn't use this," which helped the team refine ideas early
key_sources: McGurl, C. & Maisscotte, B. (2026). ATS Field Note: Using AI in Prototyping. In ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/298

article_title: Commentary on Interest-Driven Creator theory: a US perspective on fostering interest, creativity, and habit in school
citation: Roschelle, J., & Burke, Q. (2019). Commentary on Interest-Driven Creator theory: a US perspective on fostering interest, creativity, and habit in school. Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning, 14(13). https://doi.org/10.1186/s41039-019-0107-2
title: Schools should both celebrate student creations and regularly cultivate creativity
description: The commentary proposes that schools need both a focus on creation (students' novel, expressive artifacts showcased in classrooms and corridors) and a focus on creativity (regular space in assignments for creative response). The authors hypothesize the two reinforce each other: celebrating creations breathes energy into the habit of creativity, while regular cultivation leads to more authentic and meaningful creations.
requirements: Schools must create space in assignments for students to respond creatively and nurture creativity regularly, not only in showpiece production
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Creativity
Sustained creative habits
examples: The authors describe progressive US schools displaying student artifacts on shelves, walls, display cases, and district offices while teachers articulate how they nurture creativity regularly
key_sources: Roschelle, J., & Burke, Q. (2019). Commentary on Interest-Driven Creator theory: a US perspective on fostering interest, creativity, and habit in school. Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning, 14(13). https://doi.org/10.1186/s41039-019-0107-2

article_title: The IEP Project: A Strength-based, Whole Learner Teacher Guide
citation: Digital Promise. (2023, February). The IEP project: A strength-based, whole learner teacher guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/169
title: Write IEPs and teacher reports through a strength-based, whole learner lens so student strengths are used to address growth areas
description: This principle holds that IEP reporting should begin from what students can do, seen through a whole learner lens, rather than from a deficit inventory. The guide states that "A goal of this guidebook is to see student strengths through a whole learner lens and write IEPs that reflect strengths to be used to address growth areas." It frames deficit-based approaches as surfacing only struggles, especially harmful for students with learning disabilities facing stigma.
requirements: A shared understanding of the student's strengths among stakeholders, situated within the student's context
constraints: Designed for PreK-12 public education IEP processes
target_learners: PreK-12 students with learning disabilities and other IEP-eligible students
target_learning_goals: Academic growth in literacy and math
Social-emotional learning and behavior
examples: The guide's sample response bank describes Antonio, who struggles to read with fluency and accuracy but has strong listening comprehension and extensive vocabulary, with decoding instruction and text-to-speech kept on two tracks
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2023, February). The IEP project: A strength-based, whole learner teacher guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/169

article_title: Interview Protocol for Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses
citation: Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses: Interview Protocol. (2025). Digital Promise / Achieving the Dream. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: Interview coverage spanning five question domains from platform experience to belonging
description: The protocol organizes its questions into recurring domains: general platform and structure, courseware-specific features, course content, student learning behaviors, and student perceptions and sense of belonging, closing with overall impressions and 0-10 ratings. Each domain pairs experience questions with follow-ups, such as asking what impacts a student's decision whether or not to review topics suggested by Readiness Checks, and ending with recommendation and instructor ratings from 0 to 10.
requirements: Questions from each domain should be asked within one interview session
Follow-up branches are scripted for supportive, neutral, and negative student responses
target_learners: Undergraduate statistics students
target_learning_goals: Capture holistic student experience including usability, content inclusivity, learning behaviors, and belonging
examples: Domain-specific prompts cover Introduce Yourself module, Lumen Community, Readiness Checks, Apply it Exercises, Self-Checks, Worked Example Videos, and Instructor Messages
key_sources: Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses: Interview Protocol. (2025). Digital Promise / Achieving the Dream. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/05ccd902-1e80-4c94-9cd9-f706a98d0cc0

article_title: Interview Protocol for Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses
citation: Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses: Interview Protocol. (2025). Digital Promise / Achieving the Dream. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: Probe both real-world relevance and racial-cultural connection when evaluating course engagement
description: The protocol treats two levers for engagement in statistics as worth probing separately: embedding real-world examples and scenarios into course content, and connecting course content to the racial and cultural experiences of the students. Interviewers ask how well the course makes each connection and how inclusion of real-world topics or racial identity and cultural experiences impacts learning, asking hypothetically if connections have not yet been made.
requirements: Interview questions must address both real-world connections and racial and cultural connections as distinct topics
constraints: Statistics courses can often seem very theoretical and disconnected from real life, which motivates the probes
target_learners: Undergraduate statistics students from a variety of backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Increase student interest and engagement in statistics
examples: The protocol asks students to rate how well the course makes connections to real world topics and to their own racial and cultural experiences
key_sources: Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses: Interview Protocol. (2025). Digital Promise / Achieving the Dream. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/05ccd902-1e80-4c94-9cd9-f706a98d0cc0

article_title: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Break instruction into short lessons with application, reflection, feedback, and encouragement when designing for adult basic learners
description: The brief's first design principle holds that the brain learns best in brief, focused bursts: short lessons let learners chunk information into meaningful units, then apply and reflect on each chunk to recall and connect it to later material. For adult basic learners this also connects to andragogy, since adults learn more effectively when new information links to their experience. The brief urges developers to build in feedback, checks for understanding, and encouragement around each short module.
requirements: Short lessons must be followed by focused activities that require learners to apply and reflect on what they learned
Feedback and checks for understanding should accompany each module
target_learners: adult basic learners
low-skilled adults
adult English language learners
target_learning_goals: chunking new information with prior knowledge
deeper retention through application and reflection
examples: Cell-Ed developed ELL micro-modules consisting of a short audio lesson, a follow-up text reinforcing the lesson for learner reflection, and an interactive quiz for application
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/0b18a16a-2f1d-400b-9fed-df5675ba40cf

article_title: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Build in visual organizers that learners can manipulate to help adult learners visualize and organize information
description: The brief's second principle recommends visual or graphic organizers as mental scaffolding that mimics how the brain records and organizes information. The brief says visual organizers "replicate this map for learners, helping them understand and therefore strengthen the patterns being formed between old and new information," supporting four functions: clarifying thoughts, organizing and analyzing information, integrating new knowledge, and thinking critically. Although widespread in K-12, such tools are used by few adult learning products.
requirements: Tools should let learners create, manipulate, and change organizers as their learning develops
Organizers should connect learners' prior experience to new content
constraints: Visual organizers are used by few, if any, adult learning products, so designers must adapt K-12 tools
target_learners: adult basic learners
adult English language learners
target_learning_goals: organizing and analyzing information
integrating new knowledge
critical thinking
examples: K-12 visual tools such as Inspiration let learners create maps and flow charts, use templates or their own organizers, and manipulate them as learning deepens
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/0b18a16a-2f1d-400b-9fed-df5675ba40cf

article_title: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Provide adult learners a large bank of easily accessible practice resources in multiple formats
description: The brief's third principle calls for many opportunities for practice and repetition, since adult learners need increased practice to activate brain plasticity and growth. Digital products should store many resource types (documents, PDFs, videos, sound files) because audio, video, and games increase engagement by being less threatening and more fun than reading text. Resources must also be easy to access, because perceived support correlates with persistence in online learning and access struggles are major roadblocks for adults with limited time and digital confidence.
requirements: Resources of many types and in learners' languages must be available
Access must be clear and simple, avoiding difficult navigation and multiple logins
constraints: LMSs and other storage options often suffer usability problems such as difficult navigation and the need for multiple logins, which can make resources effectively unavailable to adults with low digital confidence
target_learners: adult basic learners
adult English language learners
target_learning_goals: practice and repetition
persistence in online learning
examples: Washington State adult educators found that having good resources in both English and Spanish was imperative for their largely ELL participants; LMSs, YouTube channels, and wikis are cited ways to centralize resources
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/0b18a16a-2f1d-400b-9fed-df5675ba40cf

article_title: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Design multiple modes of learner-instructor communication available outside class time and on demand
description: The brief's fourth principle is facilitating frequent communication between instructor and learner, because adult learners have a particularly strong need for connection with and encouragement from their teachers given the barriers and weaker skills they face. Technology can provide reflective activities (blogs, emails, videos), regular feedback (emails, discussion threads, videos), office-hour chats, and anytime communication so learners can reach instructors when they need support between life commitments.
requirements: Communication tools must allow learners to contact instructors when they need to, not just during class meetings
Multiple communication modes should be built in
target_learners: adult basic learners
adult English language learners
target_learning_goals: learner confidence
persistence and progress in learning
examples: myPLACE instructors contact students via personal emails, discussion boards, LMS messages, and global announcements; CyberESL students have weekly one-on-one Skype coaching sessions for individualized instruction and practice
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/0b18a16a-2f1d-400b-9fed-df5675ba40cf

article_title: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Design in tools and opportunities for peer-to-peer interaction among adult learners
description: The brief's fifth principle rests on research that students learn from peers as well as teachers, particularly peers of different abilities and backgrounds. Working with others increases the social-emotional memories of a learning experience and thus the learning, and for adult learners these connections also build confidence because they learn with others managing the same adult responsibilities. Digital tools such as wikis, discussion threads, and video and text chats can be built into products as places for peer work.
requirements: Products must include built-in spaces for peer interaction such as wikis, discussion threads, and chats
Instruction should be peppered with peer discussion, peer-review writing, and group project opportunities
target_learners: adult basic learners
adult English language learners
target_learning_goals: deepening learning through peer input and models
building a peer support system for managing learning
examples: Online courses use discussions with peers, peer-review writing activities, and group projects as peer-to-peer collaboration practices
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/0b18a16a-2f1d-400b-9fed-df5675ba40cf

article_title: Computing in rural America: Developing K-8 coding pathways for Kentucky Appalachia
citation: Computing in Rural America: Developing K-8 Coding Pathways for Kentucky Appalachia. (2020). Presentation slides, December 2nd 2020.
title: South Fayette SD's CS/STEAM pathway organized around four throughlines
description: The South Fayette School District pathway, which the Kentucky project adapts, is organized around four throughlines found in its CS/STEAM pathway: "Maker Education (artistic expression and creativity)", "Computational Thinking (computer science including coding in the virtual and physical environment)", "Spatial Reasoning & Discrete Math (the ability to imagine things in three-dimensions & understanding mathematical modeling)", and "Manufacturing and Design (engineering, human centered design thinking)". Lesson plans in the pathway include "student agency, computational thinking competencies and practices, habits of mind and examples of student artifacts."
requirements: Lesson development must attend to student agency, CT competencies and practices, habits of mind, and student artifacts
constraints: The pattern is presented as one district's model being adapted to a rural Appalachian context, not as a validated general design
target_learners: K-8 students
target_learning_goals: creativity and maker expression
computational thinking
spatial reasoning and discrete math
engineering design
examples: Glimpses of South Fayette SD's pathway were shown to the Kentucky partners as a model to adapt
key_sources: Computing in Rural America: Developing K-8 Coding Pathways for Kentucky Appalachia. (2020). Presentation slides, December 2nd 2020. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/0c77d3c7-12c8-4a9b-8583-040137f0fd3c

article_title: Computing in rural America: Developing K-8 coding pathways for Kentucky Appalachia
citation: Computing in Rural America: Developing K-8 Coding Pathways for Kentucky Appalachia. (2020). Presentation slides, December 2nd 2020.
title: Build a CT pathway from five key components: district-wide vision, annotated grade-band competencies, curated resources, competency-based PD, and formative assessment
description: The presentation enumerates the key components of a pathway: "Develop a district-wide vision for curricular integration of CT & CS in each grade band, including attention to the 'why' in the eyes of students, teachers and parents"; clear competency statements annotated with "short, illustrative examples or videos"; "Identification & adaptation of useful curricular resources"; identification of teacher professional development needs "based on stated competencies & curricula resources"; and "Articulation of formative assessment for students & teachers, guiding improvement."
requirements: Competencies must be stated per grade band and PD must be derived from those competencies and the chosen curricular resources
target_learners: K-8 students
K-8 teachers
target_learning_goals: district-wide computational thinking and computer science integration
examples: The project's three central outputs — competencies, curricula, and credentialing — map onto these components

article_title: Transforming Teachers’ Knowledge for Teaching Mathematics with Technologies through Online Knowledge-Building Communities
citation: Niess, M. L., & Roschelle, J. (2018). Transforming Teachers' Knowledge for Teaching Mathematics with Technologies through Online Knowledge-Building Communities. Proceedings of the 40th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education, Greenville, SC. https://www.pmena.org/proceedings/
title: Online knowledge-building trajectory built on two tools and two processes
description: The online TPACK learning trajectory organizes professional learning around two tools and two processes within a social metacognitive constructivist framework. As printed, "Two tools support the online professional development: (1) a community of learners and (2) reflection," supporting social and cognitive presence; the two key processes are shared/individual knowledge development and inquiry learning, in which learners move between group and individual knowledge-building and investigate worthy questions. Reflection happens through reflective essays, peer reviews, and online portfolios.
requirements: Establishing a community of learners to support communication and interaction in the asynchronous online environment
Critical reflection activities such as reflective essays, peer review, and portfolios
constraints: The primarily asynchronous nature of online learning poses additional challenges for the design of these educational experiences
target_learners: in-service mathematics teachers in graduate online courses
target_learning_goals: reframing teacher knowledge for teaching mathematics with technologies
knowledge-building through inquiry and discourse
examples: In SED 520, teachers explored an unfamiliar temperature probe through ten laboratory experiments, discussed key questions in small communities of learners, and concluded each unit with a critical reflection
key_sources: Niess, M. L., & Roschelle, J. (2018). Transforming Teachers' Knowledge for Teaching Mathematics with Technologies through Online Knowledge-Building Communities. Proceedings of the 40th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education, Greenville, SC. https://www.pmena.org/proceedings/

article_title: Transforming Teachers’ Knowledge for Teaching Mathematics with Technologies through Online Knowledge-Building Communities
citation: Niess, M. L., & Roschelle, J. (2018). Transforming Teachers' Knowledge for Teaching Mathematics with Technologies through Online Knowledge-Building Communities. Proceedings of the 40th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education, Greenville, SC. https://www.pmena.org/proceedings/
title: Combine practical classroom teaching experiences with knowledge-building discourse and extensive critical reflection to transform teachers' TPACK
description: The article's concluding design recommendation for teacher educators is that transforming teachers' TPACK requires practical experiences combined with community discourse and critical reflection. As printed, the work "identified the importance of combining practical experiences with opportunities for the teachers to engage in discourse through the knowledge-building communities of learners and extensive critical reflection on teaching in their classrooms." This combination lets teachers rethink, unlearn and relearn content and pedagogical strategies in light of technologies' affordances.
requirements: Access to teachers' own classrooms for practical implementation
Knowledge-building communities of learners for discourse
Extensive critical reflection on classroom teaching
constraints: The discussion notes a knowledge-building community is aspirational and would go beyond the results reported here, which emphasized individualized problems of practice
target_learners: in-service mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: transforming TPACK toward student-centered, technology-integrated instruction
examples: In SED 594 teachers designed and taught a five-day technology-integrated unit while weekly discussing reform-based strategies online, gathering two instruction videos, student products, and multiple critical reflections

article_title: Equity in the Driver’s Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education
citation: Babe Liberman and Viki Young, Ph.D. (2020). Equity in the Driver's Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Consultancy protocol in which a district team presents an equity challenge and peers probe it before offering suggestions
description: The article details a five-phase consultancy protocol: the district team presents its equity challenge for about ten minutes, consultants ask clarifying questions, then probing questions, then discuss the challenge in small groups while the district team listens, and finally the district team reflects and shares new thinking. Probing questions were 'deeper, open-ended questions that empowered the district teams to reflect on and think about collaboratively addressing their problem.' The protocol surfaced both common trends and context-specific observations about local policy, assets, and barriers.
requirements: A district team willing to present its equity challenge
Consultants who listen with dual purposes: helping clarify the challenge and generating their own ideas for tackling it
constraints: The authors state that in the future they would 'allow even more time for exploring and interrogating specific district challenges' and suggest probes to keep the group centered on equity
target_learners: District and school teams defining equity challenges, serving K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Clarifying and articulating equity challenges to generate relevant research questions and development priorities
examples: One district leader shared plans to use a consultancy protocol in her own district meetings after experiencing it at the convening
key_sources: Babe Liberman and Viki Young, Ph.D. (2020). Equity in the Driver's Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/1185beda-6355-47f0-b3f2-980f6541172b

article_title: Equity in the Driver’s Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education
citation: Babe Liberman and Viki Young, Ph.D. (2020). Equity in the Driver's Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Begin R&D agenda-setting from districts' specific equity challenges rather than from the research literature
description: The article recommends structuring agenda-setting so that practical field perspectives drive the framing of research questions. 'We intentionally structured the day to begin with the specific equity challenges that the invited district teams were facing, rather than starting from a research perspective,' based on the hunch that this would yield questions relevant and usable in practice. Research is then consulted in service of those challenges, with district teams first sharing what they found most useful in topic overviews and what else they would need to know.
requirements: Access to district teams who can articulate authentic equity challenges with supporting data and artifacts
Topic overviews prepared in advance so participants enter discussions with working knowledge
constraints: The authors note that published research 'often does not provide a meaningful starting point for action' on its own and must be mediated by practitioners' local knowledge
target_learners: K-12 students in participating districts, with attention to students at the margins
target_learning_goals: Producing R&D agendas that address schools' most pressing equity-related needs
examples: District teams shared viewpoints on topic overviews before researchers added additional findings, flipping the traditional dynamic in which researchers kick off such dialogue
key_sources: Babe Liberman and Viki Young, Ph.D. (2020). Equity in the Driver's Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/1185beda-6355-47f0-b3f2-980f6541172b

article_title: Equity in the Driver’s Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education
citation: Babe Liberman and Viki Young, Ph.D. (2020). Equity in the Driver's Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Select challenge topics that have an existing research base, remaining gaps, and timeliness in policy and equity conversations
description: The article recommends three criteria for selecting challenge topics for practice-driven R&D agenda-setting: a strong existing body of field knowledge with remaining research gaps, being a hot topic in policy, practice, and equity, and an ongoing need for research synthesis, solution development, or technical assistance. 'Appropriate challenge topics have a research base to start from, but are not fully developed, with meaningful gaps in the research that can be filled based on practice perspectives.' Adolescent literacy and computational thinking were selected because both met these criteria.
requirements: Topics must be relevant and urgent to both the research and practice sides
target_learners: Adolescents behind in reading proficiency and K-12 students in computational learning opportunities
target_learning_goals: Focusing R&D investment on persistent, equity-relevant challenges where practice perspectives can fill research gaps
examples: Adolescent literacy was chosen because less is known about supporting adolescents severely behind in reading, and CT because best practices for implementing CT competencies across grade levels remain unclear

article_title: Fostering Market Effciency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement
citation: Morrison, J. R., Ross, S. M., Corcoran, R. P., & Reid, A. J. (2014). Fostering Market Efficiency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563768
title: Districts should use structured pilots for discovery and evaluation of ed-tech products
description: The report recommends that districts and providers would benefit substantially from guidelines for conducting formal pilots to facilitate discovery and evaluation. Pilots that are structured and rigorous generate evidence about product efficacy that is useful locally and to other districts considering the same products. Effective strategies are needed for matching products to teachers, funding pilots, collecting qualitative and quantitative data, and analyzing results.
requirements: Strategies for matching products to be piloted to teachers based on interest and instructional needs
Funding for pilots
Collection of both qualitative and quantitative data on implementation, satisfaction, and educational outcomes
constraints: Informal pilots (demos, brief try-outs, committee reviews) may yield questionable conclusions about product quality
target_learners: K-12 school district administrators and ed-tech providers
target_learning_goals: Evaluating ed-tech product quality and effectiveness for selection decisions
examples: District participants overall reported a moderate-to-extensive reliance on pilot tryouts (mostly informal demos and field tests) within the district for ed-tech procurement.
key_sources: Morrison, J. R., Ross, S. M., Corcoran, R. P., & Reid, A. J. (2014). Fostering Market Efficiency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563768

article_title: Fostering Market Effciency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement
citation: Morrison, J. R., Ross, S. M., Corcoran, R. P., & Reid, A. J. (2014). Fostering Market Efficiency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563768
title: Districts should create guidelines for structuring instructional needs assessments
description: The report recommends districts would likely benefit from the creation of guidelines and models for structuring instructional needs assessments to ensure that selections and acquisitions are linked directly to priority areas. Districts should also more integrally involve end-users in defining needs more specifically and operationally, and should obtain guidelines for matching instructional design features of ed-tech products to needs assessments.
requirements: Guidelines and models for structuring instructional needs assessments
Greater involvement of end-users (teachers and principals) in defining needs specifically and operationally
constraints: Current needs assessments are most frequently surface in nature and do not identify specific types of support and product attributes
target_learners: K-12 school district administrators, curriculum directors, and technology directors
target_learning_goals: Linking ed-tech selection and acquisition directly to priority instructional areas
examples: The report recommends involving end-users in defining needs operationally, such as 'To teach problem-based learning more effectively in STEM classes.'
key_sources: Morrison, J. R., Ross, S. M., Corcoran, R. P., & Reid, A. J. (2014). Fostering Market Efficiency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563768

article_title: Fostering Market Effciency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement
citation: Morrison, J. R., Ross, S. M., Corcoran, R. P., & Reid, A. J. (2014). Fostering Market Efficiency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563768
title: Providers should seek third-party independent evidence to differentiate their products
description: The report recommends providers should seek opportunities to collect third-party (independent) evidence from evaluation studies, including both treatment-control group comparisons and case studies, to differentiate and support their products. As a practical alternative to complex and expensive RCTs, credible evidence for judging product fit and potential efficacy can come from pilots, case studies, and small comparison-group designs.
requirements: Engaging third-party evaluators for design reviews, case studies, or experimental comparison group studies
constraints: Few providers (except for the very large companies) can afford or win large grants to fund a randomized control trial
target_learners: Ed-tech product providers and developers
target_learning_goals: Differentiating products and supporting claims of effectiveness
examples: The report notes few providers seek opportunities for their products to be evaluated in pilots, case studies, and small comparison-group designs.

article_title: Computational Thinking for an Inclusive World: A Resource for Educators to Learn and Lead, Quick Start and Discussion Guide
citation: Mills, K., Coenraad, M., Ruiz, P., Burke, Q., & Weisgrau J. (2021, December). Computational thinking for an inclusive world: A resource for educators to learn and lead, Quick start and discussion guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/140
title: Inclusive computational thinking pedagogies in three categories: accessible instruction, connecting to homes and communities, and combating inequity
description: The guide organizes inclusive computing pedagogies into three categories emphasizing different approaches to inclusivity. Designing Accessible Instruction engages all learners; Connecting to Students' Interests, Homes, and Communities draws on student experiences to highlight computing's relevance; and Acknowledging and Combating Inequity supports students to recognize and take a stand against oppression of marginalized groups. The guide states these pedagogies are "divided into three categories to emphasize different pedagogical approaches to inclusivity."
requirements: Inclusive learning experiences must intentionally integrate connections to students' interests, homes and communities and acknowledge and challenge inequity at the outset of the learning rather than as an afterthought
target_learners: All K-12 learners, including Black, Native American, and Latinx students; students with disabilities; girls and non-binary students
target_learning_goals: Equitable participation in computational thinking and computing
examples: Example practices include using Universal Design for Learning principles, pair programming and POGIL, translanguaging and translated Scratch blocks, recruiting excluded students to CS classes, and teaching about biases in algorithms and artificial intelligence
key_sources: Mills, K., Coenraad, M., Ruiz, P., Burke, Q., & Weisgrau J. (2021, December). Computational thinking for an inclusive world: A resource for educators to learn and lead, Quick start and discussion guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/140

article_title: Computational Thinking for an Inclusive World: A Resource for Educators to Learn and Lead, Quick Start and Discussion Guide
citation: Mills, K., Coenraad, M., Ruiz, P., Burke, Q., & Weisgrau J. (2021, December). Computational thinking for an inclusive world: A resource for educators to learn and lead, Quick start and discussion guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/140
title: District and school leaders must build shared leadership and professional learning capacity to scale computational thinking integration
description: The guide argues that integrating computational thinking into every classroom cannot be left to individual educators; leaders at district and school levels must prioritize the initiative and build teacher capacity. It notes that strong CT examples often exist in isolated pockets but are rarely consistent across classrooms or schools, which yields fewer and less robust opportunities for students experiencing marginalization. The guide states that "In order to scale and sustain computational thinking integration within districts and schools, educators must promote shared leadership between districts and schools and designing professional learning experiences for pre- and in-service teachers."
requirements: Shared leadership between districts and schools and professional learning experiences for pre- and in-service teachers
constraints: Pockets of strong CT integration within districts often leave students experiencing marginalization with fewer and less robust computing learning opportunities
target_learners: K-12 students district-wide, especially those experiencing marginalization
target_learning_goals: Equitable, sustained access to computational thinking learning opportunities
examples: The guide poses reflection prompts asking educators how to engage teacher, school and district leaders to build capacity for computational thinking

article_title: Unintended Impact: How the Verizon Innovative Learning Schools Program Affected Its Educators' Job Satisfaction and Career Trajectories
citation: Chelimo, S., Cortez, C., Jackson, J., & Weaver, D. (2024, May). Unintended Impact: How the Verizon Innovative Learning Schools Program Affected Its Educators' Job Satisfaction and Career Trajectories. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/212
title: Three standout reasons for increased job satisfaction: technology access and use, student engagement, and work-life balance
description: Interviews of teachers and coaches did not uncover a single distinct reason for increased job satisfaction but a multiplicity, of which three stood out: the availability and effective use of technology, increased student engagement leading to less teacher stress, and better work-life balance from digital convenience. The report presents these as recurring themes across the six districts rather than tested factors, illustrated with teacher and coach testimonies about engagement, joy, and time management.
requirements: Program-supported devices and connectivity plus coaching that helps teachers use technology effectively
constraints: Derived from interviews and focus groups in six districts; the report notes no distinct single reason was found
target_learners: classroom teachers
instructional technology coaches
target_learning_goals: teacher retention and job satisfaction
student engagement through technology
examples: A Broward teacher reported spending less time working out of school hours because being digitally connected let her get more done in school

article_title: Micro-credentials: Driving teacher learning & leadership
citation: Barnett Berry and Karen Cator. (2016). Micro-credentials: Driving teacher learning & leadership. Center for Teaching Quality and Digital Promise. http://teachingquality.org/micro-credentials
title: Four key characteristics of the micro-credential approach: competency-based, personalized, on-demand, shareable
description: The report identifies four characteristics distinguishing micro-credentials from traditional professional development. They are "Competency-based," focusing on "evidence of educators’ actual skills and abilities, not the amount of 'seat time'"; personalized, with teachers selecting credentials based on their own needs and contexts; on-demand, responsive to teachers' schedules through an agile online system; and shareable as "portable currency for professional learning" across platforms, résumés, and blogs. Each micro-credential specifies what the teacher should know and do, recommends resources, and specifies the evidence required to demonstrate competence.
requirements: Each micro-credential must provide a competency definition, recommended resources, and a specification of the evidence an educator must submit
constraints: The report notes implementing micro-credentials will not guarantee teachers have the time they need to collaborate and learn together
target_learners: practicing K-12 teachers
teacher leaders
target_learning_goals: demonstrating discrete professional competencies
personalized professional growth
examples: Teachers identify a credential, pursue learning at a time and location they choose, gather and submit evidence such as portfolios, video, student work, or classroom observations, and earn a digital badge
key_sources: Barnett Berry and Karen Cator. (2016). Micro-credentials: Driving teacher learning & leadership. Center for Teaching Quality and Digital Promise. http://teachingquality.org/micro-credentials

article_title: Accelerating Change: How Education Technology Developers Can Jump-Start a New Adult Education Market
citation: DeSchryver, David A., with Deirdre Dlugoleski. (2015). Accelerating Change: How education technology developers can jump-start a new adult education market. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Adult ed-tech should enable stackable, portable micro-credentials and employer-connected accelerated learning
description: The report recommends that adult ed-tech developers use micro-credentials and digital badges to "breathe life into the policy objectives of “stackable credentials” and “portable credentials" emphasized under WIOA. Stackable credentials accumulate over time to build qualifications; portable credentials are recognized in other settings such as educational institutions, industries, or employers. It also recommends accelerated learning models (e.g., coding bootcamps) that give students "just enough training to get started in a new career" and connect them with partner companies for employment, extending these to low-skilled adults.
requirements: Credentials must be recognized and accepted as verifying qualifications in other settings such as educational institutions, other industries, or employing companies
constraints: The report notes accelerated learning programs currently work outside traditional workforce and higher education models, and connections to adult learning programs are only beginning
target_learners: Adult learners seeking better jobs or career advancement, including low-skilled adults
target_learning_goals: Occupational and workforce skills
Recognized, portable qualifications
examples: Digital Promise is building a coalition to develop a micro-credential system for K-12 educators; General Assembly and Flatiron are creating bridge programs and partnerships to put adult learners on track for accelerated programs
key_sources: DeSchryver, David A., with Deirdre Dlugoleski. (2015). Accelerating Change: How education technology developers can jump-start a new adult education market. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/29f39d7d-87f2-4e1e-920e-0c1ce86035cc

article_title: Pathways Unlocked: A Learner-Centered Toolkit for Usable Learning & Employment Record Technologies
citation: Digital Promise. (2025). Pathways Unlocked: A Learner-Centered Toolkit for Usable Learning & Employment Record Technologies. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Six best practices for embedding IUX across the LER project lifecycle
description: The toolkit enumerates six best practices: define inclusivity and accessibility goals early, incorporate research and user empathy early on, test and validate with learners on an ongoing basis, utilize established inclusive design principles, follow up with continuous improvement, and collaborate with a diverse project team and partners. It states that "Embedding IUX early saves time and improves outcomes by addressing barriers related to ability, background, and access." The practices span planning, development, testing, and post-launch improvement.
requirements: Goals should align with the identified needs of the intended learner audience
target_learners: project teams designing or implementing LER technologies for diverse learners and workers
target_learning_goals: accessible, authentic, and practical LER technology design
examples: The IUX Integration Planning Template operationalizes the practices across six practice areas with intent, actions, involvement, and measures of success
