title: Professional learning questionnaire characterizing curriculum-based professional learning across districts and schools
description: A questionnaire gathering information on professional learning in each district and its schools, grounded in a definition of curriculum-based professional learning (CBPL) as learning that supports implementation and sustained use of specific curriculum with integrity to the design while adapting to student needs. It includes four sections: basic district facts including built-in professional learning hours; types of professional learning structures such as PLCs and summer institutes with average monthly time; alignment with "11 CBPL features, including whether it is individualized or student focused"; and ratings of CBPL and HQIM implementation for each school. constraints: The report notes professional learning resources and supports vary dramatically across districts and remain largely hidden to external actors

article_title: The Arc of Dual Enrollment: Access, Struggle, and What Makes Success Possible
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Blanchard, A., & Roldan-Rueda, D. (2026). The arc of dual enrollment: Access, struggle, and what makes success possible. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Dual Enrollment Equity Pathway (DEEP) framework of four equity-oriented practice areas
description: The Dual Enrollment Equity Pathway (DEEP) framework, developed by the Community College Research Center, organizes what distinguishes equity-oriented dual enrollment programs from conventional ones. The brief states it "identifies four practice areas": "outreach to underserved students; alignment of dual enrollment coursework to postsecondary pathways; advising and exploration; and, most relevant here, high-quality instruction and academic support that responds quickly when students are struggling." The framework shifts focus from eligibility to supports in place, which the authors present as consistent with their findings.
requirements: Programs must invest in support infrastructure, which the authors say should be treated as a core program cost rather than an optional enhancement
constraints: The framework is attributed to Fink et al. (2023) and CCRC; the brief endorses it as consistent with its findings rather than testing it
target_learners: High school students in dual enrollment, especially students from low-income and first-generation backgrounds
target_learning_goals: College enrollment and success in college-level coursework during high school
examples: The brief cites research on high-performing programs identifying scaffolding coursework, quick response to struggling students, and structured academic support as the practices that improve outcomes
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Blanchard, A., & Roldan-Rueda, D. (2026). The arc of dual enrollment: Access, struggle, and what makes success possible. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681344

article_title: The Arc of Dual Enrollment: Access, Struggle, and What Makes Success Possible
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Blanchard, A., & Roldan-Rueda, D. (2026). The arc of dual enrollment: Access, struggle, and what makes success possible. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: OUSD open-access dual enrollment support model with the Point Person role
description: Oakland Unified School District's support model for open-access dual enrollment centers on the Point Person: "a designated K–12 staff member in each dual enrollment classroom whose explicit role is to stay in proactive contact with dual enrollment students throughout the semester, track progress in coordination with both high school and college instructors, and reach out before small difficulties become insurmountable ones." It is paired with school-day academic support, navigation assistance, and professional development, and the program reports an average pass rate of 83 percent, reaching 90 to 91 percent in recent semesters.
requirements: Investment in proactive outreach staffing, integrated academic support, navigation assistance, and instructor professional development
constraints: The model is described in a companion case study (Terrell et al., 2026b); this brief reports it as a single-district example without causal evaluation
target_learners: High school students across a wide range of academic backgrounds, including many from low-income and first-generation backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Passing dual enrollment courses and navigating college systems and expectations
examples: OUSD achieved an average pass rate of 83 percent across the program while maintaining open access, with recent semesters reaching 90 to 91 percent

article_title: The Arc of Dual Enrollment: Access, Struggle, and What Makes Success Possible
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Blanchard, A., & Roldan-Rueda, D. (2026). The arc of dual enrollment: Access, struggle, and what makes success possible. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Build intentional support infrastructure for dual enrollment rather than restricting access as a protective strategy
description: Because achievement-based eligibility thresholds screen out capable students while leaving underlying barriers intact, the brief recommends investing in deliberate student supports instead of tightening readiness criteria. It states that "Scaffolding coursework, responding quickly when students are struggling, and providing structured academic support—rather than imposing enrollment screens—are the practices that improve outcomes," and that "Support infrastructure should be treated as a core program cost, not an optional enhancement added after enrollment decisions are made."
requirements: Districts must fund support infrastructure as a core program cost and prepare faculty and staff for college-concurrent environments
constraints: Applies where dual enrollment is designed as an on-ramp for students who would not otherwise access advanced coursework; the brief notes findings may feel like edge cases where it functions mainly as acceleration
target_learners: High school students in or considering dual enrollment, particularly students from low-income and first-generation backgrounds
target_learning_goals: College enrollment, dual enrollment course success, and equitable access to advanced coursework
examples: The brief recommends districts audit dual enrollment pass rates disaggregated by student subgroup to determine whether outcomes reflect preparation gaps or support gaps

article_title: Rethinking English Learner Reclassification in California: What Research Says about the State's Criteria
citation: Faulkner-Bond, M. (2026). Rethinking English Learner reclassification in California: What research says about the state's criteria. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resource/finding-the-sweet-spot-for-english-learner-reclassification/
title: Maintain a rigorous, validated English proficiency threshold as the statewide standard for exiting English Learner status
description: The principle holds that the statewide standard for exiting EL status should be a rigorous and validated proficiency threshold rather than additional achievement-based requirements. The study found ELPAC overall PL 4 is the "sweet spot" — the most robust indicator that language is no longer the primary driver of achievement differences — and recommends maintaining it as the Criterion 1 standard. Additional criteria may be used only for specific circumstances, such as PL 3 students already demonstrating strong academic achievement.
requirements: A validated proficiency assessment threshold (ELPAC overall PL 4) established through statistical comparison against achievement outcomes
constraints: Applies to California's EL reclassification policy context and the ELPAC assessment; the brief recommends engaging the field on Criteria 2 and 3 so they do not become unnecessary barriers if Criterion 4 is removed
target_learners: English Learner students in grades 3 through 8 and 11 in California
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification of English proficiency for reclassification and equitable access to grade-level instruction
examples: The WestEd/CDE study compared ELPAC overall performance levels against SBAC English language arts performance across grades 3 through 8 and 11 using data from more than 3 million students

article_title: What Educational Research Looked Like When Scores Were Rising: A Comparative Analysis of AERA Conference Programs, 2005-2014 and 2022-2025
citation: Quesen, S. (2026). What educational research looked like when scores were rising: A comparative analysis of AERA conference programs, 2005–2014 and 2022–2025. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Protect stable, nonpartisan federal research infrastructure because all educational research depends on it regardless of research focus
description: The principle holds that federal data systems—NAEP, longitudinal surveys, and enrollment tracking—are shared infrastructure that serves research across the ideological spectrum, so protecting them should be prioritized "independent of changing federal and state policy priorities." The author cites nearly $900 million in IES grant cuts and reports that nearly every one of the 11 most important education studies since 2002 drew on IES data infrastructure.
requirements: Sustained federal funding for data collection systems such as NAEP, longitudinal surveys, and enrollment tracking
constraints: Federal research priorities have swung in different directions across administrations, making infrastructure vulnerable to partisan shifts

Policymakers at all levels of government
target_learning_goals: Maintaining the evidence base for educational policy and practice
examples: The report cites the elimination of nearly $900 million in IES grants and three fourths of National Science Foundation education funding as threats to fundamental data collection systems.

article_title: An Evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: A 1-Year Follow-Up on Math Achievement. Findings from an Arnold Ventures Grant
citation: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2026). An Evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: A 1-Year Follow-Up on Math Achievement. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Air Tutors high-dosage math tutoring program
description: Air Tutors is a high-dosage math tutoring program evaluated in two districts (Colorado and Texas). The implementation plan "called for students to attend 45-minute sessions 4–5 times per week for at least 10 weeks, totaling approximately 30 hours of tutoring", with adequate participation defined as at least 24 hours (80 percent of full dosage). This follow-up evaluation found no measurable long-term effects on statewide math assessments 1 year after tutoring concluded.
requirements: Students were intended to receive approximately 30 hours of tutoring via 45-minute sessions 4–5 times per week for at least 10 weeks.
constraints: In District B, student participation remained far below the intended 30 hours because scheduling disruptions and session cancellations limited consistent exposure.
target_learners: Students in grades 4, 5, and 6 in two school districts (District A in Colorado, District B in Texas)
target_learning_goals: Math achievement as measured by statewide standardized summative assessments
examples: The evaluation matched treatment students to observationally similar non-tutored comparison students in District A (CMAS) and District B (STAAR).

article_title: Expanding Equitable Access to Bilingual Education in California's Silicon Valley: Analysis and Recommendations
citation: Expanding Equitable Access to Bilingual Education in California's Silicon Valley: Analysis and Recommendations. (2026). https://www.wested.org
title: Conditions-for-success framework: additive bilingualism and shared bilingual conditions benefit all English Learner programs, not only formal bilingual models
description: The report organizes its analysis around a set of conditions critical to the success of any program for English Learners, treating bilingual educational opportunity as "a range of conditions that are critical to the success of all educational programs for students who are English Learners." Central to this is additive bilingualism, "an approach whereby students acquire English while maintaining and developing their home language." The framework holds that conditions such as bilingually authorized staff assignment, staff who value other languages and cultures, home language learning opportunities, and partnerships with multilingual families support success in any English Learner program and create foundations for formal bilingual programs.
requirements: Assignment of bilingual instructors, which the report calls a requirement for bilingual programs that increases support for English Learner students in any type of program
constraints: The report notes LCAPs provide only limited information on English Learner program investments regionwide
target_learners: English Learner and Multilingual Learner students in K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: Bilingualism and biliteracy development alongside academic content learning in English and a partner language
examples: The study used this framework to examine how bilingual educational opportunities are reflected in Silicon Valley English Learner programs and resource allocation

citation: Harrington, H., Willis, J., Bishop, J. P., & Cazares-Minero, M. (2026). Highly mobile youth: How state policy and local implementation can work together to support youth. WestEd; Center for the Transformation of Schools, UCLA. https://www.wested.org
title: Cross-sector collaboration framework for supporting highly mobile youth
description: The report defines cross-sector work as "the process by which agencies/organizations across two or more areas of focus—such as education, housing, and so on—share information, resources, and activities to advance shared goals or a unified vision." It uses a framework of cross-sector collaboration with dimensions of aligned supports, monitoring and accountability, and prevention as the coding structure for interviews and policy documents. Aligned systems are argued to improve service delivery, maximize limited resources, and shift practice from reactive to preventative.

School attendance, grade-level promotion, and graduation

citation: Harrington, H., Willis, J., Bishop, J. P., & Cazares-Minero, M. (2026). Highly mobile youth: How state policy and local implementation can work together to support youth. WestEd; Center for the Transformation of Schools, UCLA. https://www.wested.org
title: Colorado Educational Stability Grant Program (HB 18-1306)
description: A state grant program established in 2018 through HB 18-1306 providing 3-year grants to districts and other education providers to build community partnerships addressing barriers to school stability for highly mobile students. The legislation "appropriated approximately $2.8 million in its first year," with roughly $800,000 per year awarded in competitive grants in the first 2 years and recent appropriations increasing to about $1.04 million in FY 2024–25. It supports strategies to improve attendance, grade-level promotion, and graduation while reducing disciplinary incidents and dropout, and requires coordination with local and state agencies.

Ongoing program subject to annual appropriations

Attendance
Grade-level promotion
Graduation and completion

article_title: Making Dual Enrollment Work: Solving the Access-Success Paradox with OUSD's Point Person Model
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: The Point Person: an embedded OUSD staff member supporting each dual enrollment classroom
description: The point person is an OUSD staff member—typically a classroom teacher, occasionally a counselor or other school employee—embedded in every dual enrollment classroom alongside the Peralta instructor. The role is defined by six functions: the point person "is present during college instruction alongside the Peralta instructor," holds the classroom on off days, monitors progress through the college's learning management system, coordinates interventions, bridges communication between instructor, students, staff, and families, and manages logistics. The model evolved organically over 11 years of problem-solving rather than from research or policy mandates, and was then systematized.
requirements: Point people must know the students, understand high school culture, and can convey differences between college expectations and adolescent learners' realities
constraints: Funding arrangements vary by site with no single formula; the report notes floating-staff arrangements result in less relationship continuity
target_learners: High school students in dual enrollment courses, predominantly first-generation students, students from low-income backgrounds, and students of color
target_learning_goals: College course success and pass rates in dual enrollment coursework
examples: In every OUSD dual enrollment classroom the point person sits alongside the Peralta instructor, holds off-day sessions, checks Canvas gradebooks weekly, and coordinates interventions for struggling students.
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681373

article_title: Making Dual Enrollment Work: Solving the Access-Success Paradox with OUSD's Point Person Model
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Embedded two-adult classroom: college instruction delivered on the high school campus with a familiar school-based adult present
description: OUSD delivers college courses on high school campuses during the school day, taught by Peralta instructors with an OUSD point person present—a dynamic some educators describe as team teaching. This "college comes to you" approach removes transportation barriers and integrates dual enrollment into students' daily schedules. During instruction the point person's presence provides students continuity and familiarity and gives instructors local knowledge and classroom management support. Point people scaffold students' agency, encouraging them to move from asking the point person questions to approaching the college instructor directly.
requirements: A funded point person (teaching line, second prep, assigned duty, or floating staff) assigned to each section, plus partnership agreements between district and college
constraints: Point person engagement varies from active classroom management to a less active but available presence; the model depends on Peralta instructors traveling to high school campuses
target_learners: High school students taking college courses, including students intimidated by or uncertain about approaching college instructors
target_learning_goals: Engagement with college-level instruction and development of student agency and confidence
examples: At one school students meet the Peralta instructor on Tuesdays and Fridays for 90-minute blocks; on Wednesdays the point person leads a shorter session for asynchronous work, quizzes, and project support.
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681373

article_title: Making Dual Enrollment Work: Solving the Access-Success Paradox with OUSD's Point Person Model
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: The access–success paradox and its resolution through embedded support infrastructure
description: The report names the access–success paradox: the assumption "that expanding access to more students who do not typically participate in advanced coursework must necessarily be accompanied by declining success, particularly for the students with the most to gain from expanded opportunity." Policy attention focuses on removing entry barriers while neglecting what enables enrolled students to succeed. OUSD's experience provides the report's answer: open-access dual enrollment can achieve equitable outcomes, but only when vague commitments to student support are transformed into concrete, systematic infrastructure—an embedded adult, continuous monitoring, proactive response to struggles, and structured communication between systems.
requirements: Intentional, resourced support infrastructure embedded in course structure rather than offered as an external add-on service
constraints: The report offers OUSD as an existence proof, "not a prescription to be replicated exactly"; support of this kind is described as not very affordable
target_learners: High school students historically underserved in advanced coursework, including Black and Hispanic students, students with disabilities, and English Learners
target_learning_goals: Equitable participation and success in college coursework while in high school
examples: OUSD pairs open eligibility (no GPA requirements, no prerequisites, no teacher recommendations) with the point person model, achieving scale of nearly 70 sections per semester with an 83 percent average pass rate.
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681373

article_title: Making Dual Enrollment Work: Solving the Access-Success Paradox with OUSD's Point Person Model
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Invest in professional learning and partnership infrastructure for both college instructors and school-based support staff
description: The report finds the point person model functions because both sides receive training. Before entering the classroom, new instructors attend a course agreement meeting; they then "participate in professional development sessions at least twice per semester on topics that include adolescent brain development, mastery-based grading, and scaffolding strategies." OUSD partners with San Francisco State University to offer courses and stipends for dual enrollment instructors, while point people receive tools, templates, and training with autonomy to adapt to context. This dual investment creates a shared understanding of student needs and instructional strategies.
requirements: A dedicated district coordination team, partnership agreements with the community college, and funding for stipends and professional development
constraints: The report quotes district staff that the model is not very affordable; scaling requires deliberate investment in staffing, professional development, and institutional commitment
target_learners: High school students in dual enrollment courses
target_learning_goals: Effective college-level instruction adapted to high school contexts; consistent support for student success
examples: A 20-year instructor described the professional development as revealing a new level of teaching, and a college dean observed that the district specialist effectively taught one instructor to teach.

article_title: Declining Enrollment in America's Public Schools: How States Can Respond Strategically
citation: Hahnel, C. & Willis, J. (2026). Declining enrollment in America's public schools: How states can respond strategically. Bellwether; WestEd. https://www.bellwether.org
title: Use dynamic hold-harmless policies or tapering mechanisms so funding adjusts gradually as enrollment shrinks, rather than permanent hold-harmless provisions
description: This principle holds that state funding formulas should phase down support gradually as enrollment declines rather than preserving past funding levels indefinitely. The brief states that hold-harmless provisions without end dates "weaken the connection between funding and current student needs, and they forestall structural adjustments". A more sustainable approach uses dynamic hold-harmless policies or tapering mechanisms, giving districts time to rightsize budgets in response to smaller student counts. States such as Colorado, Maine, Texas, and California offer temporary relief through provisions allowing use of a recent prior-year or multiyear average enrollment.
requirements: Funding formulas must be updated to account for enrollment change, and any additional investment can be drawn from savings realized from declines in total statewide enrollment
constraints: The brief notes most state funding formulas are based on historic enrollment patterns, which work reasonably well when enrollment is steady but create fiscal and planning challenges when enrollment is growing or declining
target_learners: Students in districts experiencing enrollment decline, including growing shares of English Learners and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Preserving adequate resources for instruction while districts adjust budgets and programming to smaller student counts
examples: Colorado, Maine, Texas, and California allow districts to use a recent prior-year or multiyear average enrollment for funding purposes as temporary relief
key_sources: Hahnel, C. & Willis, J. (2026). Declining enrollment in America's public schools: How states can respond strategically. Bellwether; WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681594

article_title: Declining Enrollment in America's Public Schools: How States Can Respond Strategically
citation: Hahnel, C. & Willis, J. (2026). Declining enrollment in America's public schools: How states can respond strategically. Bellwether; WestEd. https://www.bellwether.org
title: Treat enrollment decline as an opportunity for strategic investment and system redesign rather than simply reducing spending, to avoid a vicious cycle of opt-out and disinvestment
description: The brief argues that how policymakers interpret declining enrollment shapes whether systems shrink haphazardly or strengthen. Viewing decline merely as a chance to reduce spending "risks exacerbating fiscal instability and undermining quality", prompting more families to opt out and creating a vicious cycle of eroding enrollment, resources, and public trust. Instead, state leaders should treat the moment as an opportunity for strategic, sustained investments that align spending with student and community needs, potentially enabling more personalized learning environments and reallocation toward evidence-based strategies.
requirements: State leaders must act proactively, mapping responses to long-range enrollment forecasts and evolving student needs rather than temporary downturns
constraints: The brief warns that without clear and consistent messaging, enrollment declines risk being framed solely as a crisis, which could undermine trust and make it harder for local leaders to act
target_learners: Students in K–12 public school systems experiencing sustained enrollment decline
target_learning_goals: Strengthening system quality, resilience, and public confidence so districts can continue serving students effectively through demographic transition
examples: The brief recommends states spotlight districts adopting promising new school designs, facility plans, staffing models, or cross-sector partnerships amid shrinking enrollment, and encourage innovation such as personalized learning models, expanded career pathways, and flexible scheduling
key_sources: Hahnel, C. & Willis, J. (2026). Declining enrollment in America's public schools: How states can respond strategically. Bellwether; WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681594

citation: UNESCO. (2022). Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org

Ethics of AI
AI techniques and applications
AI system design

citation: Miao, Fengchun; Shiohira, Kelly; Lao, Natalie. (2024). AI competency framework for students. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-students
title: Three progression levels of AI competency: Understand, Apply, Create
description: The framework structures competency development across three progression levels: "Understand", "Apply", and "Create". article_title: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Students
citation: Miao, Fengchun; Shiohira, Kelly; Lao, Natalie. (2024). AI competency framework for students. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-students
title: Integrate AI learning objectives into official school curricula to prepare students for the AI era
description: The publication argues that because artificial intelligence is increasingly integral to life, education systems must proactively prepare students as responsible users and co-creators of AI. It states that "Integrating AI learning objectives into official school curricula is crucial for students globally to engage with AI safely and meaningfully", and offers the competency framework as a tool for this integration.
requirements: Educators and curriculum bodies adopt AI learning objectives within official school curricula
target_learners: School students globally
target_learning_goals: Safe and meaningful engagement with AI
Citizenship preparation for the AI era
examples: The framework details curricular goals and domain-specific pedagogical methodologies to support curricular integration

Lifelong AI learning

article_title: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers
citation: Miao, Fengchun; Cukurova, Mutlu. (2024). AI competency framework for teachers. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org
title: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers: 15 competencies across five dimensions
description: The AI Competency Framework for Teachers defines "the knowledge, skills, and values teachers must master in the age of AI." It organizes teacher AI competence into "15 competencies across five dimensions": Human-centred mindset, Ethics of AI, AI foundations and applications, AI pedagogy, and AI for professional learning. The framework was developed to address the gap left by countries that have not defined teacher AI competencies or built training programmes.
requirements: Countries adopting the framework should develop national AI competency frameworks and teacher training programmes based on it
constraints: Few countries have currently defined teacher AI competencies or developed national programmes to train teachers in AI
target_learners: teachers
target_learning_goals: AI-related knowledge, skills, and values for teaching in the AI era
examples: The publication outlines the five dimensions and positions itself as a global reference guiding national framework development, teacher training, and assessment parameter design

title: Three progression levels — Acquire, Deepen, Create — structure teacher AI competency development

This progression axis describes how teachers advance from initial acquisition of AI-related competencies through deepening them to creating new applications and practices. requirements: Training programmes and assessment parameters should be designed to reflect the three progression levels
target_learners: teachers

article_title: AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle
citation: Ruiz, P., and Noakes, S. (2025). AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/272
title: Four-phase AI-enabled edtech adoption cycle for districts
description: The article organizes district adoption of AI-enabled edtech into a cycle of four phases: vision and planning, implementation, ongoing evaluation, and scaling and sustaining. Each phase pairs a goal statement with key challenges and recommendations, e.g. planning requires districts to "move beyond reactive purchasing decisions and establish strategic frameworks that align technology with clear learning objectives and pedagogical goals." The cycle frames adoption as continuous rather than a one-time purchase.
requirements: Districts must establish strategic frameworks aligned with learning objectives and pedagogical goals before purchasing
constraints: The framework addresses AI-enabled edtech specifically, with criteria such as algorithmic transparency, bias mitigation, and data privacy
target_learners: K-12 district leaders and procurement staff
target_learning_goals: Effective selection, implementation, and sustained use of AI-enabled educational technology
examples: The brief lists per-phase challenges such as siloed processes, reliance on sales pitches, insufficient measurement, unused tools, funding constraints, and market fragmentation
key_sources: Ruiz, P., and Noakes, S. (2025). AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/272

article_title: AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle
citation: Ruiz, P., and Noakes, S. (2025). AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/272
title: Align edtech procurement with district needs and strategic priorities using specialized AI evaluation criteria
description: The article recommends that districts plan AI-enabled edtech purchases through formal, cross-functional processes rather than reacting to sales pitches. It states that "AI-enabled tools require specialized evaluation criteria that address unique considerations, including algorithmic transparency, bias mitigation, data privacy implications, and the need for ongoing monitoring of AI system performance and outputs." Recommendations include cross-functional teams, formal planning processes, and data-driven needs assessments.
requirements: Cross-functional collaboration so technical requirements and pedagogical objectives are both met
Data-driven needs assessments
constraints: Applies to AI-enabled tools, which the article says need specialized criteria beyond general edtech evaluation
target_learners: District administrators and procurement teams
target_learning_goals: Selecting AI-enabled edtech that aligns with learning objectives
examples: The vision and planning phase lists key challenges of siloed processes, lack of clear vision, and reliance on sales pitches

Attention to hardware requirements, scheduling constraints, and classroom logistics

title: Build evaluation frameworks with faster metrics and role-specific data access to time contract decisions
description: The article identifies a timing misalignment: districts must make contract renewal decisions before reliable outcome data arrive, since state test results typically arrive in mid- to late summer after procurement cycles conclude. It recommends that districts "establish comprehensive evaluation frameworks that provide role-specific data access and identify faster, more reliable metrics beyond annual assessments to enable timely decision-making."

Adverse incident reporting systems
Early quality indicators including keyword detection at the input and output layers

article_title: Free to Fail or On-Track to College
citation: Stevens, W. D., Allensworth, E. M., Pareja, A. S., de la Torre, M., Gwynne, J. A., Rosenkranz, T., & Sebastian, J. (2014). Free to Fail or On-Track to College: An Introduction to the UChicago CCSR Research Series. UChicago CCSR Research Brief. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Focus on Freshmen Study
description: The Focus on Freshmen Study is a UChicago CCSR research project examining the transition to high school and the school practices that contribute to ninth-grade performance. It followed a cohort "as they moved from eighth grade in spring 2008, through the ninth grade year (2008-09) and into tenth grade in 2009-10," including about 22,000 students. It combined district-wide records, student and teacher surveys, longitudinal in-depth interviews of 55 students and their teachers, and classroom observations in English and math.
requirements: District-wide student records, student and teacher surveys, longitudinal interviews, and classroom observations in eighth and ninth grade
target_learners: Ninth-grade high school students in Chicago Public Schools
target_learning_goals: Student engagement in coursework, course performance, and graduation readiness
examples: The study examined how teacher support, classroom instruction, and school practices lead students to be engaged in their work and earn good grades
key_sources: Stevens, W. D., Allensworth, E. M., Pareja, A. S., de la Torre, M., Gwynne, J. A., Rosenkranz, T., & Sebastian, J. (2014). Free to Fail or On-Track to College: An Introduction to the UChicago CCSR Research Series. UChicago CCSR Research Brief. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/free-fail-or-track-college

article_title: Free to Fail or On-Track to College
citation: Stevens, W. D., Allensworth, E. M., Pareja, A. S., de la Torre, M., Gwynne, J. A., Rosenkranz, T., & Sebastian, J. (2014). Free to Fail or On-Track to College: An Introduction to the UChicago CCSR Research Series. UChicago CCSR Research Brief. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Instruction Study classroom survey dataset and analysis
description: The Instruction Study used district-wide high school student and teacher survey reports of experiences in specific classes to identify instructional elements associated with students' grades and gains on ACT's EPAS system. Students in grades 9-12 in all CPS non-alternative high schools were surveyed in fall 2009 and grouped into classes using transcript data on course number, period, and teacher ID. The grades analysis was based on 58,824 students in 2,575 classrooms in 88 high schools; the test-score-gains analysis covered 8,754 students in 794 classrooms in 70 high schools.
requirements: Survey reports tied to specific academic classes (English, mathematics, science, social studies, world language) using transcript data on course number, period, and teacher ID
constraints: Test score gains analysis restricted to subjects and grades for which standardized test scores existed
target_learners: High school students in grades 9-12 in Chicago Public Schools
target_learning_goals: Classroom instruction quality and its relationship to grades and test score gains
examples: Relationships of classroom instruction to student achievement were discerned through statistical models adjusted for students’ background characteristics and prior achievement

article_title: College Prep for All? What We've Learned from Chicago's Efforts
citation: Elaine Allensworth, Takako Nomi, Nicholas Montgomery, & Valerie E. Lee. (2008). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Consequences of Ninth-Grade Course Taking in Algebra and English on Academic Outcomes in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Conceptual model of curriculum-policy effects flowing through the school's instructional program
description: The article proposes a conceptual model in which a curricular policy mandate affects student outcomes only through changes in the school's instructional program: "the courses, content, and pedagogy that students receive". Enrollment depends on both program structure and student background; courses plus student response shape ninth-grade learning, which should then propagate to later achievement and post-secondary outcomes. The model guided the study's proximal (end of Grade 9) and distal (end of high school, college) outcome measures.
requirements: Beneficial effects require that schools' instructional programs adjust to the policy as expected and that students respond with better freshman-year performance
constraints: The article states some schools may have difficulty enacting substantial instructional changes, and students who would otherwise take remedial classes may not respond as expected
target_learners: first-time ninth graders in urban public high schools
target_learning_goals: college-preparatory mathematics and English coursework and subsequent academic outcomes
examples: The study measured 15 student-level outcomes at ninth grade and end of high school, mapped onto the model's proximal and distal pathways
key_sources: Elaine Allensworth, Takako Nomi, Nicholas Montgomery, & Valerie E. Lee. (2008). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Consequences of Ninth-Grade Course Taking in Algebra and English on Academic Outcomes in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu

article_title: College Prep for All? What We've Learned from Chicago's Efforts
citation: Elaine Allensworth, Takako Nomi, Nicholas Montgomery, & Valerie E. Lee. (2008). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Consequences of Ninth-Grade Course Taking in Algebra and English on Academic Outcomes in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Universal college-preparatory mandates need instructional supports, not just course requirements, to improve outcomes
description: The article argues that simply mandating rigorous courses for all is insufficient: schools attempting detracking face parent resistance, technical difficulties teaching heterogeneous classrooms, and low teacher expectations. It concludes that "a policy of universalizing college-preparatory courses may have little chance of success if it does not address such issues as professional development around instruction, widespread support for the policy among the school community (teachers and parents), and extra support for low-ability students." The Chicago evaluation bears this out: enrollment changed, but achievement did not.
requirements: Professional development around instruction, school-community support, and extra support courses for struggling students accompany the mandate
constraints: The article notes successful detracking schools appear exceptional, with shared belief in diversity and inclusive pedagogical practices
target_learners: all ninth graders, including low-ability and special education students in urban districts
target_learning_goals: success in college-preparatory coursework in place of remedial tracks
examples: Chicago mandated Algebra I and English I for all ninth graders in 1997 without the accompanying instructional supports the literature identifies, and test scores and college entrance did not improve
key_sources: Elaine Allensworth, Takako Nomi, Nicholas Montgomery, & Valerie E. Lee. (2008). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Consequences of Ninth-Grade Course Taking in Algebra and English on Academic Outcomes in Chicago. article_title: Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego
citation: Babineau, K., Shah, Z., Jacobs, B., Miller, A., Alvarado, B., Aguirre, N., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., & Young, V. (2025). Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/254
title: Inclusive Innovation model: a phased process in which people closest to the challenge lead, participate in, and benefit from innovation
description: The Inclusive Innovation model is a formalized co-design framework guiding the San Diego STEM Pathways Initiative. The report defines it as "a formalized process by which the people closest to the challenge lead, participate in, and benefit from innovation". Figure 3 presents phases from Readiness and Connect & Commit through Inquire & Investigate, Design & Develop, Implement & Iterate, and Sustain & Scale, each with associated artifacts such as a Community Charter, Solution Prototype, and Codified Solution. The Community Advisory Committee used the model to structure its collaboration, moving from establishing core values and root cause analysis to developing solution concepts.
requirements: A cross-sector coalition with an organizing intermediary to convene partners and structure the process
Trust-building time, since the Connect and Commit pillar often takes time and is an ongoing process throughout the life of the project
constraints: The report describes early-phase use only: the committee was transitioning into the Implement & Iterate phase, with solution concepts not yet tested
target_learners: Excluded learners in Pre-K through postsecondary STEM pathways in the San Diego region
target_learning_goals: STEM career readiness and access to inclusive education-to-workforce pathways
examples: The CAC co-designed a Community Charter, conducted a Root Cause Analysis of past cross-sector collaborations, and developed problems of practice that became the foundation for solution statements and concepts
key_sources: Babineau, K., Shah, Z., Jacobs, B., Miller, A., Alvarado, B., Aguirre, N., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., & Young, V. (2025). Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/254

article_title: Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego
citation: Babineau, K., Shah, Z., Jacobs, B., Miller, A., Alvarado, B., Aguirre, N., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., & Young, V. (2025). Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/254
title: San Diego STEM Pathways Community Advisory Committee (CAC)
description: The CAC is a cross-sector coalition formed in 2024 to lay the groundwork for regional STEM pathway initiatives. The report describes "a robust coalition of local and regional partners working to ensure alignment with the local economy, community context, and values". This 14-member committee spans early childhood education, K-12, postsecondary, workforce development, community-based organizations, and philanthropy. Members meet monthly, connect asynchronously between meetings, and have established collaboration principles, engaged learners and industry leaders in co-design, and developed four solution concepts for STEM pathways.
requirements: Members meet on a monthly basis and connect asynchronously between meetings to work toward their goals
Commitment to long-term, sustainable leadership and transparent partnerships across sectors
target_learners: Excluded learners across Pre-K, K-12, and postsecondary education in San Diego
target_learning_goals: Building career-ready STEM competencies through community-aligned pathways
examples: Committee members developed the initiative's Core Values, co-designed a Community Charter, and voted to select four solution concepts in subgroups based on interest and expertise
key_sources: Babineau, K., Shah, Z., Jacobs, B., Miller, A., Alvarado, B., Aguirre, N., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., & Young, V. (2025). Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/254

article_title: Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego
citation: Babineau, K., Shah, Z., Jacobs, B., Miller, A., Alvarado, B., Aguirre, N., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., & Young, V. (2025). Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/254
title: Co-design principles for regional STEM pathways: Pre-K-to-career alignment, flexible entry, stackable credentials, industry recognition, and representative instructors
description: During the Inquire & Investigate phase, the CAC developed five principles to shape regional STEM pathways: "Align STEM pathways from Pre-K to career"; "Create flexible entry points for all learners"; "Offer stackable skills-focused certifications to ensure smooth credit transfer between institutions"; "Recognize diverse workforce and industry as key to K-12 education"; and "Learners see themselves in instructors, mentors, and industry professionals". The committee also adopted interaction principles for its own collaboration, including open and full collaboration, flexibility, and a win-win mindset.
requirements: Cross-sector collaboration among K-12, postsecondary, workforce, and community partners to align pathways across institutions
constraints: The principles were developed by the San Diego CAC to guide shaping and refining pathways in that region
target_learners: All learners from Pre-K through career, including excluded learners in the San Diego region
target_learning_goals: STEM skill recognition, credit transfer, and STEM identity development toward career pathways
examples: The CAC's pathway-shaping principles include stackable, skills-focused certifications designed to ensure smooth credit transfer between institutions

citation: Babineau, K., Shah, Z., Jacobs, B., Miller, A., Alvarado, B., Aguirre, N., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., & Young, V. (2025). Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/254
title: Four CAC-developed STEM pathway solution concepts (Inspire to Aspire, CIELO, ATGC, STEM SD Partner Exchange)
description: In the Design & Develop phase, advisors "voted to select four solution concepts and self-selected into subgroups based on their interest areas and expertise". Table 1 presents the concepts: Inspire to Aspire (career-connected professional learning for preschool–elementary educators to build student math and science confidence), CIELO (after-school STEM programs co-developed with families facing housing insecurity), ALL TOGETHER Get Connected (a place-based South Bay pilot spanning middle school STEM identity, high school career exploration, and paid college internships), and STEM SD Partner Exchange (an online repository of inclusive STEM pathway partners and resources).

constraints: Concepts were developed in early 2025 and had not yet been tested; members will move to testing throughout the year
target_learners: Preschool through elementary students, middle and high school students, college students, families facing housing insecurity, and homeless and foster youth in the San Diego region

examples: ATGC will pilot in South Bay leveraging Southwestern College innovations, combining expanded and work-based learning, early college credit, alternative assessments, and transfer pathways

article_title: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom
citation: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom. (2014). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/microcredentials
title: Digital Promise system of educator micro-credentials for recognizing teacher competencies
description: The article describes a system Digital Promise is building "to provide professional educators a new way to identify competencies they are developing and gain recognition for the skills they learn throughout their careers." It addresses the gap that teachers "often don't have the opportunity to demonstrate the full breadth of what they have learned, including in informal contexts." The system moves professional learning toward a competency-based model with multiple ways to learn, demonstrations of competence, and desired outcomes, and is supported by a platform for earning the credentials.
requirements: Teachers demonstrate competencies through performance-based artifacts such as lesson plans, student work samples, reflections, observations, videos, and peer or self evaluations
constraints: Receipt of a micro-credential is not a guarantee of teacher quality — it is a signal of competency with a specific skill
target_learners: practicing K-12 teachers and professional educators
target_learning_goals: demonstrating and gaining recognition for professional teaching competencies developed throughout a career
examples: Digital Promise launched a platform to support teachers in earning Deeper Learning micro-credentials
key_sources: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom. (2014). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/microcredentials

article_title: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom
citation: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom. (2014). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/microcredentials
title: Deeper Learning framework of six competency categories
description: The article presents Deeper Learning as "an umbrella term for the skills, understandings, and mindsets students must possess to succeed in today's jobs and civic life." The framework comprises "six categories of strategies that are essential for students to achieve at high levels": mastering core academic content, thinking critically and solving complex problems, working collaboratively, communicating effectively, learning how to learn, and developing academic mindsets. Each category is elaborated with observable student behaviors, such as transferring knowledge of core facts and concepts to a novel context and persisting and adjusting when an approach is not working.
requirements: Each competency is defined by observable student behaviors that can be demonstrated and assessed
target_learners: all K-12 students
target_learning_goals: mastering academic content, critical thinking and problem solving, collaboration, communication, self-directed learning, and academic mindsets
examples: The framework's six categories structure the 40 Deeper Learning micro-credentials described in the article
key_sources: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom. (2014). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/microcredentials

article_title: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom
citation: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom. (2014). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/microcredentials
title: Eight design characteristics of micro-credentials
description: The article enumerates the design characteristics of educator micro-credentials: they are "Bite-sized—focused on a specific, observable competency," subject-adaptable, research-based, teacher- and student-centered, personal and timely, portable as digital badges, transparent with publicly available assessment criteria, and performance-based. This list defines the reusable instructional design pattern the credential system follows, specifying how each credential is scoped, evidenced, and shared so that professional learning can be recognized in competency-based rather than time-based terms.
requirements: Each micro-credential targets a specific, observable competency and is demonstrated through artifacts with publicly available assessment criteria
target_learners: practicing K-12 teachers and professional educators
target_learning_goals: earning recognition for specific teaching competencies aligned to student needs
examples: Micro-credentials can be shared as digital badges in online platforms and adapted to multiple subject areas
key_sources: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom. (2014). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/microcredentials

article_title: Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception
citation: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://lvp.digitalpromiseglobal.org/
title: Learner variability as a universal characteristic embracing both struggling and thriving learners
description: The paper defines learner variability as a term describing all students, not only those with identified learning differences. It states that learner variability "embraces both students who struggle and those who thrive" because of natural variability in each person. Variability includes poverty, English learners, trauma, stereotype threat, working memory and attention challenges, and advanced learners who are bored by one-size-fits-all instruction.
requirements: Recognition that all students differ, grounded in learning sciences research showing these differences matter for learning
constraints: The paper notes the term is sometimes tightly defined to mean only struggling students, but rejects that narrower usage
target_learners: all K-12 learners, including students who struggle and those who thrive
target_learning_goals: understanding and addressing individual differences to support confident learning in school and beyond
examples: The paper illustrates variability with the student who already excels beyond the curriculum pace and is bored, and the learner with working memory or decoding challenges who retreats into silence
key_sources: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/b7b14506-0b46-4279-9f9e-675c694b06a6

article_title: Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception
citation: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://lvp.digitalpromiseglobal.org/
title: The science of the individual: pathways and context principles for understanding learner variability
description: Drawing on Todd Rose and colleagues, the paper presents the science of the individual as a framework resting on two notions: the object of interest is the individual, not the statistical average, and human individuals are remarkably variable. It depends on pathways (multiple routes exist to learn to read, so non-mainstream progress is not necessarily delay) and on the context principle, which holds that behavior results from an interaction between traits and situation.
requirements: Addressing the needs of the individual requires abandoning statistical-average thinking and attending to both pathways and context
constraints: The paper attributes this framework to Rose and colleagues rather than testing it; it is presented as a research-based account
target_learners: all learners, including children progressing on alternative reading pathways
target_learning_goals: understanding depth and breadth of learner variability to inform classroom learning
examples: Initial thought heralded a single progression for developing strong reading skills; current research shows multiple pathways exist, so children progressing differently may not have delays
key_sources: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/b7b14506-0b46-4279-9f9e-675c694b06a6

article_title: Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception
citation: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://lvp.digitalpromiseglobal.org/
title: The Learner Variability Project four-pillar framework: Content, Cognition, Social and Emotional Learning, and Student Background
description: The Learner Variability Project (LVP) at Digital Promise distills learning sciences research into Learner Factors organized under four pillars: Content, Cognition, Social and Emotional Learning, and Student Background. Each Factor includes an explanation of what it is and how it connects with other Factors, situated in the context of a learning goal, with a robust list of research-based strategies showing how research may be applied in practice and product development.
requirements: Factors must be situated in the context of a learning goal, given the context principle of variability
Strategies must be research-based and complement the Factors
constraints: Current Learner Models cover Math pre-K to 2nd grade, Reading pre-K to 3rd grade, and Reading and Writing 4th-6th grade, with others in development
target_learners: teachers and edtech developers serving the full diversity of learners rather than a mythical average
target_learning_goals: putting research insights at educators' fingertips to infuse instruction or products with evidence-based resources
examples: LVP aims to expedite addressing each learner's variability by distilling research into a comprehensive yet brief and accessible form with example strategies
key_sources: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/b7b14506-0b46-4279-9f9e-675c694b06a6

article_title: Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception
citation: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://lvp.digitalpromiseglobal.org/
title: Treat classroom challenges as design problems, not student problems, by starting from the assumption of learner variability
description: The paper argues that understanding learner variability informs design: if educators start from the assumption that there is a lot of variability among learners in each classroom, different decisions are made about how to create optimal environments to support learning. Combined with digital technology's flexibility and precision, this reframing makes classroom challenges "a design problem, not a student problem."
requirements: Start with the assumption that there is a lot of variability among learners in each classroom
constraints: The paper notes that gains have been slow to come in schools nationwide, with one-size-fits-all models continuing to under-serve nearly all students
target_learners: all K-12 learners in traditional school systems
target_learning_goals: creating optimal environments that support learning for each learner
examples: Digital Promise built the LVP systems to support teachers and edtech developers in addressing learner variability, putting evidence-based resources at their fingertips
key_sources: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/b7b14506-0b46-4279-9f9e-675c694b06a6

article_title: From Childcare to Educare: Inspiring Change in Early Childhood Education for Rural Tennessee
citation: Jacobs, B., Babineau, K., Parker, D. (2024). From Childcare to Educare: Inspiring Change in Early Childhood Education for Rural Tennessee. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/222
title: Boeren's Lifelong Learning Participation Model as a framework for adult learners' education participation
description: The article's primary guiding framework holds that 'participation in lifelong learning is determined by a number of nested and layered structural factors at the micro, meso, and macro levels.' The micro level covers individual behavioral and social characteristics such as motivation, confidence, race, gender, and geographic location; the meso level covers structures of education and training providers such as courses, class times, and online availability; the macro level covers state and country-level political and cultural climates. The study operationalizes the model by collecting data from service providers (micro) and TECTA administrators (meso) and interpreting findings against Tennessee and U.S. policy contexts (macro).
requirements: Data collection instruments must address all three levels; the study's research questions and interview schedules 'directly address aspects of these levels' to capture relationships among them.
target_learners: adult early childhood education providers, particularly rural learners and women of color
target_learning_goals: participation, persistence, and credential attainment in further education (CDA, associate, and bachelor's degrees)
examples: The study collected data from both service providers (micro level) and TECTA administrators (meso level) and presented findings considering the political and cultural realities of Tennessee and the United States (macro level).
key_sources: Jacobs, B., Babineau, K., Parker, D. (2024). From Childcare to Educare: Inspiring Change in Early Childhood Education for Rural Tennessee. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/222

article_title: From Childcare to Educare: Inspiring Change in Early Childhood Education for Rural Tennessee
citation: Jacobs, B., Babineau, K., Parker, D. (2024). From Childcare to Educare: Inspiring Change in Early Childhood Education for Rural Tennessee. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/222
title: TECTA: Tennessee Early Childhood Training Alliance
description: TECTA is 'a statewide program that provides free training and academic tuition support to childcare providers and administrators throughout the state of Tennessee.' It offers a free 30-hour orientation with instruction in five areas — center-based child care, infant/toddler care, family child care, school-age child care, and administrator training — after which participants become eligible for tuition assistance for coursework at any public higher education institution in Tennessee. Nine state and community colleges currently offer TECTA programs, which support workers pursuing the CDA, associate degree, and bachelor's degree, and provide CDA candidates with tuition assistance, textbooks, professional development, and application support.
requirements: Participation is open to any staff employed in a licensed child care facility in Tennessee; completing the free 30-hour orientation is the gateway to tuition assistance eligibility.
constraints: The program's stipend funds are limited and allocated on a first-come, first-served basis, creating financial barriers for those unable to secure funding promptly.
target_learners: childcare providers and administrators employed in licensed Tennessee child care facilities, including rural providers
target_learning_goals: early childhood education credentials (CDA, associate, bachelor's) and professional skills such as classroom management and professionalism
examples: Five focus groups with 80 service providers and one with 8 administrators were conducted between February and April 2024 to evaluate the program's benefits and barriers.
key_sources: Jacobs, B., Babineau, K., Parker, D. (2024). From Childcare to Educare: Inspiring Change in Early Childhood Education for Rural Tennessee. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/222

article_title: Recruitment and Retention: Pilot Solutions Designed by Teachers of Color (Phase I)
citation: Bland, J. & Smith, K. (2023, February). Recruitment and retention: Pilot solutions designed by teachers of color (Phase I). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/168
title: The Inclusive Innovation model: an equity-centered R&D process with five phases that prioritizes the voices of those most impacted
description: The report describes the Inclusive Innovation approach as "An equity-centered R&D model that engages communities—students, parents, families, and community leaders—in partnership with district leaders, educators, researchers, and developers to create novel solutions to complex educational challenges." It encompasses five phases: connect and commit, inquire and investigate, design and develop, implement and iterate, and sustain and scale. The model intentionally prioritizes the perspectives, experiences, and ideas of those most impacted by a challenge, and in this project it structured LEA Design Teams' work from problem identification through pilot launch.
requirements: Requires building relationships, trust, and a shared commitment to tackling a challenge in the connect and commit phase
constraints: The report covers only the design and launch phases; implementation results are deferred to a subsequent 2023 report
target_learners: Teachers of color in K-12 districts and charter networks
target_learning_goals: Recruiting and retaining teachers of color through locally contextualized solution design
examples: Five districts and one charter network used the model to assemble Design Teams, define problems of practice, create solution goals and theories of action, and launch pilots
key_sources: Bland, J. & Smith, K. (2023, February). Recruitment and retention: Pilot solutions designed by teachers of color (Phase I). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/168

article_title: Recruitment and Retention: Pilot Solutions Designed by Teachers of Color (Phase I)
citation: Bland, J. & Smith, K. (2023, February). Recruitment and retention: Pilot solutions designed by teachers of color (Phase I). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/168
title: Black Male Teacher Fellowship Program
description: One LEA created a fellowship for all of its Black male teachers, administrators, and staff in service of a goal to increase Black men in LEA teaching positions "by 25 in the next 5 years." The program creates "a very authentic safe space" and builds a brotherhood to retain Black males in the profession, meeting four times during the school year for two hours each during the workday. Initial meetings use personal-vulnerability exercises, and the fellowship doubles as a recruitment vehicle through tailgates, elementary classroom appearances, and connections with Black Student Unions and educator preparation programs.
requirements: Meetings scheduled during the workday so as not to impose additional demands on members' time
target_learners: Black male teachers, administrators, and staff in K-12 LEAs
target_learning_goals: Retention of Black male educators and recruitment of additional Black male teachers
examples: The first meeting used exercises requiring personal vulnerability; a participating teacher reported it "felt genuine, and it felt real"
key_sources: Bland, J. & Smith, K. (2023, February). Recruitment and retention: Pilot solutions designed by teachers of color (Phase I). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/168

article_title: Recruitment and Retention: Pilot Solutions Designed by Teachers of Color (Phase I)
citation: Bland, J. & Smith, K. (2023, February). Recruitment and retention: Pilot solutions designed by teachers of color (Phase I). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/168
title: Grow-Your-Own credential pathway for classified staff
description: One LEA implemented a Grow-Your-Own program "structured to set up pathways for classified staff to earn credentials—in part because classified staff in the LEA are, on the whole, more diverse than classroom teachers." It focuses on teacher assistants who already hold college degrees, partnering with four higher education institutions and the state teacher's union to offer varied transition-to-teaching licensure programs. The administrator estimated the LEA currently has 15 to 20 classified staff members working toward earning their teaching license, who will "serve as a pool of individuals to feed into our teacher pipeline down the road."
requirements: Partnerships with higher education institutions offering transition-to-teaching licensure programs that fit participants' learning and work-life balance
target_learners: Classified staff and teacher assistants with college degrees seeking teaching licensure
target_learning_goals: Earning teaching credentials and entering the local teacher pipeline
examples: The initiative is already in progress, with 15 to 20 classified staff members working toward licensure
key_sources: Bland, J. & Smith, K. (2023, February). Recruitment and retention: Pilot solutions designed by teachers of color (Phase I). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/168

article_title: Recruitment and Retention: Pilot Solutions Designed by Teachers of Color (Phase I)
citation: Bland, J. & Smith, K. (2023, February). Recruitment and retention: Pilot solutions designed by teachers of color (Phase I). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/168
title: Event design details—offsite venues, elevated BIPOC vendors, compelling speakers, and intentional branding—foster pride and engagement
description: Across the LEAs, Design Teams emphasized event-planning details that make events feel high in quality and foster pride and value among participating teachers. Efforts "included selecting offsite locations that would feel more special than holding events in school or LEA spaces; making choices about food that would appeal to attendees, including taking care to select and elevate BIPOC vendors; and selecting compelling outside speakers." LEAs also invested in language and branding, such as a meaningful logo, branded hoodies, and a social media presence for the Black Male Fellowship.
requirements: Planning choices must authentically represent the experiences of teachers of color, with teachers of color themselves planning the events
target_learners: Teachers of color participating in recruitment and retention events
target_learning_goals: Fostering a sense of pride, value, and community among teachers of color
examples: Regional convenings were held at a university on a professional development day, with meals catered from minority-owned businesses and a dean who is an educator of color as a speaker

article_title: From Rural Districts to Statewide Pathways: A Blueprint for Scaling Cybersecurity Workforce Development Through Regional Collaboration
citation: Babineau, K., Aso, C., Ganoo, K., Jacobs, B., Lenderman, K., Shah, Z., Smith, K., & Young, V. M. (2025). From Rural Districts to Statewide Pathways: A Blueprint for Scaling Cybersecurity Workforce Development Through Regional Collaboration. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/263
title: East Alabama Regional Cybersecurity Alliance (EARCA)
description: EARCA is a regional alliance established through collaborative efforts in Alabama Workforce Region 2 that aims to "expand economic opportunity in rural areas by bolstering the cybersecurity workforce ecosystem across multiple rural districts". It spans seven school districts (Anniston City, Etowah County, Oxford City, St. Clair County, Sylacauga City, Talladega City, and Talladega County), with more than 35,000 students positioned to engage, over half (52.5%) qualifying for free or reduced-price lunch. During SY 2024-25 it laid groundwork across partners, teachers, curricula (Project Lead the Way, TestOut, Code.org, plus IBM SkillsBuild), and student outreach, with each district launching at least one cybersecurity course in 2025-26.
requirements: Districts engage local industry and postsecondary partners to establish a supportive network within the regional alliance
Teachers identified to teach cybersecurity engage in professional development aligned with industry needs
constraints: Rural areas typically have to do more work with less capacity and funding, limiting availability of work-based learning
target_learners: high school students in rural Alabama districts, majority economically disadvantaged
target_learning_goals: cybersecurity technical skills and industry certifications such as CompTIA Security+
career awareness and work-based learning in cybersecurity
examples: Districts evaluated curricula, upskilled current teachers for the Security+ exam, and Digital Promise worked to connect state tech hubs with rural regions for work-based learning
key_sources: Babineau, K., Aso, C., Ganoo, K., Jacobs, B., Lenderman, K., Shah, Z., Smith, K., & Young, V. M. (2025). article_title: From Rural Districts to Statewide Pathways: A Blueprint for Scaling Cybersecurity Workforce Development Through Regional Collaboration
citation: Babineau, K., Aso, C., Ganoo, K., Jacobs, B., Lenderman, K., Shah, Z., Smith, K., & Young, V. M. (2025). From Rural Districts to Statewide Pathways: A Blueprint for Scaling Cybersecurity Workforce Development Through Regional Collaboration. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/263
title: Blueprint for Statewide Pathways Scaling (five-component theory of action)
description: The report's central framework is a theory of action for scaling career pathways statewide, consisting of "three critical layers": state-level actors, models, and policy/funding mechanisms; regional-level district cohorts, pathways design, and partnerships; and measurable outcomes across education and economic systems. It is operationalized through five complementary components—ACTIVATE (state and regional policy levers), ASSESS (employment market and skills opportunity), CREATE (K-12 pathways scale-up model), ALIGN (postsecondary and credentials landscape), and CONNECT (regional infrastructure)—each illustrated with Alabama Workforce Region 2 implementation. The framework emphasizes reciprocal state-regional interplay and strengthening existing relationships rather than creating new systems.
requirements: A lead organization with deep knowledge of the state's political landscape, credibility across sectors, and capacity to provide long-term continuity
Policies that incentivize coherence across the K-12, postsecondary and industry sectors
constraints: Specific policy contexts, industry landscapes, and educational structures will vary across regions and industries; the blueprint is a transferable approach rather than a fixed model
target_learners: K-12 students statewide, including rural learners and those from historically underserved communities
target_learning_goals: career-connected learning leading to industry-recognized credentials and postsecondary or direct employment entry in high-demand fields
examples: Alabama implementation mapped each component: the Workforce Pathways Diploma and Alabama Talent Triad under ACTIVATE, market assessment under ASSESS, a statewide district network under CREATE, dual enrollment and stackable credentials under ALIGN, and the Region 2 model under CONNECT
key_sources: Babineau, K., Aso, C., Ganoo, K., Jacobs, B., Lenderman, K., Shah, Z., Smith, K., & Young, V. M. (2025). From Rural Districts to Statewide Pathways: A Blueprint for Scaling Cybersecurity Workforce Development Through Regional Collaboration. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/263
title: Collaborative Innovation model
description: Collaborative Innovation is Digital Promise's research and development model underpinning its regional pathways work: "a structured process where those most directly impacted by educational challenges lead, shape, and benefit from the solutions". As an R&D model, it engages communities and schools in the co-research and co-design of innovative approaches, centering the voices of students, families, educators, and community members alongside researchers and solution developers. The report claims the resulting solutions are more effective, relevant, and responsive, particularly for rural learners and historically underserved communities, and it grounded the co-design of district cybersecurity pathways in the national initiative.
requirements: Engagement of students, families, educators, and community members as co-researchers and co-designers, not only recipients of solutions
constraints: The report presents this as a guiding framework and rationale rather than a tested comparison; effectiveness claims are the authors' interpretation
target_learners: rural learners and students from historically underserved communities
target_learning_goals: career pathway skills co-designed with the communities they serve
examples: Ten districts co-researched and co-designed high school cybersecurity pathways programs with students, families, teachers, and community partners in the 2022 national initiative
