article_title: Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners
citation: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Five-dimension framework for strengthening Home Language Survey design and use
description: The working session structured its discussion of HLS improvement around five dimensions: "A. Purposes and intended uses B. Key constructs (aligned to purposes and uses) C. HLS question formulation (aligned to constructs) D. Administrative procedures E. Decision rules." The framework orders design work so that purposes guide construct selection, constructs guide question wording, and procedures and decision rules govern administration and interpretation of responses. The paper uses it to organize the session's consensus recommendations for states and assessment consortia.
requirements: Purposes and intended uses must be defined first, since they guide identification of key constructs and thus more precise HLS questions
constraints: Time to explore the decision-rules dimension was limited, and the paper says further discussion and elaboration of this dimension would be beneficial
target_learners: K-12 students potentially identified as English learners
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification of students entitled to specialized English language development services and English language proficiency screening
examples: The session produced consensus statements under each dimension, from the three HLS purposes to sample Tier 1-3 questions and decision-rule guidelines

article_title: Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners
citation: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Define HLS purposes and intended uses explicitly, including what the survey is not for, before designing questions
description: Session participants agreed the HLS serves three purposes: identifying potential members of a protected class under federal law, identifying who should be assessed with an English language proficiency screener, and better understanding students' language environments and use. The paper recommends that "The purposes and intended uses of the HLS should be made explicit to those administering and those completing the survey," and that states specify what the survey is not for, such as determining immigration status. Clear purposes then guide construct identification and more precise question wording.
requirements: Purposes and uses must be stated explicitly to administrators and respondents, and the HLS must be clearly distinguished from other questions when embedded in a larger intake form
constraints: The paper notes the HLS is not intended to measure English proficiency and should not pre-determine educational services or immigration status
target_learners: K-12 students potentially identified as English learners and their parents/guardians
target_learning_goals: Correct routing of potentially EL students to English language proficiency screening
examples: New York City's tiered intake form separates essential HLS questions (Tier 1) from instructional-planning questions (Tier 2) and parent communication preferences (Tier 3)
key_sources: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED565756

article_title: Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners
citation: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Three-tier relevance taxonomy of HLS constructs: essential, associated, and irrelevant
description: The paper organizes HLS constructs by degree of relevance to a student's current English abilities. Essential constructs are "student's current language(s); frequency of English language use by student; frequency of English language exposure provided by others." Associated constructs include languages spoken among adults in the home, linguistic history, and years in U.S. schooling. Country of origin is classed as irrelevant. Participants considered student language dominance outmoded, focusing instead on contexts of exposure to English across home, school/child care, and recreational settings.
requirements: Essential constructs should appear as Tier 1 questions on a tiered intake form and associated constructs as Tier 2, with the HLS clearly demarcated in any multi-purpose intake form
constraints: Parents' language use among themselves but not with the student may be misleading, and reported first language may be inaccurate due to cultural pride
target_learners: K-12 students potentially identified as English learners
target_learning_goals: Gauging the language environments a student has been exposed to and the likelihood the student has acquired English abilities before enrolling
examples: Tier 1 sample questions ask which languages the child currently understands, speaks, most often uses, and most often hears across home, school, and outside-of-school settings
key_sources: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED565756

article_title: Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners
citation: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Suggested Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 HLS question sets
description: The paper presents candidate HLS questions organized by tier: Tier 1 questions on the student's current receptive and productive language use and exposure across home, school, and outside-of-school contexts; Tier 2 questions on English variety names, adult home language, first language spoken, literacy in English and other languages, and years in U.S. schools; Tier 3 questions on parents' preferred languages for written and oral school communication. The paper cautions that "None of these questions has been piloted for ease of comprehension; they are only suggested starting points."
requirements: Questions should be piloted with parents/guardians and school personnel across a wide range of language groups, in both print and oral forms, and in translation and interpreter formats
constraints: The questions are untested starting points requiring refinement based on focus groups and piloting
target_learners: Parents/guardians of K-12 students at initial school enrollment
target_learning_goals: Identifying students who should proceed to English language proficiency screening
examples: Tier 1 sample question: Which language does your child most often use at home, in school/educational settings, and outside of school

article_title: Strengthening Policies and Practices for the Initial Classification of English Learners: Insights from a National Working Session
citation: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: States and districts should provide common guidance on purposes, policies, and practices for initial EL classification
description: The report recommends that states and districts issue shared guidance for the locally administered initial EL classification process, because its "rigor and consistency within a state is critical" for cross-state comparability. Common guidance should include a clear statement of purpose, a flowchart and checklist of the classification process, a screening timeframe, allowed instruments with scoring guidelines, evidence standards for detecting and correcting misclassifications, and required qualifications and training.
requirements: Guidance must cover purpose, process flowchart and checklist, screening timeframe, permitted instruments and score interpretation, misclassification evidence standards, and staff qualifications and training
constraints: EL classification remains a locally administered process and local decision
target_learners: Potential English learners in K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: Accurate initial classification of English learner status and access to entitled language instructional services
examples: Working session participants described wide variability in classification across schools, districts, and states and supported policies fostering greater standardization and consistency
key_sources: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org

article_title: Strengthening Policies and Practices for the Initial Classification of English Learners: Insights from a National Working Session
citation: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Differentiate initial EL classification procedures for Kindergarten and grade 1 students from later grades while monitoring classification accuracy
description: Several states assess only oral language domains for K-1 students, or assess all four domains but heavily underweight literacy (e.g., a composite that is 90% oral, 10% literacy), reflecting concern that young children's literacy reflects prior literacy experiences rather than English proficiency. The report cautions that students "classified as initially fluent English proficient based solely or largely on oral language skills may experience difficulty in developing foundational literacy skills", making this a tension point requiring ongoing monitoring and validation.
requirements: Ongoing monitoring and validation of classification procedures and decisions for early elementary language-minority students in particular
constraints: Determining the appropriate level of literacy assessment for young children is a tension point that should be approached carefully
target_learners: Kindergarten and grade 1 language-minority students
target_learning_goals: Accurate initial EL classification and foundational literacy development
examples: States use composites weighted as much as 90% oral language and 10% literacy for early-grade classification decisions
key_sources: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org

article_title: Strengthening Policies and Practices for the Initial Classification of English Learners: Insights from a National Working Session
citation: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: The initial classification screener should align to state ELP standards and strongly predict performance on the annual ELP summative assessment
description: The report proposes a two-step validation process: first, an alignment study (or a test-blueprint comparison) establishing proportionately comparable match, depth, and breadth of coverage between the screener and state ELP standards; second, a formal study of the predictive relationship between classifications from the initial assessment and the annual summative assessment, examined through correlation and/or regression analyses. Moderate to low associations would suggest the assessments measure different aspects of English language proficiency.
requirements: The predictive study should administer both assessments to already confirmed ELs within a few days, so that instruction during the interval does not measurably change proficiency
constraints: For brief screener instruments the alignment will not be as extensive as with the annual summative assessment, though coverage should be proportionately comparable
target_learners: Potential English learners undergoing initial classification
target_learning_goals: Consistent, defensible English learner classification decisions
examples: The report suggests giving the initial classification assessment and, a few days later, the annual summative ELP assessment to the same confirmed ELs and checking score and proficiency-category relationships
key_sources: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org

article_title: Strengthening Policies and Practices for the Initial Classification of English Learners: Insights from a National Working Session
citation: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Districts within a state and states within an ELP consortium should use a single ELP assessment for initial EL classification unless comparability evidence exists
description: Because commercially available ELP assessments measure and weight language domains differently, multiple classification instruments can produce multiple understandings of English language proficiency and complicate interpreting transferring students' proficiency levels. The report states that "Practically all participants agreed that having a common initial classification assessment was preferred", and that states allowing multiple instruments should first provide compelling empirical evidence that the instruments' scores are comparable, such as a table of comparative scores.
requirements: If multiple instruments are allowed, compelling empirical evidence of score comparability must be provided first
constraints: States using multiple instruments face challenges understanding transferring ELs' proficiency levels from districts using different instruments
target_learners: Potential English learners moving within and across states and consortia
target_learning_goals: Comparable initial EL classification decisions across districts, states, and consortia
examples: Seven states permit LEAs to choose among multiple commercial screeners, and half of WIDA Consortium member states allow a choice between two consortium screeners
key_sources: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org

article_title: The Effects of the Elevate Math Summer Program on Math Achievement and Algebra Readiness
citation: Snipes, J., Huang, C.-W., Jaquet, K., & Finkelstein, N. (2016). The effects of the Elevate Math summer program on math achievement and algebra readiness. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org/
title: Elevate Math summer program
description: Elevate Math is a math support program by the Silicon Valley Education Foundation whose core is "an intensive 75-hour (19 days over four weeks) summer preparatory course" for rising grade 8 students. It has four components: a Common Core–based curriculum with four content modules; about 19 days of four hours of blended instruction with one daily hour on Khan Academy; a college field trip and family college information night; and 40 hours of Common Core–based professional development for teachers and teacher assistants.
requirements: Credentialed teachers and college-level teacher assistants who receive the 40 hours of Common Core State Standards–based professional development
constraints: The study reports the program is not sufficient by itself for ensuring students are ready for challenging middle school math courses
target_learners: rising grade 8 students scoring at the high basic or low proficient level on the grade 6 math CST
target_learning_goals: middle school math achievement
algebra readiness
examples: In summer 2014 the program was evaluated in a randomized controlled trial at eight schools in six Silicon Valley districts
key_sources: Snipes, J., Huang, C.-W., Jaquet, K., & Finkelstein, N. (2016). The effects of the Elevate Math summer program on math achievement and algebra readiness. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567052

article_title: The Effects of the Elevate Math Summer Program on Math Achievement and Algebra Readiness
citation: Snipes, J., Huang, C.-W., Jaquet, K., & Finkelstein, N. (2016). The effects of the Elevate Math summer program on math achievement and algebra readiness. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org/
title: MDTP Algebra Readiness test
description: The Mathematics Diagnostic Testing Project (MDTP) Algebra Readiness test was used to measure math achievement and define algebra readiness in the study. It "consists of 45 multiple-choice items in seven topic areas" and was administered on the first and last days of participation. Previous research cited by the authors found it highly predictive of success in grade 8 algebra I, with passing three or more topic areas indicating a greater than 50 percent chance of algebra success.
requirements: Administration to students at defined points in the program (first and last days)
target_learners: rising grade 8 students
target_learning_goals: algebra readiness assessment
examples: Used in this study to define math achievement (total score) and algebra readiness (three or more topic areas passed)

article_title: Using Assessment Data to Guide Math Course Placement of California Middle School Students
citation: Chun-Wei Huang, Jason Snipes, Neal Finkelstein, WestEd. (2016). Using assessment data to guide math course placement of California middle school students. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Use continuous scale scores and immediately available diagnostic assessments rather than proficiency status alone to guide grade 8 algebra I placement
description: The article recommends that districts making grade 8 algebra I placement decisions move beyond the binary proficiency indicator on the grade 6 math CST and rely on scale scores identifying students with at least a 50 percent chance of success, supplemented by immediately available diagnostics. It states that "immediately available, easily administered assessments such as MDTP scores are potentially effective tools for making placement decisions," since CST results are not available until August or later.
requirements: Access to continuous scale scores from prior math assessments, and a diagnostic test such as the MDTP that can be administered online with results available immediately after completion
constraints: Grade 7 CST data are not typically available in time for initial placement decisions
Simply scoring at the proficient level (a scale score of 350) is not enough to give a student a greater than 50 percent chance of achieving proficiency
target_learners: Grade 8 middle school students being placed into algebra I
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification of students likely to achieve proficiency in grade 8 algebra I
examples: SVRA districts participating in the study had agreed under a 2010 memorandum of understanding to use multiple criteria including course performance, teacher recommendations, diagnostic tests, and CST performance for placement
key_sources: Chun-Wei Huang, Jason Snipes, Neal Finkelstein, WestEd. (2016). Using assessment data to guide math course placement of California middle school students. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567123

article_title: Using Assessment Data to Guide Math Course Placement of California Middle School Students
citation: Chun-Wei Huang, Jason Snipes, Neal Finkelstein, WestEd. (2016). Using assessment data to guide math course placement of California middle school students. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Mathematics Diagnostic Testing Project (MDTP) grade 7 assessments
description: The MDTP is a diagnostic assessment of grade 7 students’ math performance and possibly algebra readiness that some SVRA districts began using in 2010 to assist algebra I placement decisions. The article describes that "The MDTP tests can be administered online, and the results are available immediately after completion," in contrast to CST results, which are not available until August or later. Three types of results are available: the number of MDTP topics mastered, the level of mastery of each topic, and the topic scores.
requirements: Online administration to produce immediately available results
target_learners: Grade 7 students being assessed for grade 8 algebra I placement
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing mathematics topic mastery and algebra readiness for course placement
examples: Some SVRA districts began using MDTP tests in 2010 to assist with initial algebra I placement decisions before grade 7 CST results become available

article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts
citation: Guckenburg, S., Hurley, N., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts. San Francisco: WestEd. http://jprc.wested.org/
title: Four key features define restorative justice in schools per expert consensus
description: The report distills expert interviews into four defining features of RJ in schools: "Focus on repairing harm rather than punishing the offender," including student voice, a whole-school approach, and building students' social/emotional skills. RJ is described as rebuilding relationships and collaboratively solving problems rather than punishing offenders, with circles exemplifying how student voice is valued.
requirements: Trained facilitators conduct RJ circles so all participants can hear about and understand the harm from different points of view
constraints: The report notes RJ is difficult to define and that measuring fidelity of implementation requires tools still in the development stage
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. elementary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Repairing harm from offenses
social and emotional skill building
valuing student voice
key_sources: Guckenburg, S., Hurley, N., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts. San Francisco: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED568378

article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts
citation: Guckenburg, S., Hurley, N., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts. San Francisco: WestEd. http://jprc.wested.org/
title: Five specific restorative justice practices implement RJ goals in schools
description: Experts identified specific program components intended to achieve RJ goals: restorative circles, restorative conferencing, peace rooms, restorative questioning, and active listening. Circles are "facilitated meetings that allow students and others to come together for problem solving, resolving disciplinary issues, receiving content instruction, and discussing concerns related to difficult topics."
requirements: Facilitation and, in some schools, dedicated "peace rooms" as safe spaces where circles and conferences may be held
constraints: Some labeled-restorative strategies, such as peer courts and peer juries, are considered inconsistent with RJ philosophy by some experts because they focus on the offender rather than the victim
target_learners: K-12 students
teachers
school staff
target_learning_goals: Conflict resolution
disciplinary problem solving
classroom content instruction
examples: Circles use a talking piece so only the holder may speak; peace rooms provide safe space for circles and conferences
key_sources: Guckenburg, S., Hurley, N., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts. San Francisco: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED568378

article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts
citation: Guckenburg, S., Hurley, N., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts. San Francisco: WestEd. http://jprc.wested.org/
title: Implement restorative justice as a whole-school integrated approach rather than a stand-alone program
description: The majority of experts agreed RJ should be integrated within a broader school culture in which everyone uses the same language and techniques. Stand-alone disciplinary approaches with minimal training "may have less positive impact than a whole-school approach." Some suggested teachers begin using RJ in staff meetings and with each other before introducing it to students.
requirements: The entire school environment must be restorative in its approach to students, staff, parents, and community members for RJ to be sustainable or successful
constraints: Simplified models that appear easier to implement may win administrator buy-in but were cautioned against by experts
target_learners: All students, staff, and administrators in a school community
target_learning_goals: School culture change
consistent restorative language and techniques
examples: Experts suggested teachers practice RJ in staff meetings and with each other before introducing it to students

article_title: Change in Practice in Maryland: Student Learning Objectives and Teacher and Principal Evaluation
citation: Slotnik, W. J., Bugler, D., & Liang, G. (2015). Change in Practice in Maryland: Student Learning Objectives and Teacher and Principal Evaluation. Mid-Atlantic Comprehensive Center (WestEd and Community Training and Assistance Center).
title: Student Learning Objectives (SLOs) as an evidence-based instructional process
description: The report frames SLOs as “an evidence-based instructional process for improving educator effectiveness and student achievement,” and the predominant measure of student growth for teachers and principals within Maryland's TPE system. State models allot 30%-50% of the total evaluation rating to SLOs, with no single SLO counting for more than 35% of the total performance score. The Maryland Teacher and Principal Evaluation Guidebook, Version 3 emphasizes using SLOs as an ongoing, iterative, and collaborative process spanning data review, SLO development, conferences, and integration of results.
requirements: Districts must establish processes for setting, reviewing, assessing, and aligning SLOs, provide SLO training per state guidelines, and document a verification process to validate consistency, comparability, quality and rigor of SLOs and evaluation results
constraints: No single SLO may count for more than 35% of the total performance score
SLO weighting in overall ratings varies by district under local control
target_learners: teachers
principals
target_learning_goals: setting measurable growth targets for student learning
selecting learning content and research-based instructional strategies
data-driven instructional improvement
examples: MSDE provided tools including SLO templates, guiding questions, a quality rating rubric, and crosswalks between SLOs and observations and College and Career-Ready Standards
key_sources: Slotnik, W. J., Bugler, D., & Liang, G. (2015). Change in Practice in Maryland: Student Learning Objectives and Teacher and Principal Evaluation. Mid-Atlantic Comprehensive Center (WestEd and Community Training and Assistance Center). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED568386

article_title: Evidence-Based Improvement: A Guide for States to Strengthen Their Frameworks and Supports Aligned to the Evidence Requirements of ESSA
citation: Hale, S., Dunn, L., Filby, N., Rice, J., & Van Houten, L. (2017). Evidence-based improvement: A guide for states to strengthen their frameworks and supports aligned to the evidence requirements of ESSA. San Francisco: WestEd. http://www.wested.org/resources/evidence-based-improvement-essa-guide-for-states
title: Five-step continuous improvement framework for evidence-based school and district improvement
description: The guide presents a five-part continuous improvement framework that brings together two ideas: that decisions should be based on data and evidence, and that "a continuous improvement process is fundamental to engaging in and sustaining improvements in school and district practice." The five steps are Inform (analyze needs), Select (identify and examine evidence-based interventions), Plan (develop implementation strategies), Implement (carry out with formative adjustment), and Analyze (conduct summative assessment of performance and effectiveness). Evidence-based decision-making and reflection are described as "the core of the entire continuous improvement process and are used in each step," with steps that overlap rather than run in strict sequence.
requirements: Decisions should be nested within a larger continuous improvement process rather than treated as isolated choices
constraints: The authors state that some versions of continuous improvement processes include more or fewer steps, and they do not require models to use these same five steps
target_learners: State education agency staff
Local education agency leadership teams
target_learning_goals: Evidence-based selection and implementation of school and district improvement interventions
examples: Figure 1 depicts the cycle; tools 1 and 2 ask SEAs and LEAs to map their own improvement process steps onto these five steps and identify gaps

citation: Hale, S., Dunn, L., Filby, N., Rice, J., & Van Houten, L. (2017). San Francisco: WestEd. http://www.wested.org/resources/evidence-based-improvement-essa-guide-for-states
title: ESSA four-tier evidence hierarchy for intervention selection
description: The guide explains that "ESSA defines four levels of evidence" as elaborated in the U.S. Department of Education's September 2016 nonregulatory guidance. Strong evidence requires a statistically significant effect from at least one well-designed and well-implemented experimental study; moderate evidence rests on a quasi-experimental study; promising evidence rests on a correlational study with statistical controls for selection bias; and the lowest tier, "demonstrates a rationale," requires a rationale based on high-quality research findings or positive evaluation plus ongoing efforts to examine effects. This hierarchy is the evaluative standard used in the guide's evidence-review tools.
requirements: Users must assess both the quality of individual research studies and the body of evidence on an intervention
constraints: Some programs and funding streams allow all four levels; the Title I set-aside for low-performing schools does not allow use of the fourth level
target_learners: SEA and LEA staff selecting interventions for school improvement
target_learning_goals: Judging the strength of research evidence supporting candidate interventions
examples: Tool 5 (Intervention Evidence Review) has users assess an intervention's level of evidence against these ESSA definitions

title: Six-tool starter set for state and district evidence-based improvement
description: The guide offers "a starter set of six tools to support this work, with an emphasis on the process of selecting evidence-based interventions." The first two tools (SEA and LEA Inventory of Current Practice) guide examination of the whole improvement cycle; the middle two guide SEA and LEA approaches to advising lower levels on selecting interventions; and the last two, as the guide states, "support selection of evidence-based interventions." Tools are provided as Word documents so they can be modified to fit local needs and contexts, and each tool includes purpose, intended outcome, materials, participants, time, instructions, and facilitation guidance.
requirements: Preparation should include building understanding of ESSA evidence guidance and the state's own policy context before using the tools
constraints: The guide is explicitly not comprehensive: it is a starting point, and tools 3-6 cover only the Select step of the cycle

LEA/district leadership teams
target_learning_goals: Building capacity for evidence-based decision-making and intervention selection
examples: Example uses include an SEA cohort improvement academy with its 10 lowest-performing LEAs, and an SEA using tools 3, 5, and 6 to update an intervention list

title: Start continuous improvement with the problem, not the solution
description: The guide's framework principle is that improvement should begin with diagnosing needs rather than adopting a pre-chosen program: "A continuous improvement process starts with the problem, rather than the solution." The process addresses a discrete issue by systematically testing potential solutions while tracking well-defined and measurable goals, iterating as data are collected, analyzed, and discussed frequently so adjustments can be made and data collected again.

constraints: The initial effort often begins small and expands over time as fit to local conditions is better understood

target_learning_goals: Selecting interventions that fit locally diagnosed problems
examples: The five-step framework's Inform step requires analyzing needs with input from leadership, staff, parents, community members, and students before the Select step

article_title: Early Indicators and Academic Mindsets in the Clark County School District
citation: Snipes, J., & Tran, L. (2016). Early indicators and academic mindsets in the Clark County School District. San Francisco, CA: REL West @ WestEd. http://relwest.wested.org/
title: Districts implementing early warning systems should consider composite indicators and weigh the true-positive/false-positive tradeoff
description: The report recommends that districts using early warning systems focus on composite indicators combining attendance, credits, Fs, and GPA, because simple composites identified more than three quarters of eventual off-track students before high school entry. It also advises that "districts might consider trying to minimize false-positives in order to conserve resources" or, alternatively, "erring on the side of casting a broader net," since flagged students may still face elevated academic risk.
requirements: Student records data on attendance, credits earned, GPA, and semester Fs must be available for 8th graders before they enter high school.
constraints: Every indicator generated false-positives; the report states the results "consistently show a tradeoff" between correct identification and false-positive rates, and the choice among indicators is a policy decision about costs and benefits.
target_learners: 8th grade students transitioning to 9th grade in large urban districts
target_learning_goals: Staying on track for on-time high school graduation
examples: CCSD could share early risk indicators with high schools so supports could begin before or at the start of 9th grade; table 2 estimates per-school identified students, true-positives, and false-positives for each indicator.

article_title: The Racial School-Climate Gap
citation: Voight, A. (2013). The Racial School-Climate Gap. A report from the Region IX Equity Assistance Center at WestEd. San Francisco: WestEd. http://cal-schls.wested.org
title: School climate as a four-theme construct associated with achievement and a candidate lever for reducing racial achievement gaps
description: The article treats school climate as "a broad term used to describe the school environment" with "no consensus definition" but several recurring themes: "(a) order, safety, and discipline; (b) teaching and learning supports; (c) social relationships; and (d) school connectedness." It uses this construct to organize six WestEd studies showing climate perceptions vary by race, and proposes a three-step logic linking climate to achievement: climate is associated with achievement, climate experiences vary by race, and reducing racial climate disparities would reduce achievement disparities.
requirements: Regular assessment and monitoring of school climate as perceived by different racial/ethnic student groups, e.g., using the Cal-SCHLS system
constraints: The studies provide empirical support for the first two points of the logic; proving that reducing climate disparities reduces achievement disparities "necessitates further research"
target_learners: K-12 students in California public schools, grades 7, 9, and 11 in the studies cited
target_learning_goals: Reducing racial achievement gaps through improved school climate and equity in students' school experiences
examples: WestEd researchers analyzed Cal-SCHLS student and staff data collected biennially in nearly two thirds of California public schools from 2004 to 2010
key_sources: Voight, A. (2013). The Racial School-Climate Gap. A report from the Region IX Equity Assistance Center at WestEd. San Francisco: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED580366

title: Cal-SCHLS survey system for assessing student and staff perceptions of school climate
description: The California School Climate, Health, and Learning Survey (Cal-SCHLS) System, developed by WestEd with funding from the California Department of Education, consists of three comparable surveys: the California Healthy Kids Survey (CHKS) for students, the California School Climate Survey (CSCS) for staff, and the California School Parent Survey. Survey items "gauged respondents’ perceptions of their school environment (e.g., supportiveness, safety), as well as students’ grades, truancy, and risk behaviors." During the analysis years the CHKS was administered in approximately 840 school districts to an average of 500,000 students per year in grades 7, 9, and 11.
requirements: Available nationally as the Healthy Kids School Climate Surveys for schools wanting to regularly assess and monitor climate by racial/ethnic group
constraints: During the years the analyzed data were collected, the CHKS was administered in grades 7, 9, and 11
target_learners: California public school students in grades 7, 9, and 11, school staff, and parents
target_learning_goals: Identifying climate-related needs and guiding school-climate improvement efforts to reduce inequity

article_title: High-Quality Science Instruction: Building Conceptual Understanding and Language Skills for English Learners
citation: DiRanna, K., & Gomez-Zwiep, S. (2013). High-Quality Science Instruction: Building Conceptual Understanding and Language Skills for English Learners. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Modified 5E lesson design planning template with concept, teacher, and student columns and Evaluate embedded in every phase
description: The Montebello project built on the 5E Instructional Model (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate) and modified its lesson design planning template. WestEd's K–12 Alliance added a "concept" column so teachers kept the lessons' conceptual flow in mind, and teachers included the Evaluate phase in every stage to monitor and assess student understanding. The template organizes planning around "Concept Teacher Student" rows for each E stage, with the Engage row targeting the prior-knowledge concept and the Explore row connecting it to the lesson concept.
requirements: Teachers complete the template stage by stage, keeping conceptual flow in mind while planning activities and discussion prompts
constraints: The template is adapted from the 5E lesson design planning template (Bybee, 1997) as used in elementary science lessons in the Montebello project
target_learners: elementary students, including high populations of English learners and low-income students
target_learning_goals: science conceptual understanding
academic language development
examples: Figure 1 shows the modified 5E template with concept, teacher, and student columns and an Evaluate entry in each of the Engage, Explore, Explain, and Elaborate rows
key_sources: DiRanna, K., & Gomez-Zwiep, S. (2013). High-Quality Science Instruction: Building Conceptual Understanding and Language Skills for English Learners. San Francisco: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED580368

article_title: High-Quality Science Instruction: Building Conceptual Understanding and Language Skills for English Learners
citation: DiRanna, K., & Gomez-Zwiep, S. (2013). High-Quality Science Instruction: Building Conceptual Understanding and Language Skills for English Learners. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Treat ELD proficiency levels as descriptions of what a student knows and can do at a stage, not as labels for students, since second-language acquisition is not strictly linear
description: The report advises structuring language development strategies to meet students' proficiency levels in California's ELD Proficiency Level Descriptors (emerging, expanding, bridging), while cautioning that the linear progression across levels is for purposes of presentation and understanding. Actual second-language acquisition does not necessarily occur in a linear fashion within or across proficiency levels. A proficiency level identifies what a student knows and can do at a particular stage, so it is inaccurate to speak of an "emerging student" but accurate to say a student's listening comprehension is at the emerging level.
requirements: Language supports should be matched to the proficiency level of the relevant skill, not applied as a blanket student label
constraints: The linear progression across proficiency levels reflects presentation conventions, not the actual course of second-language acquisition
target_learners: English learners at all proficiency levels
target_learning_goals: English proficiency
access to high-level, cognitively demanding academic work with appropriate linguistic support
examples: The report contrasts saying a teacher has an "emerging student" (inaccurate) with saying a student's listening comprehension ability is at the emerging level (accurate)

article_title: Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation
citation: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies
title: Four-domain framework for leading NGSS implementation
description: The Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation answers the question of what leaders need to know and be able to do to lead NGSS implementation. It comprises four domains: Leadership Knowledge (six knowledge areas), Critical Actions (eleven actions), Impacting NGSS Teaching and Learning (classroom interactions among teachers, NGSS, and students surrounded by six system drivers), and Sustaining Implementation of NGSS. The article states it "provides a vision of the four major domains that leaders focus on as they lead the implementation of the NGSS." Domains interact through a continuous improvement cycle connecting leaders' actions to classroom impact.
requirements: Leaders must develop and use new knowledge unique to the NGSS; the framework assumes possessing this leadership knowledge is necessary for carrying out the critical actions.
constraints: Developed for NGSS or closely aligned state science standards implementation in K-12 systems in the United States.
target_learners: Science education leaders at state, district, regional, school, and teacher-leader levels
target_learning_goals: Leading standards implementation
Planning and sustaining NGSS-aligned science education reform
examples: Used as a self-assessment for leaders to identify knowledge gaps and as a planning guide for critical actions.
key_sources: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies

article_title: Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation
citation: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies
title: Six foundational leadership knowledge areas for NGSS implementation
description: Domain 1 of the framework identifies six distinct but related knowledge bases leaders need: NGSS and the Innovations in NGSS; Equity and Access for All Learners; Instructional Materials, Curriculum, and Assessment; Professional Learning; Systems Change; and Continuous Improvement. The article states "leaders need in-depth knowledge within six distinct, but related knowledge bases (Figure 1.1)." These areas were identified through a summit with national experts and interviews with leaders in two states, and they inform all critical actions in Domain 2.
requirements: Leaders at all levels need to develop knowledge in each of the six areas and understand intersections among them; depth needed may vary by role and system level.
constraints: No prior guidance existed on what knowledge leaders need for NGSS implementation; the areas were derived from the project's own literature review, summit, and interviews.
target_learners: State, district, regional, and school science education leaders
target_learning_goals: Understanding NGSS innovations, equity, curriculum and assessment quality, professional learning, systems change, and continuous improvement
examples: Regional and district leaders designing professional learning need deeper understanding of the NGSS and how to design and facilitate professional learning.
key_sources: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies

article_title: Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation
citation: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies
title: Six system drivers influencing NGSS use in classroom practice
description: Domain 3, Impacting NGSS Teaching and Learning, places standards-based teaching and learning at the center, with interactions among teachers, the NGSS, and students, surrounded by six system drivers: Standards; Curriculum, Instruction, and Assessment; Policies; Key Stakeholders; Funding; and Professional Learning. The article states "Surrounding this center are six system drivers that most influence the use of the NGSS in classroom practice." Leaders' critical actions are both informed by and focused on these drivers, with equity and access encompassing the classroom.
requirements: Leaders gather data to gauge the extent to which their actions are influencing and leveraging each system driver.
constraints: The focus of NGSS implementation should always be on standards-based teaching and learning in the classroom for all students.
target_learners: Leaders charged with supporting and implementing the NGSS at all system levels
target_learning_goals: Focusing implementation efforts on the levers that most influence classroom NGSS teaching and learning
examples: The framework graphic shows arrows connecting leaders' critical actions to the Impacting NGSS Teaching and Learning domain.
key_sources: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies

article_title: Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation
citation: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies
title: Sustaining implementation through people, policies, processes, and practices
description: Domain 4 represents the overall goal of leaders' work: sustainable implementation of the NGSS. Leaders continuously assess whether effective implementation has been achieved and what is needed next, examining their impact on four key areas: People, Policies, Processes, and Practices. The article states "leaders examine their impact on four key areas that influence sustaining the use of the NGSS." Based on their continuous improvement cycle, leaders gauge movement toward sustainable implementation and may enhance their own knowledge and refine their critical actions.
requirements: Leaders must engage in continuous improvement cycles and use data to inform improvements to ensure sustainability.
constraints: Sustainability is assessed within the framework's overall continuous improvement cycle rather than as a one-time determination.
target_learners: State, district, and school leaders responsible for long-term standards implementation
target_learning_goals: Sustaining NGSS implementation over time
examples: Leaders determine whether they need to further enhance their own knowledge and refine their use of critical actions.

title: Treat equity for all students as fundamental to science education leadership
description: The framework's developers identified equity as the first shared value underlying the framework: all students should have access to education that prepares them for success, in student-centered environments with equitable, engaging, rigorous, and coherent opportunities. The article states "Ensuring equitable access requires educators to create the cultural and local relevance for students to engage in the practices and to understand the ideas of science," and leaders must recognize where inequity exists and find solutions to address it.
requirements: Leaders and educators must recognize areas where inequity exists and find solutions to address the inequity.
constraints: Equitable access depends on addressing environmental, cultural, and familial contexts of a wide range of students.
target_learners: All K-12 science students, with attention to economically disadvantaged students, students with disabilities, English language learners, and other groups named in the framework
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to rigorous standards-based science learning
examples: An elementary teacher leader refused to let students be pulled out for intervention during the science block, and the district mandated a science block so every child had access to science.

article_title: Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings
citation: Nakamoto, J. & Rice, J. (2017). Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: NFTE's entrepreneurial mindset framework of eight core domains
description: NFTE conceptualizes the entrepreneurial mindset as a 21st century skill set comprising eight core domains: Future Orientation, Comfort with Risk, Opportunity Recognition, Initiative and Self-Reliance, Communication and Collaboration, Creativity and Innovation, Critical Thinking and Problem Solving, and Flexibility and Adaptability. The report states that "an individual who acts and thinks like an entrepreneur has an entrepreneurial mindset." NFTE grounds the framework in the claim that non-cognitive skills are malleable and can improve with instruction, and its programs pair entrepreneurial-mindset skill growth with small-business-management content instruction.
requirements: Programs must provide students the support and experiences needed to develop the mindset, via project-based lessons and experiential activities
constraints: The framework is NFTE's own articulation (NFTE, 2016b); the report treats it as a program-defined construct rather than an independently validated taxonomy
target_learners: middle and high school students in under-resourced communities
target_learning_goals: entrepreneurial mindset skills such as opportunity recognition, communication and collaboration, and critical thinking
examples: NFTE programs teach the domains through business plan creation, business plan competitions, experiential activities such as the Buying and Selling Event and the Product Innovation Game, and Community Walks
key_sources: Nakamoto, J. & Rice, J. (2017). Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED582976

article_title: Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings
citation: Nakamoto, J. & Rice, J. (2017). Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: NFTE Startup Summer intensive business startup program
description: Startup Summer is NFTE's most intensive startup program, targeting a select group of students ready to launch the business they planned in Owning Your Future or Startup Tech. It begins with a Boot Camp week in which students set goals, create marketing materials, and plan initial launch steps; participants then meet three times per week for six weeks, receive an investment grant and stipend, meet volunteer business coaches, and can pitch in a Shark Tank-style event. Since 2011 approximately 150 students have participated.
requirements: Students complete an application toward the end of their classroom program and are selected as ready to launch with mentoring and eventual funding
constraints: The program is selective and small (approximately 150 participants since 2011), offered initially in New York City and later Los Angeles and South Florida
target_learners: high school students from under-resourced communities ready to launch a planned business
target_learning_goals: business launch skills, marketing, goal setting, and entrepreneurial mindset application
examples: The 2016 alumni survey found 71 percent of Startup Summer respondents launched a business and 83 percent frequently used what they learned at NFTE at their current work
key_sources: Nakamoto, J. & Rice, J. (2017). Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED582976

article_title: Using Data to Ensure That Teachers Are Learner Ready on Day One
citation: Data Quality Campaign. (2017). Using Data to Ensure That Teachers Are Learner Ready on Day One. https://www.dataqualitycampaign.org
title: AACTE and Westat pilot survey of beginning teachers and their supervisors
description: In spring 2017 the American Association of Colleges for Teacher Education and Westat piloted a new state survey instrument for beginning teachers and their supervisors. Developed with input from state partners, it "aims to provide more detailed information about graduates' experiences in the classroom and help states make more meaningful comparisons across programs." The instrument is intended to give EPPs and states better information about graduates' performance and needs than existing collections provide.

target_learners: beginning teachers (teachers of record in their first years)
target_learning_goals: informing EPP program improvement and state comparisons of preparation program quality
examples: Piloted in spring 2017 for beginning teachers and their supervisors

article_title: Using Data to Ensure That Teachers Are Learner Ready on Day One
citation: Data Quality Campaign. (2017). Using Data to Ensure That Teachers Are Learner Ready on Day One. https://www.dataqualitycampaign.org
title: High-quality teacher-student data link (TSDL) built at the state level
description: A teacher-student data link connects teachers to students by course at the state level, which the brief calls "critical to understanding the connection between student academic growth and teacher training and practice." It describes a best-practices TSDL as "a linchpin of state success in policy implementation and evaluation of educator preparation quality," and lists six focus areas: data linkages, teacher of record definition, roster verification, K–12 course scheduling and codes, governance, and teacher ID number. Assigning the educator ID at program enrollment is suggested to ease sharing.

description: In 2014, as part of its teacher equity plan, Missouri developed a shortage predictor model that "identifies where the state is likely to see teacher shortages in the coming years," pinpointing specific content areas and geographic locations most likely to experience shortage. DESE targets districts identified by the model and supports their recruitment of potential teacher candidates at the high school level, while EPPs train those candidates in high-need content areas, ideally sending teachers back to their home districts.

description: Maryland's statewide educator evaluation system combines measures of professional practice and student growth. It frames competency as a continuum on which leader proficiency varies, and reports that in complex work, underlying competencies drive success more than observable skills and knowledge. The framework organizes the brief's discussion of assessment and development of turnaround leaders.

article_title: Thought Leadership Forum Brief: Talent Development and Opportunity Culture
citation: Center on School Turnaround at WestEd. (2018). Thought Leadership Forum Brief: Talent Development and Opportunity Culture. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://WestEd.org
title: Opportunity Culture defined-role staffing structure (MCLs, MRTs, Elementary Specialists, Team Teachers, Teacher Residents, Reach Associates)
description: Opportunity Culture is "an approach to school design based on a tiered teaching structure within a content area or across one or more grade levels in a school," intended to increase teacher leadership and expand the instructional impact of teachers recognized for strong instruction. Multi-Classroom Leaders lead teacher teams through feedback, coaching, modeling instruction, co-planning, and modeling data analysis, and are accountable for all team student results. Supporting roles include Master Reach Teachers with larger classes aided by technology and interns, Elementary Specialists teaching specific content, Team Teachers, year-long Teacher Residents, and Reach Associates (redesigned paraprofessionals) who supervise students during digital, skills-practice, or project-based learning.
requirements: MCLs must be teachers with excellent instructional practice and adult leadership responsibilities
regular school budgets are repurposed to fund increased pay for leadership roles
constraints: larger class sizes are the norm for Master Reach Teachers, offset by technology, intern teachers, and paraprofessional support
support strategies such as time-technology swaps and remote teaching are adopted in part to offset higher numbers of students
target_learners: K-12 students in turnaround and high-needs schools
target_learning_goals: increase instructional impact of excellent teachers
develop teacher leadership and instructional practice across teams
examples: Charlotte-Mecklenburg's Project LIFT implemented multi-classroom teachers as instructional leaders, elementary specialists, time-technology swaps, and remote teaching across 30 schools
Figure 2 shows seven classroom teacher positions repurposed into an MCL-1, team teachers, a learning coach, a lab monitor, and blended learning teachers using the same funds

description: The brief lists five design principles that "characterize the Opportunity Culture school structure": reach more students with excellent teachers and their teams; increase compensation for teachers who extend their impact; utilize regular budgets to increase pay for teachers in leadership roles; provide protected in-school time and clarity about using that time for planning, collaboration, and professional development; and match authority and accountability to each teacher's responsibilities. The pattern operates at whole-school staffing level, redistributing existing teacher positions into tiered roles.

title: VITAL (Visibly Improve Teaching and Learning) professional learning service
description: VITAL is a WestEd service "to build teachers' capacity to engage in effective collaboration focused on teacher and student learning." It provides tools and processes establishing a professional teaching/learning cycle in four phases: prepare for inquiry, engage in a teaching-and-learning cycle, study impact on student and teacher learning, and take action to share findings. In phase 2, teachers plan lessons, seek peer feedback, teach and observe lessons (e.g., through video), analyze student work, and offer collaborative feedback.

target_learning_goals: Improving instructional practice through collaborative inquiry and formative peer feedback

title: Coburn's four dimensions of scale for scaling instructional change
description: The brief describes ADE's statewide formative assessment implementation plan as organized around Coburn's (2003) four dimensions of scale: depth ("deepening understanding of formative assessment to generate a change in teachers' beliefs, norms of social interaction, and pedagogical principles"), spread (more teachers, schools, districts, plus policies reflecting changed practice), shifts in ownership (from SEA/LEA or outside provider to teachers and students), and sustainability (institutionalizing the changes). The framework treats scale as more than numbers, encompassing deep and lasting change.

District leaders
Teachers

examples: ADE designed its statewide formative assessment implementation plan using the four dimensions, reporting accomplishments along each: shared definitions, policy changes, increased participation, committed staff, more professional learning, and a statewide community of practice

description: Figure 1 of the brief reproduces the formative assessment feedback loop (Source: Heritage & Gerzon, 2015), which became "the central core of instructional practice" in Sunnyside School District. The loop is organized around three questions — Where am I going? Where am I now? Where to next? — and includes steps: determine learning goals, develop success criteria, elicit evidence of learning, interpret evidence, take responsive action, close the gap, and create building blocks.

article_title: Five Misconceptions about School Shootings
citation: Langman, P., Petrosino, A., & Persson, H. (2018). Five misconceptions about school shootings. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/five-misconceptions-about-school-shootings/
title: Langman's three-category typology of school shooters: psychopathic, psychotic, and traumatized
description: The brief presents a typology in which, although no single psychological profile fits all school shooters, perpetrators "tend to fall into one of three categories: psychopathic, psychotic, or traumatized." Psychopathic shooters are narcissistic and lack empathy; psychotic shooters show symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions; traumatized shooters come from severely dysfunctional families with abuse, substance abuse, or criminal behavior. The brief uses the typology to organize case examples while cautioning it does not by itself explain shootings.
requirements: Used as a classification framework for perpetrators, not as a standalone causal explanation of attacks
constraints: The brief states the typology "does not — by itself — explain school shootings"; most people in these categories or with mental illness do not commit mass murders
target_learners: Educators
School safety personnel
Reporters and the public
target_learning_goals: Understanding the psychological diversity of school shooters to counter the single mental-illness stereotype
examples: The brief classifies one Columbine killer as psychopathic, the Thurston High School killer as psychotic with auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions, and a Bethel, Alaska shooter as traumatized based on family abuse history

article_title: What Do We Know about the Effects of School-Based Law Enforcement on School Safety?
citation: Stern, A., & Petrosino, A. (2018). What do we know about the effects of school-based law enforcement on school safety? San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/effects-of-school-based-law-enforcement-on-school-safety
title: Two common types of school-based law enforcement strategies: school resource officers and school district police
description: The brief organizes school-based law enforcement into two common U.S. strategies. The most common is the school resource officer (SRO), where a school or district partners with the local police department so municipal police devote time to a presence on school property. The alternative is school district police, where districts establish their own sworn police departments, as large urban districts like Miami-Dade County Public Schools do. Officers' roles vary by school and district policy, including coordinating security, monitoring and responding to criminal activity, building relationships, and referring students to external services.
requirements: Personnel must be sworn officers who carry firearms, have arrest powers, and carry a police department badge
constraints: The brief excludes security guards, who are not an extension of law enforcement, and officers who only teach prevention curricula such as D.A.R.E. or G.R.E.A.T.
target_learners: K-12 students, including at the elementary school level
target_learning_goals: School safety and student well-being
examples: The brief cites Miami-Dade County Public Schools as an example of a large urban district with its own sworn police responsible for school grounds
