citation: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions
title: Children and Youth Behavioral Health Initiative (CYBHI)
description: The CYBHI, adopted in California's 2021/22 budget, aims to transform children and youth behavioral health into an upstream-focused ecosystem in which all children and youth are routinely screened, supported, and served. "Approximately $4 billion has been allocated over 5 years; funding grants are one-time and will be spent over 5 years, from 2022 through 2026." It has four focus areas: expanding equitable access with no wrong door, building prevention and treatment capacity, raising awareness, and delivering evidence-based care. Services target Californians aged birth through 25 via commercial plans and Medi-Cal, including a 24/7 virtual platform.
requirements: Partnerships across CalHHS and outside agencies, including K–12 and higher education systems
constraints: The guide notes the CYBHI does not provide immediate resources for direct services; it focuses on infrastructure
target_learners: All Californians aged birth through 25
target_learning_goals: Behavioral health screening, support, and service access that enables children and youth to learn and thrive
examples: Components connected to student mental health include incentive grants to Medi-Cal managed care plans to partner with LEAs, funding for school-based counselors and coaches, and a virtual access platform
key_sources: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). article_title: Supporting California's Children through a Whole Child Approach: A Field Guide for Creating Integrated, School-Based Systems of Care
citation: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions
title: Use one-time funds for long-term-impact investments and plan early for sustainable funding
description: Because much of California's historic influx of funding is short term, the guide advises leaders to treat sustainability as a planning component from the start rather than a future goal. "Consider how to use these funds for short-term investments that can have long-term impacts, such as facilities or digital infrastructure, intensive short-term interventions for students, and staff capacity building." Leaders should also plan early for acquiring new resources or shifting existing long-term funding sources to sustain new initiatives, and Chapter 3 details blending and braiding funds across siloed streams.
requirements: Early planning for how to acquire new resources or shift existing long-term funding sources to sustain initiatives
constraints: If historic funding flows through the state's historically siloed system of separate agencies, LEAs and partners can expect the same barriers to integrated services
target_learners: Students and families served by LEAs using one-time federal and state relief funds
target_learning_goals: Sustained access to integrated academic, social-emotional, mental health, and health supports
examples: The guide notes professional development funding can bolster student-support staff positions and align school policies with PACEs science as disaggregated data reveal needs

article_title: Expanding the Expository Reading and Writing Curriculum: An Evaluation of an Investing in Innovation Validation Grant
citation: Fong, A., Porterfield, A., Skjoldhorne, S., & Hadley, L. (2022). Expanding the Expository Reading and Writing Curriculum: An evaluation of an Investing in Innovation Validation grant. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/expanding-the-erwc-evaluation/
title: ERWC Assignment Template arc: a recursive scaffold from Reading Rhetorically through Preparing to Respond to Writing Rhetorically
description: The ERWC theory of action posits that the curriculum and professional learning enable grades 11-12 teachers to support students' communication across genres, increasing literacy learning opportunities and college, career, and civic readiness. Its core structure, the Assignment Template, "progresses along what its developers call an 'arc'" through three phases: Reading Rhetorically, Preparing to Respond, and Writing Rhetorically. The Template "outlines a scaffolded process for helping students read, comprehend, and respond to nonfiction and literary texts" and guides module writers, with reading and writing interwoven throughout the modules.
requirements: Teachers implement modules following the full arc from reading professional (mentor) texts to students writing their own texts
constraints: Full-length modules cover the full arc of the Assignment Template; mini-modules cover only specific rhetorical concepts and skills
target_learners: Grades 11 and 12 high school students in college-preparatory English courses
target_learning_goals: Rhetorical analysis of expository, analytical, and argumentative texts
College readiness in reading and writing
examples: The evaluation studied 67 modules organized by this template across grade 11 and 12 courses
key_sources: Fong, A., Porterfield, A., Skjoldhorne, S., & Hadley, L. (2022). Expanding the Expository Reading and Writing Curriculum: An evaluation of an Investing in Innovation Validation grant. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/expanding-the-erwc-evaluation/

article_title: Expanding the Expository Reading and Writing Curriculum: An Evaluation of an Investing in Innovation Validation Grant
citation: Fong, A., Porterfield, A., Skjoldhorne, S., & Hadley, L. (2022). Expanding the Expository Reading and Writing Curriculum: An evaluation of an Investing in Innovation Validation grant. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/expanding-the-erwc-evaluation/
title: ERWC 3.0 curriculum: 67 selectable modules for yearlong grade 11-12 courses
description: The ERWC 3.0 is a college-preparatory English language arts curriculum developed by the California State University, designed to prepare students as critical consumers of texts and effective communicators. "It consists of 67 modules that teachers can choose from to design a yearlong course." Modules integrate reading, writing, and discussion and move from professional texts to student texts; the edition adds grade 11 full-length modules, concept and portfolio mini-modules, integrated and designated English Language Development, and Universal Design for Learning features such as student goal-setting.
requirements: Teacher participation in required professional learning: annual Summer Institutes, coaching cycles, and community of practice meetings
constraints: Few teachers taught the full curriculum with fidelity due to time constraints and pandemic-related instructional shifts
target_learners: Grades 11 and 12 high school students in California and Washington
target_learning_goals: Readiness for college-level English
Rhetorical literacy and effective communication across genres
examples: Full-length modules are classified as book, drama, foundational document, or issue modules; 65 modules were published in the final version

article_title: Pivoting an In-Person Multiplatform Science Program to a Virtual Program during a Pandemic: Lessons Learned
citation: Li, L., Hayakawa, M., Freese, J., Daniels, B., Weiser, G., Luttgen, K., Lor, M. C., Schneider, M., Huang, C.-W., & Jensen, E. (2022). Pivoting an in-person transmedia science program to a virtual program during a pandemic: Lessons learned. Children, Youth and Environments, 32(3), 53-81. http://www.jstor.org/action/showPublication?journalCode=chilyoutenvi
title: Hero Elementary multiplatform science program and its playlist structure
description: Hero Elementary is a multiplatform, equity-focused educational initiative providing science and literacy instruction to kindergarten through second-grade learners from underserved communities, funded by a U.S. Department of Education Ready to Learn grant. Its central structure is the playlist: "Each playlist focuses on a given science concept" and contains an animated television story, a live-action song-based video on a Science and Engineering Practice, a digital or analog game, two hands-on activities, a digital journal, and a non-fiction e-book. Content types and their in-person implementations are summarized in Table 1, and distance-learning supports and modifications in Table 2.
requirements: Educators are encouraged to customize the program by selecting high-interest playlists aligned with their community's goals rather than following a predetermined sequence; professional development for educators is provided on media resources, program design, and equity strategies.
constraints: During distance learning, digital games and non-fiction eBooks required no modifications, but hands-on activities, analog games, and the Science Power Notebook needed modified home versions, discussion guides, and video demonstrations.
target_learners: Students ages five to eight in kindergarten through second grade
Race-ethnic minorities, children in low-income households, children with disabilities, and English learners
target_learning_goals: Early science engagement aligned with Next Generation Science Standards
Science and literacy skills, including communication skills aligned with Common Core English Language Arts standards
examples: Study 1 implemented the program in 12 treatment second-grade classrooms that continued in distance learning; Study 2 implemented it in 14 classrooms across six summer or after-school programs in six states.
key_sources: Li, L., Hayakawa, M., Freese, J., Daniels, B., Weiser, G., Luttgen, K., Lor, M. C., Schneider, M., Huang, C.-W., & Jensen, E. (2022). Pivoting an in-person transmedia science program to a virtual program during a pandemic: Lessons learned. Children, Youth and Environments, 32(3), 53-81. http://www.jstor.org/action/showPublication?journalCode=chilyoutenvi

article_title: Pivoting an In-Person Multiplatform Science Program to a Virtual Program during a Pandemic: Lessons Learned
citation: Li, L., Hayakawa, M., Freese, J., Daniels, B., Weiser, G., Luttgen, K., Lor, M. C., Schneider, M., Huang, C.-W., & Jensen, E. (2022). Pivoting an in-person transmedia science program to a virtual program during a pandemic: Lessons learned. Children, Youth and Environments, 32(3), 53-81. http://www.jstor.org/action/showPublication?journalCode=chilyoutenvi
title: Design multiplatform science programs for flexible implementation so educators can adapt delivery to their learning community
description: The article presents flexibility as a core design feature that enabled Hero Elementary's pivot to virtual delivery across formal and informal settings. "Educators are encouraged to customize Hero Elementary to suit their learning community by selecting high-interest playlists that align with their community’s goals, rather than presenting the materials in a specific, predetermined sequence." The developers reinforced this by providing distance-implementation documents, home versions of activities, and a train-the-trainer professional development model that "highlighted flexibility and adaptation," letting each site fit the program to its schedules, resources, and communities.
requirements: Modified resources must be presented to educators as learning materials that can be modified to accommodate a broad range of students, with supports such as Distance Implementation overview documents, Live Demo documents, Home Co-viewing Guides, and Discussion Guides.
constraints: The article stresses that each implementation was unique and all sites struggled with technology issues, whether unreliable internet connectivity or lack of technology support; flexibility does not remove access barriers.
target_learners: Kindergarten through second-grade students in formal and informal learning environments
Educators in formal classrooms and informal summer or after-school programs
target_learning_goals: Maintaining science learning access and engagement during abrupt transitions to virtual instruction
examples: Informal educators logged onto Zoom at scheduled times, shared screens on hands-on activities or animated episodes, reserved other activities for asynchronous use with debriefs, and used the advance and pause features of recorded videos to discuss activities with home materials.

article_title: Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools Can Develop Systems That Support Student Mental Health
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Three-category framework for organizing school mental health and well-being supports
description: The report organizes school mental health and well-being efforts into three categories of school support: creating a welcoming, affirming environment that enables a sense of safety for every student; providing responsive mental health, well-being, and SEL supports for all students; and partnering with the community to extend mental health and well-being supports. It states charter school leaders "can organize their efforts into three categories of school support," and Section 2 unpacks each category with strategies, reflection questions, and charter school spotlights.
requirements: School leaders assess their own school community's practices and needs within each of the three support areas using the reflection questions provided
constraints: The report frames the framework for charter school leaders, noting charters may have different access to mental and behavioral health resources than traditional public schools
target_learners: K-12 students in public charter schools
target_learning_goals: Student mental health and well-being
social-emotional learning
readiness to learn
examples: Section 2 spotlights Valor Collegiate Academy, Rocky Mountain Prep, and Uplift Education delivering supports aligned to the three categories
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED625528

article_title: Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools Can Develop Systems That Support Student Mental Health
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Six design components of welcoming and affirming school environments for student mental health
description: The report identifies six strategies as important components of comprehensive approaches to creating welcoming and affirming environments: culturally responsive practices, predictable routines, positive expectations, explicit SEL instruction, supportive relationships, and self-care strategies such as mindfulness, exercise, meditation, yoga, and calming routines. It states these have been "identified as important components of comprehensive approaches to creating welcoming and affirming environments to improve student mental health in schools."
requirements: Strategies must correspond with school and community values and be implemented through programmatic support and commitments that shape school climate and culture
target_learners: K-12 students in charter schools, with attention to historically marginalized students and students of color
target_learning_goals: Sense of safety and belonging
self-regulation
social-emotional skills
examples: Valor Collegiate Academy implements welcoming-environment practices through its Compass Model, restorative-justice discipline policies, and weekly Compass Circles of 15 to 20 students
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED625528

article_title: Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools Can Develop Systems That Support Student Mental Health
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Valor Collegiate Academy Compass Model with badge system and Compass Circles
description: The Compass Model is Valor Collegiate Academy's whole-school SEL and mental health approach, consisting of five interdependent domains that help students develop an inner compass for a purposeful life. Students earn badges marking key disciplines, habits, and mindsets from 5th grade to graduation, and participate in weekly Compass Circles of 15 to 20 students facilitated by a mentor. Survey data showed "more than 80% of students report that Circles help them feel less alone," and approximately 80% of faculty reported the program changed how they think about emotions; 64 schools have adopted the model.
requirements: Weekly peer groups (Compass Circles) facilitated by a mentor
integration with the academic curriculum and student choice of pathways
constraints: The report describes Valor as intentionally diverse by income and race since opening in 2014, serving Grades 5-12 in Nashville, Tennessee
target_learners: Students in Grades 5-12
target_learning_goals: Positive identity development
self-awareness and social awareness
purpose, kindness, determination, and curiosity
examples: Valor has ranked in the top 5% of Tennessee schools in growth and achievement since 2014, with lower socio-economic students outperforming middle- and upper-income peers in the state
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED625528

article_title: Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools Can Develop Systems That Support Student Mental Health
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Rocky Mountain Prep Family Advocacy Support Team (FAST) emergency family supports
description: FAST is Rocky Mountain Prep's referral-based team of teachers, social workers, and operations staff that responds to family hardship affecting student well-being. Staff with deep family relationships submit referrals; the team provides stopgap supports, including up to $300 in cash assistance for food, laundry, clothing, or other needs, while connecting families to long-term resources. Each campus has approximately $20,000 in flexible funds; in 2020-2021 FAST supported "nearly 125 families with resources for basic needs around food, shelter, mental health, and more."
requirements: Flexible emergency funds at each campus (approximately $20,000)
staff who hold deep relationships with families to submit referrals
a needs audit conducted alongside a social worker
constraints: The report describes FAST within RMP's four pre-K through 5th grade campuses in the Denver, Colorado area
target_learners: Pre-K through 5th grade students and their families
target_learning_goals: Family well-being as a foundation for student attendance, enrollment stability, and learning
examples: As of December 2021, zero students who had received FAST support had unenrolled from school
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED625528

article_title: How 2017-2019 State Entity Grantees Are Using Technical Assistance Set-Aside Funds
citation: National Charter School Resource Center. (2022). How 2017-2019 State Entity Grantees Are Using Technical Assistance Set-Aside Funds. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://www.qualitycharters.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/CorePerformanceFrameworkAndGuidance.pdf
title: Twelve common TA set-aside activities supporting quality authorizing, led by contracting providers and evaluating current practices
description: The report identifies 12 common activities SE grantees funded to improve authorizer quality, ranging from contracting external providers and evaluating current authorizing practices to individualized TA, professional development, and purchasing software such as Epicenter. It states "Sixteen grantees reported contracting (or planning to contract) with the National Association of Charter School Authorizers (NACSA), SchoolWorks, the National Charter Schools Institute, or similar organizations to support quality authorizing practices." Fifteen grantees reported evaluating current authorizing practices using internal and external evaluators.
requirements: Grantees must allocate at least 7% of CSP funds to TA to applicants and TA to support quality authorizing
constraints: Some grantees represent states with a single authorizer, so their use of funds to support quality authorizing was appropriately limited
target_learners: State educational agencies and statewide charter support organizations administering CSP grants
target_learning_goals: Improving the quality of charter school authorizing practices
examples: Sixteen grantees contracted providers such as NACSA and SchoolWorks; thirteen offered on-demand individualized TA to authorizers; thirteen provided professional development including boot camps for new authorizers

citation: National Charter School Resource Center. (2022). How 2017-2019 State Entity Grantees Are Using Technical Assistance Set-Aside Funds. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://www.qualitycharters.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/CorePerformanceFrameworkAndGuidance.pdf
title: Eleven common TA set-aside activities for charter school applicants, led by pre-award workshops and webinars
description: The report identifies 11 common activities grantees funded to support subgrant applicants, spanning pre-award workshops and webinars, application-process TA, grants-management resources and training, school-opening resources, governing board training, and vendor contracts. It reports "Seventeen grantees reported holding pre-award workshops and webinars for potential applicants to support them through the application process." Fifteen grantees each shared grants-management resources, shared applicant resources, and provided post-award grants management training.

constraints: The two grantees not using TA set-aside funds for pre-award workshops used 3% administrative funds or state funds instead
target_learners: Charter school developers and applicants for CSP subgrants
target_learning_goals: Successfully applying for and managing CSP subgrants and opening and operating charter schools
examples: Seventeen grantees held pre-award workshops; fourteen offered individualized application assistance including pre-review of applications; eleven hosted subgrantee learning communities

citation: National Charter School Resource Center. (2022). How 2017-2019 State Entity Grantees Are Using Technical Assistance Set-Aside Funds. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://www.qualitycharters.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/CorePerformanceFrameworkAndGuidance.pdf
title: Seven activity types by which SE grantees equip subgrantees to serve students with disabilities and English learners
description: From open-ended survey responses, the report tallies seven activity types grantees used to ensure subgrantees can serve all students: technical assistance, partnering with the SEA, monitoring and audits, training, application requirements, contracted services, and dissemination. It states "Eleven of 19 SE grantees reported providing TA to the subgrantees." Activities were similar for both student populations, with only the topics changing, so results are reported in aggregate.
requirements: Under ESSA, SEs are responsible for ensuring charter schools receiving subgrants meet the educational needs of their students, including those with disabilities
constraints: These numbers were derived from an analysis of responses to an open-ended item, so it is possible this is an under-representation of the SE grantees engaged in each activity
target_learners: Students with disabilities and English learners in charter schools receiving CSP subgrants
target_learning_goals: Equipping subgrantees to meet the educational needs of students with disabilities and English learners

article_title: Redefining Approaches for Engaging English Learners with Mathematical Ideas
citation: Chu, H., Tran, T., & Hamburger, L. (2022). Redefining approaches for engaging English Learners with mathematical ideas. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Three Moment Architecture for secondary mathematics lessons with English Learners
description: Three Moment Architecture is a bounded instructional sequence in which a lesson, possibly spanning several class periods, moves through three distinct moments with different pedagogical purposes: Preparing the Learners, Interacting With the Concept, and Extending Understanding. The brief uses it to structure how defining evolves: working definitions generated early enable exploration, and more formal definitions emerge later. The authors present it as "a bounded instructional sequence" that may help rethink how definitions are handled in secondary mathematics.
requirements: Lessons must connect students' prior knowledge with the main ideas during Preparing the Learners, then provide exploration across multiple representations, procedures, and contexts before formalizing definitions in Extending Understanding.
target_learners: secondary English Learners in 8th–9th grade mathematics
target_learning_goals: accessing and exploring mathematical ideas deeply
developing and formalizing mathematical definitions
engaging in deductive reasoning
examples: The brief elaborates the sequence using the topic of outliers within bivariate data: broad arrays of data with and without outliers in Preparing the Learners, exploration connecting outliers to measures of center and spread in Interacting With the Concept, and formalizing via interquartile-range or standard-deviation criteria in Extending Understanding.
key_sources: Chu, H., Tran, T., & Hamburger, L. (2022). Redefining approaches for engaging English Learners with mathematical ideas. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED625747

article_title: Redefining Approaches for Engaging English Learners with Mathematical Ideas
citation: Chu, H., Tran, T., & Hamburger, L. (2022). Redefining approaches for engaging English Learners with mathematical ideas. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Concept images and example spaces as the basis for an ongoing process of defining
description: The brief draws on Vinner's notion of concept images—the working examples and illustrative instances learners use to make meaning—and on Watson and Mason's example spaces, proposing that students explore different example spaces from which they can later articulate concise descriptions of key properties. Through an ongoing process of defining, students develop what Molina terms "simple but deep" definitions or working definitions that are just enough to offer access to ideas for deeper exploration.
requirements: Students need opportunities to explore examples, including borderline cases, before verbal descriptions of essential properties are formalized.
target_learners: secondary English Learners in mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: generating and refining working definitions of mathematical concepts
connecting informal uses of terms to formal definitions
examples: Students may explore the arithmetic mean as a point of balance and later connect this idea to the standard algorithm for calculating the mean, a procedure the brief says is often conflated with the definition.

article_title: Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools That Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees
citation: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD.
title: Three-type taxonomy of newcomer schools: programs-within-a-school, transitional, and comprehensive
description: The report organizes newcomer schools into three structural types. "These newcomer schools use a standalone facility" distinguishes transitional and comprehensive schools, while programs-within-a-school are "embedded programs co-located at a traditional school" where newcomers join recess, meals, electives, and sports with host-school students. The types differ in enrollment duration and exit pathways: transitional schools are designed for 1-2 years, while comprehensive schools let students remain through graduation.
requirements: Serve newly-arrived immigrant English Learners with voluntary enrollment
constraints: Characteristics vary by district vision, economic resources, teacher talent, approach to supporting English Learners, facilities, and newcomer numbers and circumstances
target_learners: Recently-arrived K-12 immigrant, refugee, and asylee students not proficient in English
target_learning_goals: English language acquisition
acculturation to American schools
core content remediation and grade-level instruction
examples: Lewiston High School and Winooski are programs-within-a-school; Newcomer Academy and Rochester International Academy are transitional; The Manhattan International High School is comprehensive
key_sources: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627813

article_title: Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools That Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees
citation: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD.
title: Newcomer schools as self-contained learning environments for recently-arrived immigrant English Learners
description: Newcomer schools are "an alternative, relatively self-contained learning environment specifically for newcomer students," created because "traditional schools are not organized to meet the needs and challenges that newcomer students face." Per the report, "All of these schools serve newly-arrived immigrant English Learners, have voluntary enrollment," and share goals: acculturation to American schools, foundational academic English, remediation or grade-level core content, native language literacy development, and wide-ranging culturally-appropriate academic, health, social, emotional, and family supports. Most are transitional, with clear entry and exit points.
requirements: Clear entry and exit points for transitional designs
specialized supports addressing academic, social, and emotional needs
constraints: Enrollment is voluntary; most students attend 1-2 years before transitioning to traditional schools that continue English language development supports
target_learners: Newcomer students in grades K-12, including SLIFE and unaccompanied minors
target_learning_goals: Foundational academic English language skills
learning-to-learn skills
grade-level content mastery
examples: The five profiled schools range from 49 to 669 students and were founded between 1993 and 2012
key_sources: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627813

article_title: Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools That Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees
citation: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD.
title: Orienting newcomers to be students through structured school-norms onboarding
description: The first promising practice is explicit orientation to schooling itself, since many newcomers lack practical classroom skills such as holding a pencil, writing on paper, and sitting at desks. Schools welcome students "into our family" by orienting them to attendance, transportation, grading, homework, behavior expectations, and emergency procedures, delivered by administrators, teachers, cultural liaisons, and classmates at year opening and on a rolling basis. Newcomer Academy runs a week-long structured orientation addressing practical matters and belonging; The Manhattan International High School embeds orientation in its Grade 9 foundations curriculum.
requirements: Combination of site administrators, teachers, cultural liaisons, and classmates to convey norms
rolling orientation as students enter any day of the year
constraints: Orientation content varies by school; for adolescent SLIFE the starting line is "wherever they're at" because they are unaccustomed to all aspects of school life
target_learners: Recently-arrived K-12 newcomers, including SLIFE with little or no formal schooling
target_learning_goals: School norms and practices
classroom survival skills
learning-to-learn skills
social connection with teachers and classmates
examples: Newcomer Academy's 'week of welcome' teaches students to use a binder, keyboard, locker, restorative circles, and to say their name, phone number, and address in English
key_sources: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627813

article_title: Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools That Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees
citation: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD.
title: Staff newcomer schools with skilled, purposeful, visionary leaders who build teams and innovate
description: The report's second promising practice holds that effective newcomer schools depend on leaders who are instrumental to realizing the vision of student success. "The five bright spots have skilled and purposeful leaders" who share characteristics: they are visionary, visible and available, consistently supportive, build teams, routinely communicate about schoolwide issues, and innovate. Leadership was centered at the district level for programs-within-a-school and with principals at standalone schools; all leaders have deep expertise in curriculum and instruction for English Learners.
requirements: Deep expertise in curriculum and instruction for English Learners
shared instruction and professional learning responsibilities across teams
constraints: Leadership structure differed by school type: district-level directors of English Learners led the programs-within-a-school, while principals and leadership teams led standalone schools
target_learners: K-12 newcomer students in immigrant-, refugee-, and asylee-serving schools
target_learning_goals: English proficiency
grade-level content mastery
successful transition to traditional schools or college
examples: Manhattan International High School's principal, an alumna, supported teacher-initiated instructional looping in Grades 10 and 11, yielding more time to master content and stronger student-teacher ties
key_sources: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627813

article_title: Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools That Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees
citation: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD.
title: Multi-approach English language and content instruction: SIOP, native-language leveraging, and scaffolding
description: The report's fourth promising practice is instruction guided by shared beliefs: it should be culturally responsive, meet students at their levels while providing high-challenge, high-support opportunities, give continuous practice in reading, writing, speaking, and listening, incorporate multiple learning modalities, use data to guide decisions, and be collaboratively planned. "Across the grades, teachers are trained in and routinely implement SIOP," with content and language objectives posted and reviewed each lesson. Schools also leverage students' native languages and differentiate and scaffold instruction toward more independent performance.
requirements: Teachers trained in SIOP
collaborative planning between ESL and content-area teachers
evidence-based conceptual frameworks and materials vetted for English Learners
constraints: None of the bright spot schools are bilingual programs because their student populations are linguistically diverse; native-language use varies by school
target_learners: K-12 newcomers with limited or no English proficiency, including SLIFE
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency in tandem with content learning
grade-level content standards mastery
college and career preparation
examples: Winooski integrates the multisensory Fundations program with SIOP for phonics and spelling; Manhattan International requires seniors to produce a graduation portfolio including work in their native language

article_title: Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies
citation: Mattson, H., Zoffel, J., & McCormick, M. (2023). Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: The Systems Review approach: a three-phase, five-element iterative process for SEA systems change
description: The Systems Review is an iterative organizational-improvement approach created by R15CC that "incorporates principles of organization development, improvement science, systems and design thinking, and overall continuous improvement." It unfolds in three phases—discovery, change effort development, and implementation—stretched across a repeating cycle of five elements: identify the issue; analyze the current system; identify and prioritize change efforts; implement key change efforts; and assess and deliberate on effectiveness. Feedback and reflection points are embedded throughout, and each step is guided by data from the previous step.
requirements: A Systems Review Team representative of the system being improved, with periodic feedback loops to broader staff
Engagement over 6–12 months with regular meetings with the division director and collaborative work sessions
constraints: Each review has its own individual scope, components, and timing because no two systems are exactly alike
target_learners: State education agency division directors, managers, and staff
target_learning_goals: Building capacity to solve adaptive challenges and lead systems change toward coherent, efficient organizational function
examples: R15CC meets with the division director every 2 weeks and holds SRT work sessions approximately every 3 weeks over 6–12 months
key_sources: Mattson, H., Zoffel, J., & McCormick, M. (2023). Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628329

article_title: Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies
citation: Mattson, H., Zoffel, J., & McCormick, M. (2023). Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Systems Review working agreements that ground teams in an inquiry-based, systems-focused stance
description: R15CC developed Systems Review Working Agreements that "guide all Systems Review projects" and delineate how teams commit to working together on improving the system. The six agreements are: stay focused on the system; prioritize equity of voice (all teach, all learn); keep an open mind with an inquiry focus and give activities a genuine try; experience discomfort and treat struggles as learning opportunities; be present and participate with a right to process; and acknowledge impact and consider intent. Facilitators verbally add italicized elaborations when working with groups.
requirements: Facilitators emphasize at the outset and throughout that the review analyzes the complete system, not individuals, to create a climate of safety for honest conversation
target_learners: SEA division and department teams participating in a Systems Review
target_learning_goals: Engaging in honest, inquiry-based systems analysis and collaborative improvement work
examples: The agreement to stay focused on the system is verbally elaborated as being about how the entire system functions, not any individuals
key_sources: Mattson, H., Zoffel, J., & McCormick, M. (2023). Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628329

article_title: Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies
citation: Mattson, H., Zoffel, J., & McCormick, M. (2023). Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Focus organizational review on the system rather than individuals to create psychological safety for honest inquiry
description: Because looking inward can be challenging and staff may fear being singled out, R15CC emphasizes that the Systems Review is about analyzing the complete system and the results it produces. The report states that "the emphasis on the system, rather than anyone within it, contributes to a climate of safety, enabling teams to engage in honest and sometimes difficult conversations that build towards shared goals and improved results." This principle underpins the working agreements and the entire review stance.
requirements: Significant upfront time and recurring touchpoints reinforcing the systems framing with SEA teams
target_learners: SEA division and department staff undergoing a Systems Review
target_learning_goals: Honest engagement in systems analysis and shared goal-setting for improvement
examples: R15CC spends significant time at the beginning of the process, and as a touchpoint throughout, emphasizing the system-level focus

article_title: A Standardized, Equitable, and Transparent High-Quality Instructional Materials Review Process
citation: Melinda Wallace and Sheila Arredondo. (2022). A Standardized, Equitable, and Transparent High-Quality Instructional Materials Review Process. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567789
title: Content Area Review Panels (CARPs)
description: CARPs are the Nevada panels that "Evaluate and rate instructional materials submitted by publishers." Per Table 1, they include subject-matter experts, content-area and special education teachers, curriculum directors, technology specialists, and English language development experts. Panelists correlate content standards to materials, participate in training and rubric calibration, conduct independent reviews, and take part in full-group deliberations to reach a unified recommendation.
requirements: Panelists must know and understand the NVACS, participate in training and rubric calibration, and submit ratings and summary reports on time to the panel facilitator
constraints: Panels are recruited at 5–7 panelists per content area, with RPDP representation secured for English language arts, mathematics, and science
target_learners: K-12 students who will use the adopted instructional materials
target_learning_goals: Reliable, calibrated evaluation of instructional materials for statewide adoption
examples: CARP findings were consolidated into a recommendation list presented to Cabinet and then the State Board of Education for adoption
key_sources: Melinda Wallace and Sheila Arredondo. (2022). A Standardized, Equitable, and Transparent High-Quality Instructional Materials Review Process. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628368

article_title: A Standardized, Equitable, and Transparent High-Quality Instructional Materials Review Process
citation: Melinda Wallace and Sheila Arredondo. (2022). A Standardized, Equitable, and Transparent High-Quality Instructional Materials Review Process. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567789
title: Nevada eight-step instructional materials adoption step matrix
description: Table 2 lays out an eight-step adoption process: issuing a Nevada-specific Request for Quote, publisher submission of digital materials, internal technical review, CARP evaluation and rating, forwarding recommendations to Cabinet, SBE adoption, publication of the SBE-approved list, and debrief/evaluation. Each step names the entity, tasks, outcomes, and a timeframe, from a 30-day submission window through publication no later than April 30.
requirements: Publishers must submit materials in digital/online formats within the specified window; publishers of rejected materials may appeal within 30 days of notification
constraints: The process is specific to Nevada statute and the State Board of Education adoption cycle, running roughly June through June of the following year
target_learners: K-12 students in Nevada public schools
target_learning_goals: Transparent, predictable statewide adoption of standards-aligned materials
examples: Step 8 requires NDE SIS to synthesize findings and debriefs, document issues and strategies, and consider potential process refinements
key_sources: Melinda Wallace and Sheila Arredondo. (2022). A Standardized, Equitable, and Transparent High-Quality Instructional Materials Review Process. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628368

article_title: A Standardized, Equitable, and Transparent High-Quality Instructional Materials Review Process
citation: Melinda Wallace and Sheila Arredondo. (2022). A Standardized, Equitable, and Transparent High-Quality Instructional Materials Review Process. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567789
title: State instructional materials review designed around statewide core values of equity, access, inclusivity, community, and transparency
description: The refined Nevada process organizes materials adoption around the SEA strategic plan's core values — "equity, access to quality, success, inclusivity, community, and transparency" — and defines high-quality curricula as standards-aligned and culturally engaging: accurate, content-rich, free from bias, and supportive of students' linguistic and cultural lenses. The design responds to prior review inequities, especially for rural districts, by standardizing rubrics, training, and public participation opportunities.
requirements: Review process design must define reviewer qualifications and trainings, process timing, public participation opportunities, and consistent reviewer expectations
constraints: What counts as high quality is defined against Nevada's own statutes, strategic plan, and NVACS; the report draws on approaches from eight other states and organizations such as RAND, Achieve, EdReports, and WestEd
target_learners: K-12 students, including students from different experiences and backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Improved learning outcomes through access to high-quality curriculum
examples: NDE and R15CC designed the process using district-leader interviews, other states' approaches, research from RAND and others, OER Commons study, and pilot reviews of primary core materials

article_title: Reimagining School Safety: A Guide for Schools and Communities
citation: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Reimagined paradigm of safety: safety as the presence of connection and systems of mutuality and care
description: The guide proposes shifting from a deficit-based paradigm in which safety is the absence of harm and violence to one in which "Safety, therefore, is not just the absence of harm and violence, but the creation of systems that acknowledge humans’ inherent indispensability, connectedness, and dignity." In this paradigm, an individual's safety is rooted in others' safety and needs being met, and safety is grounded in self-care, collective care, and mutuality. Table 1 contrasts traditional safety (exclusionary, punitive, technical, top-down) with reimagined safety (inclusive, restorative, adaptive, codesigned at the margins).
requirements: Reimagining requires new ways of doing and also new ways of thinking and being, achieved through unlearning and relearning via small, daily choices.
constraints: The guide states this definition comes from activists and movement makers, particularly those most harmed by systemic oppression, and is not new.
target_learners: K-12 students
educators
school leaders
district administrators
target_learning_goals: social-emotional learning
belonging and school safety
equity in school climate
examples: The guide profiles Curie High School in Chicago, whose students and staff share in a video the shifts they made to transform their understanding of school safety.
key_sources: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628885

article_title: Reimagining School Safety: A Guide for Schools and Communities
citation: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: School safety as a complex, adaptive system on the simple–complicated–complex continuum
description: Adapting Glouberman and Zimmerman, the guide places problems on a continuum from simple to complex and locates school safety at the complex end: "Complex problems or systems are based on relationships and their properties of self-organization, interconnections, and evolution (“adaptive”) (e.g., school safety)." Because safety is inherently adaptive and nonlinear, it cannot be achieved by linear steps, top-down policies, or experts alone. The guide recommends systems thinking and an engineering or systems design approach that iterates as conditions evolve, rather than the linear determine-intervene-evaluate method traditionally used in education.
requirements: Educators must engage in formal and informal processes of emergence with their community, observing how properties and behaviors emerge as parts interact.
constraints: The guide states complicated challenges have a time and place, such as determining truancy policies or lockdown procedures.
target_learners: educators
school leaders
district administrators
target_learning_goals: systems thinking
understanding school safety as a complex adaptive system
examples: The guide offers a sticky-note exercise in which participants brainstorm ten or more leverage points for a school safety issue and map the individuals and groups most affected.
key_sources: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628885

article_title: Reimagining School Safety: A Guide for Schools and Communities
citation: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Restorative justice as a framework for community-centered harm prevention and a new paradigm of safety
description: The guide describes restorative justice, a framework originating from Indigenous communities, as redefining harm, conflict, and broken rules as harm to relationships: "By redefining harm, conflict, violence, and broken rules or laws as harm to relationships and reimagining justice as addressing the root issues of harm, restorative justice offers a framework for community-centered harm prevention and a new paradigm of what safety means." In this model, healing-centered accountability is achieved for all involved, relationships are restored, reintegration occurs, and communities remain intact. The guide illustrates the contrast with a four-school scenario in which School D addresses unmet needs at personal, collective, and systemic levels.
requirements: Safety is achieved when those who cause harm have the community support to engage in accountability practices that meet the needs of those impacted by the harm.
constraints: The guide notes that responses addressing harm only at personal and interpersonal levels, like School C's quick fixes, lack a systemic lens and do not fully transform the harm.
target_learners: K-12 students
educators
school leaders
target_learning_goals: restorative accountability
harm prevention and healing
community building
examples: The guide points to a reintegration circle from Oakland Unified School District supporting a student's return to their community after causing harm.
key_sources: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628885

article_title: Reimagining School Safety: A Guide for Schools and Communities
citation: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Balance the technical, adaptive, and relational elements of school safety rather than emphasizing only technical implementation
description: The guide defines technical elements as policies, plans, structures, and models handed down to be implemented; adaptive elements as the mindsets, values, and belief systems needed to tailor them; and relational elements as social capital, belonging, collectivism, and trust. It warns that "Implementing school safety through only a technical lens is like sitting on a stool with two of its legs missing; all three are needed for success." Without the adaptive mindsets in place, implementation can be inconsistent and unsustainable over time.
requirements: Deep levels of community engagement and collectively shared values and beliefs are needed for the technical elements of transformational school safety to function at their best.
constraints: The guide states that tools and practices put in place for reimagined safety may be oppositional to the values, mindsets, and practices schools have been operating with systemically.
target_learners: educators
school leaders
district administrators
target_learning_goals: sustainable implementation of school safety initiatives
school climate and culture change
examples: The guide's practice exercise has participants draw three concentric circles to map a technical element, the people it affects, and the beliefs that led to its creation.
key_sources: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628885

article_title: Reimagining School Safety: A Guide for Schools and Communities
citation: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Codesign school safety with those kept farthest from institutional power as equal collaborators
description: Because human systems are designed by humans and are inherently not neutral, the guide argues that safety is typically defined by people operating at a satellite level and implemented top-down. Equitable design requires "zooming in" to the voices and experiences of those on the margins: "Centering those who are kept farthest from institutional power means more than just inviting them to offer their feedback or to be part of the conversation; instead, they should be codesigners, equally participating as collaborators in the process of reimagining school safety." It also requires "zooming out" to examine the larger systems and structures that cause harm.
requirements: Those kept farthest from institutional power must participate as equal codesigners and collaborators, not only as feedback providers.
constraints: The guide states that without zooming out to institutional structures, policies only address harm at individual or interpersonal levels, so the harm is likely to happen again.
target_learners: K-12 students
families and community members
educators
school leaders
target_learning_goals: equitable school safety policy design
shared power and agency in design processes
examples: The guide suggests using the Relationship Mapping Strategy to identify which students have at least one positive connection to at least one adult, and profiles Forest Park Middle School staff codesigning school climate with students.

article_title: Research and Evaluation on School Safety: The Structure, Services, and Products of State School Safety Centers
citation: McKenna, J. M., Russo, S., Sutherland, H., Muñoz, E., Boal, A., & Petrosino, A. (2023). Research and evaluation on school safety: The structure, services, and products of state school safety centers. WestEd. https://www.ojp.gov
title: Two-phase SSSC activity data collection protocol (Qualtrics survey plus Smartsheet workspaces)
description: The evaluation's activity data collection is a two-phase instrument for retrospectively documenting SSSC services over calendar year 2021. Phase 1 is a Qualtrics survey with 23 questions across five sections covering training events, technical assistance, resources, compliance activities, and grant administration; Phase 2 provides each center a customized Smartsheet workspace for service-level detail. The report states that "Seventeen SSSCs from 16 states completed the Qualtrics survey portion of the activity data collection, and 9 SSSCs from 9 states submitted at least one type of Smartsheet." The interview analysis used a codebook with 33 code families and 208 subcodes.
requirements: Centers must complete the Qualtrics survey before receiving Smartsheets, which are provided based on survey responses about which services the center provides
constraints: Participation in the Smartsheet phase was partial: 9 SSSCs submitted training data, 4 technical assistance data, 9 resources data, 3 compliance data, and 3 grant administration data
target_learners: State school safety center staff
State educational agency staff
target_learning_goals: Documenting and characterizing the services, activities, and outputs of state school safety centers
examples: The training events Smartsheet documented event name, dates, length in hours, description, training type and modality, number and types of participants, topics, presenters, and funding sources

article_title: Technology-Based Support Shows Promising Long-Term Impact on Math Learning: Initial Results from a Randomized Controlled Trial in Middle Schools
citation: Feng, M., Huang, C.-W., & Collins, K. (2023). Technology-based support shows promising long-term impact on math learning: Initial results from a randomized controlled trial in middle schools. WestEd. https://osf.io/exqpn
title: Four-step formative assessment loop for technology-supported math homework
description: The ASSISTments intervention is organized around "a four-step loop that can be readily integrated into day-to-day instructional practices." Teachers (1) find and assign standards-aligned content, (2) students work with instant feedback and support, (3) teachers examine performance data to inform instructional decisions, and (4) teachers share and review data with students, discussing common misconceptions. Teachers were expected to assign 20–30 minutes of assignments at least twice a week and regularly review data reports.
requirements: Teachers need systematic professional development and ongoing coaching to implement the loop; teachers were trained to encourage students to rework problems they initially got wrong and to discuss commonly missed questions.
constraints: Developed and evaluated for middle school math homework support aligned to a state curriculum.
target_learners: Grade 7 and 8 middle school math students
target_learning_goals: Grade 7 and 8 mathematics proficiency on state standards
examples: Intervention teachers assigned ASSISTments homework twice weekly with a local coach visiting classrooms three times per school year.
key_sources: Feng, M., Huang, C.-W., & Collins, K. (2023). Technology-based support shows promising long-term impact on math learning: Initial results from a randomized controlled trial in middle schools. WestEd. https://osf.io/exqpn

article_title: Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department
citation: Jenna Howard Terrell, Sarah Barzee. (2023). Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Align performance-based assessments with standards, curriculum, and instruction
description: The report's first cross-state lesson is that "Intentional work should be done to align performance-based assessments with standards, curriculum, and instruction." Interviewees in every state emphasized embedding performance assessments in classroom curriculum and instruction so they evaluate "content and standards together using authentic, student-centered methods." Misalignment risks assessments being perceived as add-on activities for teachers and feeling jarring to students.
requirements: Performance assessments should be embedded in the classroom's curriculum and instruction and aligned with state standards, including embedded skills such as communication and collaboration.
constraints: Interviewees cautioned that misalignment between assessment and curriculum could make the assessments feel like add-on activities for teachers and jarring to students.
target_learners: K-12 students in states implementing performance-based graduation or classroom assessment options
target_learning_goals: Demonstration of mastery of content standards and transferable or essential skills
examples: State interviewees advised incorporating both content and skills into the performance assessment process, noting content is the vehicle through which students demonstrate essential skills.
key_sources: Jenna Howard Terrell, Sarah Barzee. (2023). Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED633310

article_title: Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department
citation: Jenna Howard Terrell, Sarah Barzee. (2023). Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Invest in ongoing capacity building and professional learning, including intermediaries, for performance assessment design and scoring
description: The report's third lesson states that "States and districts need to invest in building the capacity of teachers and leaders to effectively design and implement performance-based assessments." Developing, piloting, and testing assessments and rubrics takes significant time plus initial and ongoing professional learning. Four states (Colorado, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Virginia) had established systems for ongoing professional learning, and intermediaries such as the New Hampshire Learning Initiative and MCIEA provided guidance, professional development, and resources.
requirements: Initial professional learning to transition teachers to a performance assessment mindset, plus ongoing professional learning, and time for developing, piloting, and testing assessments and rubrics.
constraints: States without intermediaries reported staffing and capacity limitations and relied on regional service districts or district-led professional learning, leaving some interviewees feeling disconnected from district needs.
target_learners: Teachers and school and district leaders designing and scoring performance assessments
target_learning_goals: High-quality design, scoring, and implementation of performance-based assessments
examples: Colorado, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire use professional learning communities and intermediaries; Virginia relies on desk audits to inform technical assistance.
key_sources: Jenna Howard Terrell, Sarah Barzee. (2023). Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED633310

article_title: Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department
citation: Jenna Howard Terrell, Sarah Barzee. (2023). Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Performance-based assessment as defined by NYSED: demonstrating knowledge by creating a response or product or doing a task, judged against rubric criteria
description: The report adopts NYSED's definition: "A performance-based assessment requires students to demonstrate or apply their knowledge, skills, and strategies by creating a response or product or doing a task." Responses or performances are judged against standards or criteria in a checklist or rubric focused on skill development stages. The report describes performance assessments as a continuum ranging from constructing a response to creating a product to performing an activity, including essays, authentic demonstrations, portfolios, exhibitions, and capstone projects.
requirements: Judging against standards or criteria in a checklist or rubric focusing on the stages of skill development and what a student can do.
constraints: The report notes there are nuances in the literature about what a performance-based assessment must entail, and the definition is adopted for the purposes of this report to NYSED.
target_learners: High school students demonstrating mastery for graduation or classroom purposes
target_learning_goals: Demonstrating and applying knowledge, skills, and strategies through products, performances, or tasks
examples: Colorado defines performance assessments as an authentic demonstration of student knowledge and skills through the creation of a complex product or presentation.
key_sources: Jenna Howard Terrell, Sarah Barzee. (2023). Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED633310

citation: Jenna Howard Terrell, Sarah Barzee. (2023). Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Table 1 summary of performance assessment implementation across Colorado, New Hampshire, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Massachusetts, and Vermont
description: Table 1 summarizes implementation across the seven case-study states on initiative, policy, rollout (voluntary or mandatory), purpose, subject and grade level, developer, common scoring rubric, and ongoing support. All seven states report assessments "Locally developed by educators." Rollout is mandatory in Oregon and Virginia and voluntary in Colorado, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and Vermont; common scoring rubrics are reported as yes in Colorado, New Hampshire, Oregon, and Virginia, no in Rhode Island and Massachusetts, and in development in Vermont.
requirements: States differ in whether ongoing support exists: Colorado, New Hampshire, Virginia, and Massachusetts report ongoing support structures, while Oregon and Rhode Island report none.
constraints: Vermont's common scoring rubric and ongoing support are listed as in development phase.
target_learners: Students in grades 3 through high school across the seven case-study states
target_learning_goals: Demonstrating college and career readiness and content mastery through performance assessment
examples: Virginia's mandatory policy applies to grade 3 history and science, grade 5 writing, U.S. history to 1865, and U.S. history from 1865 to the present.

article_title: Resourcing Supports for Young Multilingual Learners with Suspected Disabilities in California: Learning Collaborative Recommendations
citation: Burr, E., & Burho, J. (2022). Resourcing supports for young multilingual learners with suspected disabilities in California: Learning collaborative recommendations. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: California Practitioners' Guide for Educating English Learners with Disabilities (CDE, 2019)
description: A state practitioner guide the report describes as reflecting "state-of-the-art research in supporting young multilingual learners" and incorporating promising practices with guidance for implementing them. The Learning Collaborative noted there is not currently widespread implementation of the strategies and practices reflected in the guide, and the report's central recommendation is to fund professional learning for consistent, widespread implementation of its practices.
requirements: Proper funding and resourcing to support sustainable statewide implementation of the research-based strategies and practices it reflects
constraints: According to Learning Collaborative members, there is neither uniform awareness of the guidance that exists nor access to professional learning to inform implementation

target_learning_goals: Accurate assessment, pre-referral supports, and special education referral practices for multilingual learners
examples: The report recommends implementing processes described in the guide, citing Imperial County SELPA's Improving Outcomes for English Learners with Disabilities as a promising model
